items.title: RDP: Forensic analysis of Windows Remote Desktop Protocol artifacts
items.summary: By Jeff Rutherford Key takeaways: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) leaves evidence on both sides of a connection. The source system can show where a user tried to connect and which account they may have used. The destination can show who connected, where the connection came from, and when the session started and ended. No single RDP artifact tells the whole story. Some artifacts only show that a connection was attempted, while others show that a session became interactive. Conclusions are strongest when multiple artifacts point to the same event. Treat the RDP session as an investigative window. RDP evidence establishes access and a timeframe. Execution, file system, network, and data movement artifacts, including possible file transfer through drive or clipboard redirection, show what happened during that window. Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) can be one of the most valuable sources of evidence in a Windows digital forensic investigation. RDP is commonly used for legitimate system administration, remote work, troubleshooting, and access to servers and workstations. The same functionality also makes it valuable to threat actors. Once an attacker obtains credentials or compromises a system, RDP can provide an interactive desktop that allows the attacker to move between systems, access files, execute tools, transfer data, establish persistence, or carry out ransomware deployment. For the digital forensic examiner, this creates an important opportunity. Windows can leave evidence of RDP activity on both sides of a connection. The system initiating the connection may contain evidence identifying where a user connected, while the destination system may document who connected, where the connection originated, when a session began, and when it disconnected or ended. Correlated with other Windows evidence, these artifacts can do more than confirm RDP was used. They can help reconstruct how someone moved through an environment and what happened during the remote session. This post explores the RDP artifacts found on the source and destination systems, what each one can and can’t prove, and how to correlate them into a timeline of remote activity. It also looks at how these artifacts support ransomware, data breach, insider threat, and intellectual property theft investigations. What is Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP)? Remote Desktop Protocol, commonly abbreviated RDP, is Microsoft’s protocol for providing interactive remote access to a Windows system. A typical RDP connection involves two roles: RDP client: The computer initiating the connection. RDP host or destination: The computer being remotely accessed. On Windows, the traditional built-in Remote Desktop Connection client is mstsc.exe. Rather than simply transferring commands between computers, RDP can provide the remote user with an interactive Windows desktop. The user can operate applications, browse files, execute programs, and interact with the destination computer much as if physically seated in front of it. RDP also supports several forms of resource redirection. Depending on the configuration, a remote session may provide access to resources on the originating computer, including local drives, the clipboard, printers, cameras, smart cards, and other devices. Microsoft specifically documents file system and clipboard redirection as capabilities of RDP. Those capabilities are particularly important during an investigation. An RDP session may be more than a remote login. It can potentially provide a path for: Moving files between systems Accessing files on a user’s local computer Copying text or files through the clipboard Executing administrative tools Accessing sensitive applications Moving laterally between computers Deploying malware or ransomware Exfiltrating information Conducting hands-on-keyboard activity Remote printing of sensitive material This is why RDP evidence should rarely be examined in isolation. Investigating the RDP source The source may help answer: Did this user attempt to connect using RDP? What computer or IP address did they connect to? What username may have been used? Was mstsc.exe executed? In this example, we can see the username that was utilized and the destination IP (LAN). If we look at additional artifacts, like Jump Lists, we can see additional details: Here we see one artifact from the incoming connection: The destination may help answer: Who connected? What IP address did the connection originate from? Was authentication successful? Was an interactive session created? When did the session start? When was it disconnected? When possible, the strongest reconstruction comes from examining both systems. How RDP artifacts are generated RDP artifacts aren’t created by one single Windows component. Instead, several components participate in the connection and session lifecycle. A simplified connection might look like: Each stage of the RDP session lifecycle can create different forensic evidence. Some artifacts document an attempted connection, while others provide much stronger evidence that the remote session actually became interactive. That distinction is critical. A hostname appearing in RDP history does not necessarily mean the user successfully authenticated. Likewise, an initial connection event should not automatically be interpreted as proof that someone received an interactive Windows desktop. Digital forensic conclusions become stronger when multiple artifacts describe the same event. From a forensic perspective, these registry locations can become a map of potential outbound RDP activity associated with a Windows user profile. An important limitation is that these artifacts should not automatically be interpreted as proof that authentication succeeded. They identify destinations associated with the RDP client and should be correlated with additional evidence. TerminalServices-RDPClient event logs The source system can also contain a dedicated RDP client event log. A common location is: Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-RDPClient/Operational The underlying EVTX file can typically be found beneath: C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs\ One particularly useful event is Event ID 1024 , which records the RDP client attempting to connect to a server. It can contain information identifying the destination server and the user SID associated with the connection attempt. Other RDP client events can provide additional information surrounding the connection lifecycle, including successful connection activity and disconnects. Investigators should therefore examine the entire group of events surrounding an RDP connection rather than searching for one Event ID in isolation. MSTSC execution evidence Determining that the Windows Remote Desktop client was executed can provide additional context. The executable used by Microsoft’s traditional Remote Desktop Connection client is: mstsc.exe Depending on the Windows configuration and investigative timeframe, execution evidence may appear in artifacts including: Prefetch UserAssist Amcache ShimCache SRUM Windows event logs EDR telemetry Process creation auditing For example, Prefetch evidence for MSTSC.EXE can support a finding that the application executed. However, execution of mstsc.exe alone does not establish: Which computer was accessed Whether authentication succeeded What the user did remotely It becomes significantly more useful when combined with RDP registry history and event logs. From the SRUM artifact for an RDP session: RDP bitmap cache One of the more interesting RDP artifacts exists because Windows attempts to improve the performance of the remote desktop experience. Instead of repeatedly retransmitting every portion of the screen, RDP can cache graphical information on the client computer. Depending on the Windows version and RDP implementation, cache files may be found beneath locations such as: C:\Users\ \AppData\Local\Microsoft\Terminal Server Client\Cache\ File names may include patterns such as: bcache*.bmc or Cache0000.bin These files can contain small fragments of the remote desktop display. This can occasionally provide remarkable evidence. Recovered fragments might show portions of: File Explorer Application windows Command prompts Documents Desktop icons Administrative tools Web applications However, bitmap cache analysis has important limitations. The cache is not a recording of the user’s session. It contains graphical fragments used by the RDP client for performance optimization. Images may be incomplete, overwritten, duplicated, or lack sufficient context. For that reason, bitmap cache evidence is generally most useful as corroborating visual evidence rather than as the sole basis for determining what occurred. Investigating the RDP destination The destination computer often contains the most valuable evidence for determining whether a remote session actually occurred. Several Windows event logs can contribute to that reconstruction. Security Event ID 4624: Successful logon Windows Security Event ID 4624 records the creation of a successful logon session. A 4624 event may provide information including: Username Domain Logon ID Authentication package Source network address Source port Process information Elevated token information, depending on event version and configuration Failed RDP logons Failed authentication attempts can also be significant. Security Event 4625 records failed logon attempts. During an intrusion investigation, repeated failed attempts followed by a successful RemoteInteractive login may indicate: Password guessing Credential spraying Mistyped credentials Use of newly acquired credentials Attempts to access multiple systems Context is important. Administrators and legitimate users mistype passwords too. A series of failed attempts from an unusual IP address followed shortly afterward by a successful RDP session, however, may deserve substantially more attention. TerminalServices-RemoteConnectionManager Another valuable log is: Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-RemoteConnectionManager/Operational One commonly examined event is Event ID 1149 . Depending on the Windows version and authentication configuration, Event 1149 can provide information related to an inbound RDP connection including the username and originating network address. It’s important not to treat Event 1149 by itself as absolute proof that a complete interactive desktop session occurred. A stronger approach is to correlate it with: Security 4624 Type 10 LocalSessionManager Event 21 Other session events This illustrates a broader rule of RDP forensics: Connection, authentication, session creation, and user interaction are related but separate events. TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager The following log can be extremely useful for reconstructing the actual RDP session lifecycle: Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager/Operational Several events may be particularly valuable: Event 21: Session logon. Indicates that a Remote Desktop Services session logon succeeded. Event 22: Shell start. Indicates the user’s session shell started. This can be particularly useful because it helps move the interpretation beyond authentication toward an interactive user session. Event 23: Session logoff. Indicates a session successfully logged off. Event 24: Session disconnect. Indicates a session was disconnected. Disconnecting is not necessarily the same thing as logging off. A disconnected RDP session may remain alive on the destination system. Event 25: Session reconnection. Indicates that a disconnected session was reconnected. Additional events such as 39 and 40 can provide information concerning disconnect behavior and session transitions. Together, these events can help create something resembling: 10:42 — RDP logon 10:42 — Windows shell starts 11:18 — Session disconnected 13:07 — Session reconnected 13:42 — User logs off That sequence is far more informative than simply stating that RDP was used. This is where timeline analysis can be so helpful to the case. RDP can be the doorway into a large behavioral timeline: Cases where RDP artifacts can be valuable Ransomware investigations RDP has historically been an important mechanism for hands-on-keyboard activity and lateral movement in a ransomware attack . An attacker may compromise one endpoint and then use RDP to move to: File servers Backup servers Domain administration systems Additional workstations RDP artifacts can help investigators determine: The initial pivot system Systems accessed afterward Accounts used for lateral movement When interactive attacker activity began Which systems should receive priority examination This can be particularly valuable when the attacker later encrypts or destroys evidence on destination systems. Data breach investigations During a data breach investigation , RDP artifacts can help establish whether an attacker had interactive access to systems storing sensitive information. For example, investigators might identify: Compromised workstation → RDP → database server The RDP connection itself does not prove that data was exfiltrated. But it can establish an investigative window. The examiner can then focus on activity during that period, including: File access Database access Archive creation Cloud uploads Browser activity SMB transfers PowerShell activity External storage Network connections RDP provides the context around which additional evidence can be evaluated. Insider threat investigations RDP history can also be useful in insider threat investigations. Consider an employee whose normal workstation suddenly contains RDP history showing connections to: Another employee’s workstation An engineering server A financial system A privileged administrator workstation Those connections may be entirely legitimate. But the artifact provides a lead. Correlating the destination with session timestamps, authentication events, and file access evidence may help determine whether the activity was expected. Intellectual property (IP) theft Suppose an employee is suspected of accessing engineering documents shortly before resigning. RDP evidence might establish that the employee remotely accessed an engineering workstation or server outside their normal workflow. The examiner could then correlate that RDP session with: Recent Files Jump Lists Shellbags LNK files Browser activity USB artifacts Cloud storage Archive utilities Network shares The strength of the evidence comes from the combination. RDP may demonstrate access to the system. Other artifacts demonstrate what occurred after access Lateral movement RDP is particularly useful when reconstructing lateral movement. Consider the following pattern: By examining the outbound RDP history on each computer and the inbound session evidence on the destination systems, investigators may be able to reconstruct a chain of interactive movement through the environment. Source-side RDP artifacts can be especially valuable here because the Terminal Server Client registry history may reveal destinations that investigators had not yet identified. A compromised computer may therefore serve as both a victim and a pivot point. File transfer through RDP Another issue investigators should consider is file movement. RDP supports several forms of resource redirection, including clipboard and drive redirection. Depending on the system’s policy configuration, local client drives may be exposed within the remote session. Microsoft documents redirected drives as allowing the remote computer to read from and write to drives located on the RDP client. This means files may potentially move: client → remote system or remote system →client without using a traditional SMB share, FTP client, or browser download, which can complicate investigations. Evidence of an RDP session should therefore prompt investigators to consider whether resource redirection was available during the session. Look for corroborating evidence such as: File creation timestamps $MFT $UsnJrnl LNK files Recent Files Jump Lists EDR file events Sysmon file creation events Archive creation Unusual filesystem paths Execution of rdpclip.exe, which supports clipboard redirection during RDP sessions, may also provide useful contextual evidence, although its presence alone does not prove that a file or specific clipboard content was transferred. Magnet Forensics has documented Prefetch, ShimCache , and SRUM as possible sources of RDP-related execution evidence including rdpclip.exe. RDP investigation tips A few quick checks can make RDP evidence much more useful: Pivot on the source IP: Identify which endpoint owned the address at the relevant time using DHCP, EDR, VPN, firewall, or asset records, then examine that system for client-side RDP artifacts. Follow the Logon ID: In Security Event 4624, the Logon ID can help correlate activity tied to the same Windows logon session. Differentiate disconnect from logoff: A disconnected RDP session may continue running and can later be reconnected. LocalSessionManager events can help distinguish the two. Look for chained RDP activity: A compromised system may have been used as a pivot to connect to additional hosts. Review more than Security.evtx: Dedicated Terminal Services logs may preserve connection, session, disconnect, and reconnect evidence even when the main Security log is incomplete or cleared. Validate logging before relying on absence: Missing events may reflect audit settings, log rollover, system configuration, or log clearing rather than proof that the activity did not occur. Build a multi-artifact RDP timeline No single RDP artifact should carry the entire conclusion. Instead, consider combining: Question Potential evidence Was the RDP client launched? Prefetch, UserAssist, process logs Where was the user connecting? Terminal Server Client registry, RDPClient logs Which account was used? UsernameHint, Security logs, RDP events Where did the session originate? Source IP in destination logs Did authentication succeed? Security 4624 Was an interactive session created? LocalSessionManager events Was the desktop shell started? LocalSessionManager Event 22 When did the session disconnect? Events 24, 40, 4779 Was the session resumed? Events 25, 4778 What happened during the session? Process, filesystem, registry, network, EDR and application artifacts Were files potentially transferred? File-system evidence, redirected-drive evidence, rdpclip context What may have appeared on screen? RDP bitmap cache The objective is to reconstruct the behavior surrounding the remote session, rather than to find one definitive “RDP artifact”. What RDP artifacts don’t prove Digital forensic examiners should also be careful about over-interpreting RDP evidence. Consider the following examples: RDP registry history Can support that a destination was entered or associated with the client. It doesn’t necessarily prove a successful session occurred. 4624 Logon Type 10 Provides strong evidence of a successful RemoteInteractive logon. It does not by itself establish everything the person did afterward. RDP bitmap cache May show graphical fragments displayed through an RDP session. It doesn’t necessarily establish who performed every visible action. rdpclip.exe execution Can support the presence of RDP clipboard functionality. It doesn’t prove that a particular file was copied. Digital forensic conclusions should describe what an artifact supports rather than extending the artifact beyond what it can demonstrate. RDP as part of the larger Windows evidence picture Remote Desktop evidence becomes considerably more powerful when viewed alongside other key Windows artifacts. Following an RDP session, investigators should consider examining: Execution artifacts Prefetch UserAssist Amcache ShimCache BAM/DAM SRUM File system activity $MFT $UsnJrnl LNK files Jump Lists Recent Files Shellbags Authentication Security event logs Domain controller logs Kerberos events NTLM authentication Network activity Firewall logs DNS VPN Proxy EDR telemetry Sysmon Command execution PowerShell Windows Terminal Command Prompt Scheduled Tasks Services WMI Data movement SMB USB Cloud storage Browser uploads RDP redirection This allows the investigator to move from identifying remote access to understanding what occurred because of that access. Final thoughts Remote Desktop Protocol is not inherently suspicious. It’s an essential component of legitimate Windows administration and remote work. But because RDP provides interactive access to another computer, it can also become an important part of ransomware, data breach, insider threat, intellectual property theft, unauthorized access, and lateral movement investigations. The most important forensic lesson is to treat RDP as a sequence of activity rather than a single artifact. This approach helps answer: Who connected? From where? To what system? Using which account? When did the session begin? Did the desktop become interactive? When did the user disconnect or log off? Did they reconnect? What occurred during that window? Client-side registry history, RDP client event logs, security events, Terminal Services logs, execution artifacts, filesystem evidence, and even bitmap cache data can contribute different pieces to the story. When those pieces are correlated, RDP artifacts can do much more than prove that remote access occurred. They can help show how someone moved through an environment, identify the systems they touched, establish the timeframe in which they operated, and provide the investigative context needed to determine what happened next. About the author Jeff Rutherford, Forensic Consultant at Magnet Forensics, is a retired FBI Supervisory Special Agent with more than twenty years of experience in organized crime, crimes against children, counterterrorism and cybersecurity related investigations. Jeff achieved specialized certification as a Technically Trained Agent and an FBI Certified Digital Forensic Examiner and holds certifications from IACIS (CFCE) and SANS (GCFA). While assigned to the North Texas Regional Computer Forensic Laboratory, Jeff conducted digital forensic examinations for various agencies (state, local, and federal) across North Texas. Jeff also led the FBI Dallas Technical Operations Squad responsible for the capture, processing, and preservation of electronic surveillance evidence.

  • Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) leaves evidence on both sides of a connection. The source system can show where a user tried to connect and which account they may have used. The destination can show who connected, where the connection came from, and when the session started and ended.

Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) can be one of the most valuable sources of evidence in a Windows digital forensic investigation.

RDP is commonly used for legitimate system administration, remote work, troubleshooting, and access to servers and workstations. The same functionality also makes it valuable to threat actors. Once an attacker obtains credentials or compromises a system, RDP can provide an interactive desktop that allows the attacker to move between systems, access files, execute tools, transfer data, establish persistence, or carry out ransomware deployment.

The system initiating the connection may contain evidence identifying where a user connected, while the destination system may document who connected, where the connection originated, when a session began, and when it disconnected or ended.

Correlated with other Windows evidence, these artifacts can do more than confirm RDP was used. They can help reconstruct how someone moved through an environment and what happened during the remote session.

This post explores the RDP artifacts found on the source and destination systems, what each one can and can’t prove, and how to correlate them into a timeline of remote activity. It also looks at how these artifacts support ransomware, data breach, insider threat, and intellectual property theft investigations.

What is Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP)?

Remote Desktop Protocol, commonly abbreviated RDP, is Microsoft’s protocol for providing interactive remote access to a Windows system.

A typical RDP connection involves two roles:

  • RDP client: The computer initiating the connection.
  • RDP host or destination: The computer being remotely accessed.

On Windows, the traditional built-in Remote Desktop Connection client is mstsc.exe. Rather than simply transferring commands between computers, RDP can provide the remote user with an interactive Windows desktop. The user can operate applications, browse files, execute programs, and interact with the destination computer much as if physically seated in front of it.

RDP also supports several forms of resource redirection. Depending on the configuration, a remote session may provide access to resources on the originating computer, including local drives, the clipboard, printers, cameras, smart cards, and other devices. Microsoft specifically documents file system and clipboard redirection as capabilities of RDP.

Those capabilities are particularly important during an investigation. An RDP session may be more than a remote login.

It can potentially provide a path for:

  • Moving files between systems
  • Accessing files on a user’s local computer
  • Copying text or files through the clipboard
  • Executing administrative tools
  • Accessing sensitive applications
  • Moving laterally between computers
  • Deploying malware or ransomware
  • Exfiltrating information
  • Conducting hands-on-keyboard activity
  • Remote printing of sensitive material

This is why RDP evidence should rarely be examined in isolation.

Investigating the RDP source

The source may help answer:

  • Did this user attempt to connect using RDP?
  • What computer or IP address did they connect to?
  • What username may have been used?
  • Was mstsc.exe executed?

In this example, we can see the username that was utilized and the destination IP (LAN).

If we look at additional artifacts, like Jump Lists, we can see additional details:

Here we see one artifact from the incoming connection:

The destination may help answer:

  • Who connected?
  • What IP address did the connection originate from?
  • Was authentication successful?
  • Was an interactive session created?
  • When did the session start?
  • When was it disconnected?

When possible, the strongest reconstruction comes from examining both systems.

How RDP artifacts are generated

RDP artifacts aren’t created by one single Windows component. Instead, several components participate in the connection and session lifecycle.

A simplified connection might look like:

Each stage of the RDP session lifecycle can create different forensic evidence. Some artifacts document an attempted connection, while others provide much stronger evidence that the remote session actually became interactive. That distinction is critical.

A hostname appearing in RDP history does not necessarily mean the user successfully authenticated. Likewise, an initial connection event should not automatically be interpreted as proof that someone received an interactive Windows desktop.

Digital forensic conclusions become stronger when multiple artifacts describe the same event.

From a forensic perspective, these registry locations can become a map of potential outbound RDP activity associated with a Windows user profile.

An important limitation is that these artifacts should not automatically be interpreted as proof that authentication succeeded. They identify destinations associated with the RDP client and should be correlated with additional evidence.

TerminalServices-RDPClient event logs

The source system can also contain a dedicated RDP client event log.

A common location is:

Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-RDPClient/Operational

The underlying EVTX file can typically be found beneath:

C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs\

One particularly useful event is Event ID 1024, which records the RDP client attempting to connect to a server. It can contain information identifying the destination server and the user SID associated with the connection attempt.

Other RDP client events can provide additional information surrounding the connection lifecycle, including successful connection activity and disconnects.

Investigators should therefore examine the entire group of events surrounding an RDP connection rather than searching for one Event ID in isolation.

MSTSC execution evidence

Determining that the Windows Remote Desktop client was executed can provide additional context. The executable used by Microsoft’s traditional Remote Desktop Connection client is:

mstsc.exe

Depending on the Windows configuration and investigative timeframe, execution evidence may appear in artifacts including:

  • Prefetch
  • UserAssist
  • Amcache
  • ShimCache
  • SRUM
  • Windows event logs
  • EDR telemetry
  • Process creation auditing

For example, Prefetch evidence for MSTSC.EXE can support a finding that the application executed.

However, execution of mstsc.exe alone does not establish:

  • Which computer was accessed
  • Whether authentication succeeded
  • What the user did remotely

It becomes significantly more useful when combined with RDP registry history and event logs.

From the SRUM artifact for an RDP session:

RDP bitmap cache

One of the more interesting RDP artifacts exists because Windows attempts to improve the performance of the remote desktop experience. Instead of repeatedly retransmitting every portion of the screen, RDP can cache graphical information on the client computer.

Depending on the Windows version and RDP implementation, cache files may be found beneath locations such as:

C:\Users\\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Terminal Server Client\Cache\

File names may include patterns such as:

bcache*.bmc

or

Cache0000.bin

These files can contain small fragments of the remote desktop display. This can occasionally provide remarkable evidence.

Recovered fragments might show portions of:

  • File Explorer
  • Application windows
  • Command prompts
  • Documents
  • Desktop icons
  • Administrative tools
  • Web applications

However, bitmap cache analysis has important limitations. The cache is not a recording of the user’s session. It contains graphical fragments used by the RDP client for performance optimization. Images may be incomplete, overwritten, duplicated, or lack sufficient context. For that reason, bitmap cache evidence is generally most useful as corroborating visual evidence rather than as the sole basis for determining what occurred.

Investigating the RDP destination

The destination computer often contains the most valuable evidence for determining whether a remote session actually occurred. Several Windows event logs can contribute to that reconstruction.

Security Event ID 4624: Successful logon

Windows Security Event ID 4624 records the creation of a successful logon session.

A 4624 event may provide information including:

  • Username
  • Domain
  • Logon ID
  • Authentication package
  • Source network address
  • Source port
  • Process information
  • Elevated token information, depending on event version and configuration
Failed RDP logons

Failed authentication attempts can also be significant. Security Event 4625 records failed logon attempts.

During an intrusion investigation, repeated failed attempts followed by a successful RemoteInteractive login may indicate:

  • Password guessing
  • Credential spraying
  • Mistyped credentials
  • Use of newly acquired credentials
  • Attempts to access multiple systems

Context is important. Administrators and legitimate users mistype passwords too.

A series of failed attempts from an unusual IP address followed shortly afterward by a successful RDP session, however, may deserve substantially more attention.

TerminalServices-RemoteConnectionManager

Another valuable log is:

Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-RemoteConnectionManager/Operational

One commonly examined event is Event ID 1149. Depending on the Windows version and authentication configuration, Event 1149 can provide information related to an inbound RDP connection including the username and originating network address.

It’s important not to treat Event 1149 by itself as absolute proof that a complete interactive desktop session occurred.

A stronger approach is to correlate it with:

  • Security 4624 Type 10
  • LocalSessionManager Event 21
  • Other session events

This illustrates a broader rule of RDP forensics: Connection, authentication, session creation, and user interaction are related but separate events.

TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager

The following log can be extremely useful for reconstructing the actual RDP session lifecycle:

Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager/Operational

Several events may be particularly valuable:

  • Event 21: Session logon. Indicates that a Remote Desktop Services session logon succeeded.
  • Event 22: Shell start. Indicates the user’s session shell started. This can be particularly useful because it helps move the interpretation beyond authentication toward an interactive user session.
  • Event 23: Session logoff. Indicates a session successfully logged off.
  • Event 24: Session disconnect. Indicates a session was disconnected. Disconnecting is not necessarily the same thing as logging off. A disconnected RDP session may remain alive on the destination system.
  • Event 25: Session reconnection. Indicates that a disconnected session was reconnected.

Additional events such as 39 and 40 can provide information concerning disconnect behavior and session transitions.

Together, these events can help create something resembling:
10:42 — RDP logon
10:42 — Windows shell starts
11:18 — Session disconnected
13:07 — Session reconnected
13:42 — User logs off
That sequence is far more informative than simply stating that RDP was used.

This is where timeline analysis can be so helpful to the case. RDP can be the doorway into a large behavioral timeline:

Cases where RDP artifacts can be valuable Ransomware investigations

RDP has historically been an important mechanism for hands-on-keyboard activity and lateral movement in a ransomware attack.

An attacker may compromise one endpoint and then use RDP to move to:

  • File servers
  • Backup servers
  • Domain administration systems
  • Additional workstations

RDP artifacts can help investigators determine:

  • The initial pivot system
  • Systems accessed afterward
  • Accounts used for lateral movement
  • When interactive attacker activity began
  • Which systems should receive priority examination

This can be particularly valuable when the attacker later encrypts or destroys evidence on destination systems.

Data breach investigations

During a data breach investigation, RDP artifacts can help establish whether an attacker had interactive access to systems storing sensitive information.

For example, investigators might identify: Compromised workstation → RDP → database server

The RDP connection itself does not prove that data was exfiltrated. But it can establish an investigative window.

The examiner can then focus on activity during that period, including:

  • File access
  • Database access
  • Archive creation
  • Cloud uploads
  • Browser activity
  • SMB transfers
  • PowerShell activity
  • External storage
  • Network connections

RDP provides the context around which additional evidence can be evaluated.

Insider threat investigations

RDP history can also be useful in insider threat investigations. Consider an employee whose normal workstation suddenly contains RDP history showing connections to:

  • Another employee’s workstation
  • An engineering server
  • A financial system
  • A privileged administrator workstation

Those connections may be entirely legitimate. But the artifact provides a lead.

Correlating the destination with session timestamps, authentication events, and file access evidence may help determine whether the activity was expected.

Intellectual property (IP) theft

Suppose an employee is suspected of accessing engineering documents shortly before resigning.

RDP evidence might establish that the employee remotely accessed an engineering workstation or server outside their normal workflow.

The examiner could then correlate that RDP session with:

  • Recent Files
  • Jump Lists
  • Shellbags
  • LNK files
  • Browser activity
  • USB artifacts
  • Cloud storage
  • Archive utilities
  • Network shares

The strength of the evidence comes from the combination. RDP may demonstrate access to the system. Other artifacts demonstrate what occurred after access

Lateral movement

RDP is particularly useful when reconstructing lateral movement. Consider the following pattern:

By examining the outbound RDP history on each computer and the inbound session evidence on the destination systems, investigators may be able to reconstruct a chain of interactive movement through the environment.

Source-side RDP artifacts can be especially valuable here because the Terminal Server Client registry history may reveal destinations that investigators had not yet identified.

A compromised computer may therefore serve as both a victim and a pivot point.

File transfer through RDP

Another issue investigators should consider is file movement. RDP supports several forms of resource redirection, including clipboard and drive redirection. Depending on the system’s policy configuration, local client drives may be exposed within the remote session. Microsoft documents redirected drives as allowing the remote computer to read from and write to drives located on the RDP client.

This means files may potentially move: client → remote system or remote system →client

without using a traditional SMB share, FTP client, or browser download, which can complicate investigations.

Evidence of an RDP session should therefore prompt investigators to consider whether resource redirection was available during the session.

Look for corroborating evidence such as:

  • File creation timestamps
  • $MFT
  • $UsnJrnl
  • LNK files
  • Recent Files
  • Jump Lists
  • EDR file events
  • Sysmon file creation events
  • Archive creation
  • Unusual filesystem paths

Execution of rdpclip.exe, which supports clipboard redirection during RDP sessions, may also provide useful contextual evidence, although its presence alone does not prove that a file or specific clipboard content was transferred. Magnet Forensics has documented Prefetch, ShimCache, and SRUM as possible sources of RDP-related execution evidence including rdpclip.exe.

RDP investigation tips

A few quick checks can make RDP evidence much more useful:

  • Pivot on the source IP: Identify which endpoint owned the address at the relevant time using DHCP, EDR, VPN, firewall, or asset records, then examine that system for client-side RDP artifacts.
  • Follow the Logon ID: In Security Event 4624, the Logon ID can help correlate activity tied to the same Windows logon session.
  • Differentiate disconnect from logoff: A disconnected RDP session may continue running and can later be reconnected. LocalSessionManager events can help distinguish the two.
  • Look for chained RDP activity: A compromised system may have been used as a pivot to connect to additional hosts.
  • Review more than Security.evtx: Dedicated Terminal Services logs may preserve connection, session, disconnect, and reconnect evidence even when the main Security log is incomplete or cleared.
  • Validate logging before relying on absence: Missing events may reflect audit settings, log rollover, system configuration, or log clearing rather than proof that the activity did not occur.
Build a multi-artifact RDP timeline

No single RDP artifact should carry the entire conclusion. Instead, consider combining:

QuestionPotential evidenceWas the RDP client launched?Prefetch, UserAssist, process logsWhere was the user connecting?Terminal Server Client registry, RDPClient logsWhich account was used?UsernameHint, Security logs, RDP eventsWhere did the session originate?Source IP in destination logsDid authentication succeed?Security 4624Was an interactive session created?LocalSessionManager eventsWas the desktop shell started?LocalSessionManager Event 22When did the session disconnect?Events 24, 40, 4779Was the session resumed?Events 25, 4778What happened during the session?Process, filesystem, registry, network, EDR and application artifactsWere files potentially transferred?File-system evidence, redirected-drive evidence, rdpclip contextWhat may have appeared on screen?RDP bitmap cache

The objective is to reconstruct the behavior surrounding the remote session, rather than to find one definitive “RDP artifact”.

What RDP artifacts don’t prove

Digital forensic examiners should also be careful about over-interpreting RDP evidence.

Consider the following examples:

RDP registry history

Can support that a destination was entered or associated with the client. It doesn’t necessarily prove a successful session occurred.

4624 Logon Type 10

Provides strong evidence of a successful RemoteInteractive logon. It does not by itself establish everything the person did afterward.

RDP bitmap cache

May show graphical fragments displayed through an RDP session. It doesn’t necessarily establish who performed every visible action.

rdpclip.exe execution

Can support the presence of RDP clipboard functionality. It doesn’t prove that a particular file was copied.

Digital forensic conclusions should describe what an artifact supports rather than extending the artifact beyond what it can demonstrate.

RDP as part of the larger Windows evidence picture

Remote Desktop evidence becomes considerably more powerful when viewed alongside other key Windows artifacts.

Following an RDP session, investigators should consider examining:

Execution artifacts
  • Prefetch
  • UserAssist
  • Amcache
  • ShimCache
  • BAM/DAM
  • SRUM
File system activity
  • $MFT
  • $UsnJrnl
  • LNK files
  • Jump Lists
  • Recent Files
  • Shellbags
Authentication
  • Security event logs
  • Domain controller logs
  • Kerberos events
  • NTLM authentication
Network activity
  • Firewall logs
  • DNS
  • VPN
  • Proxy
  • EDR telemetry
  • Sysmon
Command execution
  • PowerShell
  • Windows Terminal
  • Command Prompt
  • Scheduled Tasks
  • Services
  • WMI
Data movement
  • SMB
  • USB
  • Cloud storage
  • Browser uploads
  • RDP redirection

This allows the investigator to move from identifying remote access to understanding what occurred because of that access.

Final thoughts

Remote Desktop Protocol is not inherently suspicious. It’s an essential component of legitimate Windows administration and remote work. But because RDP provides interactive access to another computer, it can also become an important part of ransomware, data breach, insider threat, intellectual property theft, unauthorized access, and lateral movement investigations.

The most important forensic lesson is to treat RDP as a sequence of activity rather than a single artifact. This approach helps answer:

  • Who connected?
  • From where?
  • To what system?
  • Using which account?
  • When did the session begin?
  • Did the desktop become interactive?
  • When did the user disconnect or log off?
  • Did they reconnect?
  • What occurred during that window?

Client-side registry history, RDP client event logs, security events, Terminal Services logs, execution artifacts, filesystem evidence, and even bitmap cache data can contribute different pieces to the story.

When those pieces are correlated, RDP artifacts can do much more than prove that remote access occurred. They can help show how someone moved through an environment, identify the systems they touched, establish the timeframe in which they operated, and provide the investigative context needed to determine what happened next.

About the author

Jeff Rutherford, Forensic Consultant at Magnet Forensics, is a retired FBI Supervisory Special Agent with more than twenty years of experience in organized crime, crimes against children, counterterrorism and cybersecurity related investigations. Jeff achieved specialized certification as a Technically Trained Agent and an FBI Certified Digital Forensic Examiner and holds certifications from IACIS (CFCE) and SANS (GCFA). While assigned to the North Texas Regional Computer Forensic Laboratory, Jeff conducted digital forensic examinations for various agencies (state, local, and federal) across North Texas. Jeff also led the FBI Dallas Technical Operations Squad responsible for the capture, processing, and preservation of electronic surveillance evidence.

The post RDP: Forensic analysis of Windows Remote Desktop Protocol artifacts appeared first on Magnet Forensics.

items.title: Origin Range Requests: Serving large files without range-request tuning
items.summary: A video player seeking to the middle of a movie asks for a few megabytes. Under our old range caching, that one request could make Cloudflare pull 128 MiB from the origin and move it between data centers, sometimes after the viewer had already left. Range requests are how large files get delivered, and caching them naively easily leads to wasted network bandwidth and wasted disk operations when running a CDN at scale. So we rebuilt how our cache handles them. For R2, Cloudflare's object storage, p99 time to first byte dropped by about half, and a follow-up improvement cut tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads by about 6%. Today, we're making that new implementation available as Origin Range Requests , a self-service feature on all plans. There's no range size to tune and no need to contact support. Turn it on with a Cache Rule , and Cloudflare handles the rest. A request for part of a file An HTTP range request asks for part of a resource instead of the whole resource. The client sends a normal GET with a Range header: GET /movie.mp4 HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com Range: bytes=1048576-2097151 If the server supports the request, it returns 206 Partial Content and identifies the returned bytes with Content-Range : HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content Content-Range: bytes 1048576-2097151/524288000 Content-Length: 1048576 Range requests are common for large objects. A video player can request bytes around a seek position instead of the whole file. A download manager can resume after an interruption. A package manager can fetch part of an artifact. A client can inspect the end of a file without downloading everything before it. The client decides whether to request a range, and Cloudflare does not change that request. Instead, Origin Range Requests changes how Cloudflare satisfies it. The range-size problem Cloudflare has supported range-request caching for years via static zone configuration. The previous implementation resembled the cache-slicing described in an nginx blog post : each client request was mapped to fixed-size ranges of the file, with the range size and file extensions configured per zone. The size of each range created a tradeoff: small ranges led to many small origin requests and memory pressure on Cloudflare from coalescing all of the requests in-memory, while large ranges caused Cloudflare to download much more data than the client requested. Updates to the range size itself would invalidate cache entries, since the size was part of the cache key. This design also meant people requesting content through our network could have unpleasant experiences accessing these files. Concurrent requests that fell inside the same range, no matter how far apart each client’s requested range was, could block each other. Our nginx-based cache also couldn’t combine range caching with concurrent streaming , a feature we built to let multiple clients read a file from cache while it's still being written. Turning both on together cut responses short, so each range had to be fully downloaded before anyone could read it, and popular files needed a separate origin fetch for every range. The extra bytes could also cross several parts of our distributed cache: from the origin to one data center, between cache tiers, and then toward the client. Every hop multiplied the waste. No value works equally well for a small seek, a sequential download, a large media file, and every origin and cache topology. Our internal cache limitations were directly exposed to customers, who should not need to understand our capabilities in-depth to have files served efficiently. Fortunately, our transition from nginx to a Pingora -based caching server created an opportunity to address the implementation problems that had forced a hard-to-use setting onto customers. Fixed-size cache chunks The fix came from something Pingora was already doing. To make it easy to resume interrupted downloads, it stores every cached file on disk in fixed-size chunks. If the cache already thinks in chunks, the range size doesn't need to be a setting at all, it can just be the chunk! For a range request, Cloudflare checks which requested bytes are already cached. It serves those bytes directly. For missing bytes, it fetches origin ranges aligned to the cache's fixed-sized-chunk boundaries, stores the result in the same chunks used for ordinary cache storage, and returns only the bytes requested by the client. For example, a request for bytes 150-250 can cause Cloudflare to fetch the aligned chunk containing those bytes. The downstream response still contains only 150-250 . This does not eliminate extra work for requests smaller than our chunk size — such a request can still require fetching the whole chunk containing it. We also are taking on the cost of more work for non-aligned ranges. The difference is that the extra work is bounded and predictable, and no longer determined by a customer-selected range size that can cause unpredictable effects on us and origins. Coordinating cached and in-flight data Parsing the Range header is straightforward. The harder problem is producing one correct response when the requested bytes are split across cached data, an origin response, and downloads already in progress. At a high level, the edge: Looks up the asset headers and range-coverage metadata. Reads whatever part of the asset it can from disk or streaming in memory. Fetches missing coverage from the origin using aligned ranges. Writes the new bytes and records the completed range in metadata. Combines the pieces and sets Content-Range and Content-Length for the client response. This is a coordinator, not a single cache lookup. One request can use a cached prefix, an in-flight download, and a newly fetched suffix. The internal origin response can be larger than the downstream response, but the downstream status and headers describe only the requested range. If an existing download covers another request's bytes, the second request can attach to that download instead of starting another origin fetch. This shares work during bursts for popular large files. The design uses the existing cache data model. Headers identify the asset version, the body is stored in bounded chunks, and metadata records which ranges were written successfully. Validate before composing Composed range responses are valid only when all bytes belong to the same representation. The coordinator checks that each origin response matches the requested range, that the total asset size is stable, and that the entity tag remains consistent across subrequests. The If-Range header lets a client request a range only if the representation still matches a known validator. If it does not match, Cloudflare returns the full representation instead of combining bytes from different versions. Cloudflare also avoids composing ranges for a representation it is about to decompress because the range over a set of compressed bytes would be different from those selected by the range in a decompressed response. In these cases, Cloudflare serves the transformed full response rather than advertising a range it cannot honor correctly. The resulting behavior is standard HTTP: A satisfiable range receives 206 Partial Content with an accurate Content-Range . An unsatisfiable range receives 416 Range Not Satisfiable . A response that cannot safely be ranged is served as the complete representation. What changed in production Before opening Origin Range Requests to everyone, we moved existing users of the old range-caching feature onto the new implementation, starting with the workloads that hurt us most. Those workloads had a lot of concurrent range requests against very large files, often on very spiky traffic. Configured range sizes on the old system ran from tens of kilobytes to tens of gigabytes. With a large range size, a request that wouldn't fill a floppy disk could make us download a few DVDs' worth of data from the origin and move it across several data centers, sometimes after the client had already given up and gone elsewhere. With a small range size, one request turned into a long line of tiny origin requests, each holding memory while it waited. Both patterns caused real operational incidents for us. R2 was the largest internal user. Its configured range size was 64 MiB, so a small read that crossed a range boundary could cost us 128 MiB of transfer between data centers. After moving R2 to the new implementation, we saw: Faster responses. Across R2's storage regions, p99 time to first byte dropped by roughly half on both cache hits and misses. Fewer bytes on our network. Our most recent change taught the coordinator to combine bytes already on disk with bytes fetched from upstream in a single response. Before, a request was served either entirely from cache or entirely from upstream. After we turned this on for R2, tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads dropped about 6% week over week, which is petabytes less data moving between our data centers every day. Getting started Once the cache no longer depended on a customer-selected range size, the product configuration could not be simpler. Customers select matching traffic through Cache Rules . Cloudflare handles the chunking and cache coordination. Origin Range Requests is intended for traffic where clients naturally request parts of a large cacheable object: Progressive and seekable video such as MP4 Resumable large downloads Software distributions and package repositories Disk images, archives, and other multi-gigabyte objects AI training and inference workloads that transfer large model files or fetch selected regions of model artifacts Clients that fetch metadata or a small region of a larger file We intend to make this the default way certain file types are served on our network, modifiable by cache rules. This feature does not change normal cache eligibility. Enabling it does not make an otherwise uncacheable response cacheable. The origin also needs to support byte ranges for partial origin fetches to be useful. To turn it on, create a Cache Rule that matches your large-file traffic and set Origin Range Requests to On. You can do this in the dashboard under Caching > Cache Rules, or through the API with origin_range_requests: { "mode": "on" } . Customers choose the traffic; the edge handles the cache coordination and correctness requirements.

A video player seeking to the middle of a movie asks for a few megabytes. Under our old range caching, that one request could make Cloudflare pull 128 MiB from the origin and move it between data centers, sometimes after the viewer had already left. Range requests are how large files get delivered, and caching them naively easily leads to wasted network bandwidth and wasted disk operations when running a CDN at scale.

So we rebuilt how our cache handles them. For R2, Cloudflare's object storage, p99 time to first byte dropped by about half, and a follow-up improvement cut tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads by about 6%.

Today, we're making that new implementation available as Origin Range Requests, a self-service feature on all plans. There's no range size to tune and no need to contact support. Turn it on with a Cache Rule, and Cloudflare handles the rest.

A request for part of a file

An HTTP range request asks for part of a resource instead of the whole resource. The client sends a normal GET with a Range header:

GET /movie.mp4 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Range: bytes=1048576-2097151

If the server supports the request, it returns 206 Partial Content and identifies the returned bytes with Content-Range:

HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content
Content-Range: bytes 1048576-2097151/524288000
Content-Length: 1048576

Range requests are common for large objects. A video player can request bytes around a seek position instead of the whole file. A download manager can resume after an interruption. A package manager can fetch part of an artifact. A client can inspect the end of a file without downloading everything before it.

The client decides whether to request a range, and Cloudflare does not change that request. Instead, Origin Range Requests changes how Cloudflare satisfies it.

The range-size problem

Cloudflare has supported range-request caching for years via static zone configuration.

The previous implementation resembled the cache-slicing described in an nginx blog post: each client request was mapped to fixed-size ranges of the file, with the range size and file extensions configured per zone.

The size of each range created a tradeoff: small ranges led to many small origin requests and memory pressure on Cloudflare from coalescing all of the requests in-memory, while large ranges caused Cloudflare to download much more data than the client requested. Updates to the range size itself would invalidate cache entries, since the size was part of the cache key.

This design also meant people requesting content through our network could have unpleasant experiences accessing these files. Concurrent requests that fell inside the same range, no matter how far apart each client’s requested range was, could block each other. Our nginx-based cache also couldn’t combine range caching with concurrent streaming, a feature we built to let multiple clients read a file from cache while it's still being written. Our internal cache limitations were directly exposed to customers, who should not need to understand our capabilities in-depth to have files served efficiently.

Fortunately, our transition from nginx to a Pingora-based caching server created an opportunity to address the implementation problems that had forced a hard-to-use setting onto customers.

The fix came from something Pingora was already doing. To make it easy to resume interrupted downloads, it stores every cached file on disk in fixed-size chunks. If the cache already thinks in chunks, the range size doesn't need to be a setting at all, it can just be the chunk!

For a range request, Cloudflare checks which requested bytes are already cached. It serves those bytes directly. For missing bytes, it fetches origin ranges aligned to the cache's fixed-sized-chunk boundaries, stores the result in the same chunks used for ordinary cache storage, and returns only the bytes requested by the client.

For example, a request for bytes 150-250 can cause Cloudflare to fetch the aligned chunk containing those bytes. The downstream response still contains only 150-250.

This does not eliminate extra work for requests smaller than our chunk size — such a request can still require fetching the whole chunk containing it. We also are taking on the cost of more work for non-aligned ranges. The difference is that the extra work is bounded and predictable, and no longer determined by a customer-selected range size that can cause unpredictable effects on us and origins.

Coordinating cached and in-flight data

Parsing the Range header is straightforward. The harder problem is producing one correct response when the requested bytes are split across cached data, an origin response, and downloads already in progress.

At a high level, the edge:

  1. Looks up the asset headers and range-coverage metadata.
  2. Reads whatever part of the asset it can from disk or streaming in memory.
  3. Fetches missing coverage from the origin using aligned ranges.
  4. Writes the new bytes and records the completed range in metadata.
  5. Combines the pieces and sets Content-Range and Content-Length for the client response.

This is a coordinator, not a single cache lookup. One request can use a cached prefix, an in-flight download, and a newly fetched suffix. The internal origin response can be larger than the downstream response, but the downstream status and headers describe only the requested range.

If an existing download covers another request's bytes, the second request can attach to that download instead of starting another origin fetch. This shares work during bursts for popular large files.

The design uses the existing cache data model. Headers identify the asset version, the body is stored in bounded chunks, and metadata records which ranges were written successfully.

Validate before composing

Composed range responses are valid only when all bytes belong to the same representation. The coordinator checks that each origin response matches the requested range, that the total asset size is stable, and that the entity tag remains consistent across subrequests.

The If-Range header lets a client request a range only if the representation still matches a known validator. If it does not match, Cloudflare returns the full representation instead of combining bytes from different versions.

Cloudflare also avoids composing ranges for a representation it is about to decompress because the range over a set of compressed bytes would be different from those selected by the range in a decompressed response. In these cases, Cloudflare serves the transformed full response rather than advertising a range it cannot honor correctly.

The resulting behavior is standard HTTP:

  • A satisfiable range receives 206 Partial Content with an accurate Content-Range.
  • An unsatisfiable range receives 416 Range Not Satisfiable.
  • A response that cannot safely be ranged is served as the complete representation.
What changed in production

Before opening Origin Range Requests to everyone, we moved existing users of the old range-caching feature onto the new implementation, starting with the workloads that hurt us most.

Those workloads had a lot of concurrent range requests against very large files, often on very spiky traffic. Configured range sizes on the old system ran from tens of kilobytes to tens of gigabytes. With a large range size, a request that wouldn't fill a floppy disk could make us download a few DVDs' worth of data from the origin and move it across several data centers, sometimes after the client had already given up and gone elsewhere. With a small range size, one request turned into a long line of tiny origin requests, each holding memory while it waited. Both patterns caused real operational incidents for us.

R2 was the largest internal user. Its configured range size was 64 MiB, so a small read that crossed a range boundary could cost us 128 MiB of transfer between data centers. After moving R2 to the new implementation, we saw:

  • Faster responses. Across R2's storage regions, p99 time to first byte dropped by roughly half on both cache hits and misses.
  • Fewer bytes on our network. Our most recent change taught the coordinator to combine bytes already on disk with bytes fetched from upstream in a single response. Before, a request was served either entirely from cache or entirely from upstream. After we turned this on for R2, tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads dropped about 6% week over week, which is petabytes less data moving between our data centers every day.
Getting started

Once the cache no longer depended on a customer-selected range size, the product configuration could not be simpler. Customers select matching traffic through Cache Rules. Cloudflare handles the chunking and cache coordination.

Origin Range Requests is intended for traffic where clients naturally request parts of a large cacheable object:

  • Progressive and seekable video such as MP4
  • Resumable large downloads
  • Software distributions and package repositories
  • Disk images, archives, and other multi-gigabyte objects
  • AI training and inference workloads that transfer large model files or fetch selected regions of model artifacts
  • Clients that fetch metadata or a small region of a larger file

We intend to make this the default way certain file types are served on our network, modifiable by cache rules.

This feature does not change normal cache eligibility. Enabling it does not make an otherwise uncacheable response cacheable. The origin also needs to support byte ranges for partial origin fetches to be useful.

To turn it on, create a Cache Rule that matches your large-file traffic and set Origin Range Requests to On. You can do this in the dashboard under Caching > Cache Rules, or through the API with origin_range_requests: { "mode": "on" }. Customers choose the traffic; the edge handles the cache coordination and correctness requirements.

items.title: Inside the LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise: Credential theft through Python startup hooks
items.summary: In this article Attack overview Technical details Mitigation and protection guidance Indicators of compromise References Learn More On October 21, 2026, a compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 release was published to the Python Package Index (PyPI) and distributed through official container images. The malicious package added files that Python could execute during normal interpreter initialization. An application did not need to import LiteLLM for the payload to run: starting Python in an affected environment could be enough. Microsoft analyzed two execution paths in the affected wheels: a credential collector launched through a path extension, and a Unix-oriented loader persisted through site-specific configuration. The collector targeted authentication material across developer tools, AI applications, cloud environments, browsers, and infrastructure. A separate database module attempted to read selected credential and model-configuration records from the LiteLLM proxy. Endpoint observations on Windows and macOS matched the recovered collector’s discovery, encryption, and outbound-connection behavior. In one Windows example, a routine Python invocation to install an unrelated dependency activated the collector. This distinction matters for response: investigators should not start Python or pip inside a suspect environment to determine whether the malicious package is present. This blog explains the startup mechanisms, the credentials the payload could reach, and the evidence defenders can use to investigate exposure. It also provides Microsoft Defender detection information, advanced hunting queries, and recovery guidance. Removing the package or a release tag is not sufficient recovery. Organizations must address the affected Python environment, any surviving processes, and credentials accessible to the compromised identity. Attack overview LiteLLM is commonly deployed as a gateway between applications and model providers. In that position it may have access to model-provider API keys, database connection strings, workload identities, routing configuration, and tenant policy data. The same package is also used on developer workstations, build agents, test systems, and containers, which widened the set of environments that could be exposed by the compromised release. According to LiteLLM maintainers , stolen developer GitHub credentials were used to alter the release workflow and redirect it to the lookalike repository Berri-AI/litellm rather than the legitimate BerriAI/litellm repository. A credential associated with another developer account was then used to satisfy a production approval step. Microsoft has not independently determined how the attacker first accessed the upstream environment or obtained those credentials. The compromised package used Python startup mechanisms to execute malicious code automatically, meaning exposure was not limited to systems actively using a LiteLLM gateway. Developer workstations, continuous integration and continuous delivery/deployment (CI/CD) agents, test environments, containers, and other systems that started Python with the affected package installed could also execute the payload. The malicious code supported credential collection and, on Unix-based systems, retrieval and execution of additional Python code. Figure 1: Compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 execution flow. 1. Compromised package distribution The compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 release delivered malicious Python startup files to environments where the package was installed. 2. Automatic payload execution Python startup processing launched the credential collector without requiring the application to actively use LiteLLM gateway functionality. 3. Credential and sensitive-data collection The collector targeted developer credentials, cloud credentials, browser data, SSH material, environment variables, and LiteLLM database data accessible to the affected process. 4. Encryption and exfiltration Collected data was encrypted and transmitted to an attacker-controlled endpoint. 5. Conditional retrieval and execution of additional code On Unix-based systems, the payload supported retrieving and executing additional Python code, although this activity was not confirmed. Technical details Compromised package distribution and automatic payload execution The compromised wheel packaged cook.pth , cook.py , and sitecustomize.py under litellm-1.107.0.data/purelib/ . During installation, these files were relocated into the Python environment’s library directory, outside the normal litellm application directory. This placement enabled execution through Python’s normal site initialization, which processes executable import statements in .pth files and later attempts to import the sitecustomize module. The first execution path began with the single executable line in cook.pth : “import cook”. This loaded cook.py , whose wrapper Base64-decoded and zlib-decompressed an embedded Python program before executing the recovered source. The program identified itself as PRIVCOLLECT and performed credential collection in a daemon thread. Figure 2. The executable .pth line imports cook, and the recovered collector starts a daemon thread after checking its inherited environment flag. Before starting the thread, the collector checked the inherited PRIVCOLLECT_ACTIVE environment variable. A nonempty value caused it to return; otherwise, it set the flag, limiting duplicate collection in descendant processes. After an upload returned HTTP 200, it attempted to write /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb . These duplicate-suppression gates were not containment controls: startup alone did not prove collection or upload completed, because a short-lived process could exit before the thread finished, while write failures or temporary-storage changes could leave the marker absent. Figure 3. Encode Cook.py file and decoded PRIVCOLLECT credential Stealer configuration . A second startup mechanism used sitecustomize.py , providing a separate Unix-oriented execution path with an embedded collector and functionality to retrieve and execute additional Python code from a remote host. Remote retrieval and execution through this path were not confirmed. Together, these mechanisms extended potential exposure beyond active LiteLLM deployments: simply starting Python in an affected environment could activate the malicious code, even when LiteLLM itself was never imported. Because the startup files resided outside the litellm application directory, removing only the application files could leave the malicious startup components behind. Credential and sensitive-data collection The recovered collector was designed to gather sensitive authentication material across developer tools, AI applications, cloud environments, browsers, and infrastructure. It runs multiple collection modules sequentially with independent error handling, allowing collection to continue even when individual targets are unavailable or inaccessible. Target Recovered collection behavior Developer and AI tools Reads selected authentication and configuration files for AI assistants, integrated development environments (IDEs) , GitHub Copilot, VS Code, and MCP integrations. Collects fixed paths and top-level JSON files in selected tool directories under a collection budget. Source control and package ecosystems Searches Git credentials, package-manager configuration, selected dotenv files, and private-key extensions. Shallow directory walks and file-size limits constrain these searches. Cloud and workload credentials Reads AWS, Azure CLI, and Google Cloud configuration or credential caches; Kubernetes service-account files; Docker configuration; and mounted secrets. It also attempts AWS and GCP metadata credential retrieval. Browsers and user histories Accesses Chromium-family and Firefox credential-related data and browsing history, plus shell, database-client, and interactive-tool histories. Password decryption is platform- and format-dependent. Process environments Collects its own environment and, on Linux, other process environments readable through procfs. This can expose secrets beyond variables explicitly configured for the LiteLLM process. Private keys and infrastructure Targets readable Secure Shell (SSH) material and selected GNU Privacy Guard (GPG), Transport Layor Security (TLS), CI/CD, Vault, and infrastructure-tool configuration. A target appearing in the code does not establish successful access. LiteLLM proxy data When its prerequisites are satisfied, starts a Python child using Prisma to read selected fields from two proxy database tables, with a 500-row limit for each query Encryption and exfiltration After collection, the payload serializes module results and host metadata as JSON. Each run generates a 32-byte AES key and a 16-byte initialization vector. AES-256-CBC encrypts the collection document; an embedded 4,096-bit RSA public key wraps the AES key using OAEP. The OpenSSL path tries SHA-256 and then SHA-1 for OAEP, and the resulting metadata records the selected digest. Figure 4. The collector generates a fresh AES key and IV, wraps the key with RSA, and packages the encrypted collection in a gzip tar archive before attempting upload. Selected code excerpts are wrapped for readability. The collector places three members in a gzip-compressed tar archive: data.bin , containing the initialization vector (IV) and encrypted collection; key.bin , containing the wrapped AES key; and hdr.json , containing plaintext envelope metadata. It then attempts an HTTP POST to hxxp://www[.]litellm[.]dev/healthcheck , using application/octet-stream , a fixed browser-like User-Agent, and a body checksum in an X-SHA256 header. The upload routine retries and treats only HTTP 200 as success. The OpenSSL backend creates temporary directories beginning with .pc_e_ , stages input and output files and removes them after use. Conditional retrieval and execution of additional code In addition to the credential collector, the compromised package contained a separate Unix-oriented loader in sitecustomize.py , designed to retrieve and execute additional Python code. When Python starts, the loader takes an exclusive lock on /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock so that only one instance runs per host and detaches into the background. Each cycle reads a GitHub-hosted domain.txt file, which acts as a mutable pointer to an attacker-controlled server. Figure 5. The remote-loader path checks the pointer and DNS before retrieving code, then compiles and executes the response without a content-signature check. If a valid server address is returned and successfully resolved, the loader is designed to request /codepy from that server, compile the returned content, and execute it as Python code within the affected environment. This gives the attacker a mechanism to change the second-stage payload without publishing another compromised LiteLLM package. This loader is separate from the credential collector delivered directly in the compromised package.
