items.title: Signed, Sealed, and Relayed, NTLM-style: Bypassing LDAP Signing Through Reauthentication
items.summary: For years, we thought LDAP and SMB signing protected us from NTLM relay attacks. However, we found that both protocols could be relay targets through re-authentication on a connection the attacker already owned. Signing was still enforced, just with the attacker known session key. Microsoft fixed SMB quietly in September 2026 and LDAP in October 2026. Every Windows Server from 2016 to 2025 was vulnerable to NTLM relay attacks, even with signing enforced in both protocols. Introduction Traditionally, LDAP signing was considered one of the “effective mitigations” against NTLM relay attacks. So, naturally, we had to ruin it. To circumvent LDAP signing, we first establish a signed LDAP connection to the DC using valid credentials or an anonymous security context and keep the session key. We then coerce a victim and relay their NTLM authentication over that existing LDAP connection, slipping our malicious LDAP operation into the same signed SASL record as the victim’s NTLM AUTHENTICATE message. The DC verifies the signature using our session key, switches authorization to the victim’s identity, and executes the malicious LDAP operation with the victim’s privileges. Microsoft patched this in October of 2026, but every Windows Server was vulnerable until then. You’re probably thinking: “So what, Raj? Why should I care?” This bypass enables machine account NTLM authentication from a domain controller over SMB to be relayed to LDAP on another domain controller, from an unauthenticated or unprivileged context. Relay to LDAP enables the total compromise of the victim domain controller via computer takeover primitives such as Kerberos resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD) and shadow credentials, which then leads to DCSync and complete domain and forest compromise. To better understand NTLM and relay attacks in detail, please read the following blogs, as this blog post will not cover the basics: The Renaissance of NTLM Relay Attacks: Everything You Need to Know NTLM Relay Note to readers SpecterOps partners with OpenAI as part of the Daybreak Trusted Access for Cyber Program . We used OpenAI’s Daybreak Red model to assist in this research. Specifically, the model excelled at reverse engineering the DLLs under guidance and pinpointing the exact bug, which significantly reduced the research time. We reported this vulnerability to Microsoft on October 6, 2026 but we never received a response to that MSRC report. The fix shipped on October 13, 2026 update, so we can’t say whether our report had anything to do with it. We independently identified a similar vulnerability in SMB, and Microsoft patched it quietly in September 2026. Another researcher also noticed that silent patch and published a blog, Defeating Enforced SMB Signing . This blog post describes an LDAP variant that we found in September 2026. Background: Why Signing Was Supposed to Stop NTLM Relay NTLM relay attacks used to be straightforward: an attacker positioned between a client and server could relay the NTLM authentication exchange and authenticate to the server as the client. Microsoft introduced NTLMv2 to strengthen NTLMv1’s authentication and session security. NTLMv2 supports signing to protect message integrity and sealing to encrypt messages. Later, Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) added channel and service binding to help prevent relay attacks. Since then NTLM relay attacks have become more complicated, especially cross-protocol relaying. Windows Server 2025 raises the baseline further. SMB signing is now required by default for outbound connections, and new Active Directory deployments require LDAP signing by default. Relaying from SMB to LDAP is still harder because the two protocols handle signing differently. SMB negotiates signing on its own, but the Windows SMB client still sets the signing flag in its NTLM messages. LDAP has no separate negotiation, so it relies on NTLM to decide whether signing is used. When we relay that SMB authentication to LDAP, the DC honors the flag and expects every message after the bind to be signed. The ordinary relay was blocked when SMB or LDAP required signing because we did not know the victim’s exported session key. LDAP over TLS was blocked when channel binding was required. This is where relaying from HTTP became easier because HTTP does not provide per-message signing and it doesn’t even negotiate a session key; when HTTPS is used, TLS provides transport integrity instead. As a result, coercing a victim through WebClient generally produces an NTLM exchange that is easier to relay and never negotiates signing. WebDAV also allows us to capture that authentication on an external host and route it back into the target environment through attacker-controlled infrastructure. Elad Shamir calls this technique “There and Back Again,” and Logan Goins demonstrates the complete workflow in this blog post . NTLMv2 Basics: Session Keys, Signing, and the MIC We will briefly cover NTLMv2 terms so we are all on the same page when these terms come up later. During normal NTLMv2 authentication, the client uses its NT hash, uppercased username and domain name to derive the ResponseKeyNT through the NTOWFv2 function. It then builds the NTLMv2_CLIENT_CHALLENGE structure, which contains a timestamp, a client challenge, and AV pairs. The client then computes the NTProofStr by running HMAC-MD5 over the server challenge and the NTLMv2_CLIENT_CHALLENGE structure using the ResponseKeyNT as the key. The final NTLMv2 response is the concatenation of the NTProofStr and the NTLMv2_CLIENT_CHALLENGE structure. So the AV pairs are protected by the NTProofStr , and changing them would invalidate that proof. For NTLMv2, the client computes a SessionBaseKey by running HMAC-MD5 over the NTProofStr using the ResponseKeyNT as the key. The KeyExchangeKey is the same as SessionBaseKey and we will refer to it as the SessionBaseKey in this blog post. When key exchange is negotiated for signing or sealing (encryption), the client generates a random 16-byte ExportedSessionKey and encrypts it with RC4 using the SessionBaseKey . That encrypted key is included in the AUTHENTICATE message. The ExportedSessionKey is used as input to derive signing and sealing keys by both LDAP and SMB protocols, but each protocol derives its own signing and sealing keys differently. Another important concept is the Message Integrity Code (MIC). The MIC protects the entire NTLM exchange from tampering. The MsvAvFlags AV pair in the AUTHENTICATE message tells the server that a MIC is present. The client computes the MIC over all three NTLM messages using the ExportedSessionKey , so any modification to any of those messages invalidates the MIC, resulting in the server rejecting authentication. How LDAP signing and channel binding stop NTLM relay Typically, if a target DC requires LDAP signing, we cannot perform NTLM relay against LDAP because we don’t know the victim’s (client’s) session key. The signing requirement is negotiated during the SASL bind and protects the LDAP messages sent after authentication, not just subsequent Bind requests. Without the session key, we cannot generate valid signatures for LDAP messages. When relaying SMB to LDAP, things get more complicated because both protocols have their own way of negotiating signing. SMB always negotiates signing, and the NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_SIGN flag will always be set to 1 for a victim coerced via SMB. The problem arises when the LDAP server honors that request even though the DC does not require signing for LDAP. So we can’t relay SMB to LDAP because LDAP enforces the signing the victim requested. This applies to typical NTLMv2 exchanges, with exceptions such as legacy NTLMv1 or vulnerable implementations. LDAP also supports channel binding when authentication happens over LDAPS (with TLS). Signing protects the LDAP messages, while channel binding ties the authentication to the TLS channel. Channel binding only applies to LDAPS, and it doesn’t apply to LDAP. Traditionally, we could bypass LDAP signing and channel binding if only one protection is enforced. If LDAP signing is enforced but channel binding is not, we can target LDAPS, and since TLS traffic is signed, it satisfies the DC’s signing requirements. If channel binding is enforced but LDAP signing is not required, we can instead target LDAP, where there is no TLS channel to bind the authentication to. After authentication, we may upgrade that connection with StartTLS because TLS is established after the bind, and channel binding was not checked during that authentication exchange. The benefit of using StartTLS is that it allows performing sensitive operations such as password changes or resets, assuming the relayed account has the necessary permissions. With LDAP signing required and channel binding set to Always, NTLM relay to LDAP should be impossible. However, as we’ll see, the word itself says “I’m possible”. How the LDAP signing bypass works Buckle up! Now the fun begins. We identified a way to bypass LDAP signing by coercing a Windows SMB client and relaying its NTLM authentication to a domain controller that requires LDAP signing. First, we establish a signed LDAP connection with a session key we know. We can do this with valid domain account credentials, or we can even establish an anonymous NTLM SASL context. We will call this identity X. We then relay the victim’s (identity Y) NTLM authentication over that existing signed connection. You might be asking why the victim has to be an SMB client. If WebDAV can be coerced too, why not relay that? This is where the SMB client turns out to be the important part. The Windows SMB client sets the NTLM signing flag in its authentication, which is the exact thing that made SMB to LDAP relaying hard before. A WebDAV client doesn’t set that flag, and when the victim authenticates over HTTP, the DC rejects the stacked operation with operationsError (0x4DC) because a successful bind had not completed. So the signing flag that used to be the problem is what makes this technique work. Before going further, we need to explain SASL. SASL (Simple Authentication and Security Layer) is a framework that lets a protocol like LDAP plug in an authentication mechanism, such as NTLM or Kerberos, and optionally add a layer that signs and encrypts every message after the bind. Once that layer is on, LDAP sends a SASL record, which is a length-prefixed block that is signed (and optionally sealed) as one unit and can hold more than one LDAP message. NTLM SASL signing creates a signing key that is associated with X, and we know that key. The important part is that one signature covers everything inside a SASL record. The interesting part is what happens when we relay Y’s final NTLM AUTHENTICATE message. Instead of sending it on its own, we put the BindRequest carrying that message and our malicious LDAP ModifyRequest (e.g., modifying msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity or msDS-KeyCredentialLink attributes for Kerberos resource-based constrained delegation or shadow credentials, respectively) into one SASL record. These are two separate LDAP messages inside the same protected SASL record, and we sign the whole SASL record with the session key we already know (X). The DC verifies the entire SASL record once using X, then processes the BindRequest and switches the connection’s identity to Y. When it reaches our modification, it runs the LDAP operation with Y’s privileges, even though we supplied the LDAP operation and signed the SASL record with X. This does not give us the victim’s session key (Y). If we send another SASL record signed with X, the DC rejects it because the connection now requires Y’s session key. The issue is what happens inside the SASL record we already sent. Its contents pass the signature check under our original security context (X), but the modification runs under Y’s identity after the bind completes. This technique bypasses LDAP signing, not channel binding. Channel binding only applies to LDAPS, because it ties authentication to the TLS channel, and LDAP (389/TCP) has no TLS channel to bind to. The domain controller we tested against had both LDAP signing and channel binding enforced, and the attack still worked over 389/TCP. If 389/TCP is blocked then this technique will not work against LDAPS (636/TCP). So why doesn’t the signing bypass itself carry over to LDAPS? The key difference between signed LDAP on 389/TCP and LDAPS on 636/TCP is where the protection is applied. LDAPS relies on TLS to sign and encrypt the connection, while NTLM only authenticates the user inside it. The TLS keys are associated with the connection and not with X, and Windows does not allow NTLM SASL signing or sealing over an existing TLS connection. So on LDAPS there is no signing key that belongs to X, and no signed SASL record to stack Y’s authentication and our operation into. This is why the LDAP signing bypass on 389/TCP does not transfer directly to LDAPS. The attack sequence follows: The attacker coerces the victim into authenticating over SMB The victim’s SMB client connects to the attacker and begins session setup The attacker establishes a signed LDAP session through GSS-SPNEGO using either valid domain credentials or, where accepted, anonymous NTLM SASL authentication, with a session key known to the attacker The victim’s SMB client sends an NTLM NEGOTIATE message The attacker carries that message in a GSS-SPNEGO SASL BindRequest over the existing protected LDAP connection The target returns an NTLM CHALLENGE message through GSS-SPNEGO, protected by the existing LDAP session The attacker forwards the NTLM CHALLENGE message to the victim’s SMB client The victim’s SMB client returns the final SPNEGO response carrying the NTLM AUTHENTICATE message The attacker sends a GSS-SPNEGO BindRequest carrying that response, followed by a separate LDAP ModifyRequest, together in one SASL record signed using the attacker’s original LDAP session key The target verifies the SASL record using the attacker’s original session key, completes the bind as the victim, and processes the following modification using the victim’s privileges Walkthrough: Relaying SMB to LDAP With Signing Required Now let’s dive deeper into this vulnerability and analyze how it works and what made it possible. In this example, we have three hosts. The domain controller is LYS-DC (10.4.10.47), the attacker is a Kali host (10.4.10.233), and the victim is LYS-SRV22 (10.4.10.48). The DC was running build 26100.33451 (KB5129235, the September 2026 cumulative update) before the October 2026 update (KB5126646, build 26100.33648) introduced the fix. First, we coerce the victim into connecting to the attacker host. The victim opens an SMB connection and sends an SMB NEGOTIATE request, which agrees on the SMB dialect and lists the security mechanisms it supports. We don’t respond yet. The TCP layer acknowledges the packet, but the relay holds the victim at this point until our LDAP connection is ready. In frame 12, we bind to the DC over LDAP as LYS\LYS.LOW and keep the session key from that authentication. Every LDAP message after the bind has to be signed with this key, and since we authenticated as LYS.LOW we know it. The session key shown above is in encrypted format so we can’t directly use it. In frame 28, we resume the victim’s SMB connection and the victim (LYS\LYS-SRV22$) sends us its NTLM NEGOTIATE message. As with any Windows SMB client, the NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_SIGN flag is set, as you can see in the screenshot below. In frame 29, we relay that NTLM NEGOTIATE message to the DC inside a Bind request. Because the connection is already signed, the Bind travels as a SASL-protected message signed and sealed with LYS.LOW’s session key. That is why the payload looks encrypted in the screenshot. We wrote a small Wireshark plugin that decrypts these messages with the LYS.LOW key so we can see what is being sent, which we will show later. In frames 30 to 33, we finish the NTLM exchange. The DC sends a NTLM CHALLENGE message to us, we forward it to Y (LYS\LYS-SRV22$) over SMB, and Y answers with its NTLM AUTHENTICATE message. We only pass the messages between Y and the DC. We never learn Y’s password or session key. Frame 34 is where the attack happens. Instead of sending Y’s AUTHENTICATE message on its own, we put two LDAP messages into one SASL record and sign it with X’s session key. The first is a BindRequest carrying Y’s AUTHENTICATE message. The second is a ModifyRequest that writes msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on LYS-SRV22$, with a security descriptor that grants an account we control (HXRBOX2$). The DC verifies the signature on the SASL record once, using X’s key. It then completes the bind as Y and processes the ModifyRequest as Y too. So the whole resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD) attack happens in one signed SASL record. Root Cause: Inside LDAP_CONN::ProcessRequestEx To uncover what happens on the domain controller side, the core of the vulnerability lives inside the LDAP_CONN::ProcessRequestEx function. This function runs for every LDAP request received on a connection. It first checks whether signing was negotiated on the connection, and if it was, it expects the message to be signed with the negotiated signing key. It verifies this by calling LDAP_REQUEST::DecryptSignedOrSealedMessage , which checks the SASL record against the key of the connection’s current security context. One thing to note here is that signing only starts after the NTLM authentication exchange is completed. Since we were the ones who authenticated on this connection, we already possess the session key at this point. So when we perform the reauthentication, we continue the open SMB connection with the victim and relay the NTLM messages back and forth with the DC. Once we have the victim’s final NTLM AUTHENTICATE message, we relay it in a Bind request together with our own LDAP operation, both in the same SASL record signed with our key. Next, ProcessRequestEx calls the LDAP_CONN::BindRequest function, where the victim’s identity is validated. Within that function, it later calls LDAP_CONN::MoveSecurityContext , LDAP_CONN::InstallNewSecurityContext , and LDAP_CONN::SetSecurityContextAtts , which switch the connection’s authorization to the victim’s. After LDAP_CONN::BindRequest returns, there is still data left in the SASL record, so ProcessRequestEx processes the next message and calls the LDAP_CONN::ModifyRequest function. This is where our stacked LDAP operation goes, the one we wanted to perform with the victim’s authorization. Since the authorization context was already switched to the victim during the Bind, the Modify executes as the victim. So basically there is no check that notices the identity changed partway through the SASL record, or that anything after the reauthentication should be verified with the new signing key, which only the victim holds. The SASL record gets verified just once, with the session key that we control, and never again after that. How Microsoft Patched the LDAP Signing Bypass Microsoft fixed this issue by giving every LDAP connection a counter that tracks its identity. So first it captures a baseline. Whenever new client data arrives, LDAP_REQUEST::ReceivedClientData reads the connection’s current identity counter and saves a copy of it inside the request itself. This is like a snapshot of which identity the connection was authenticated as when that data came in. Nothing is validated or blocked at this point – it’s just recorded. That counter only increments when the connection’s identity actually changes, and that is exactly what our relayed Bind does. When the Bind completes, LDAP_CONN::SetSecurityContextAtts installs the victim’s security context and increments the same counter, which leaves a trace that the switch happened. Later, after the Bind in that request has switched the connection over to the victim, the counter on the connection has increased, but the copy saved in the request hasn’t. So when ProcessRequestEx compares the two, and they don’t match, it knows the identity changed partway through the SASL record. It then throws away the rest of the SASL record, which means our stacked Modify never runs. Proof of Concept: Running the Attack With ntlmrelayx To test out the above described attack, we are releasing “The LDAP Switcheroo” that wraps ntlmrelayx.py with our custom modifications to make this attack work. https://github.com/grayhatkiller/switcheroo How to Defend Against NTLM Relay to LDAP Signing alone was never a complete defense against NTLM relay. To close the gap this research exposed: Patch domain controllers first. Install the October 2026 cumulative update (KB5126646) on every domain controller. This fixes the LDAP signing bypass. Patch for the SMB fix. Install the September 2026 update (KB5122882) on every server to close the SMB signing bypass. Enforce LDAP signing and channel binding together. Either one on its own leaves a path open. With both enforced, an attacker can’t switch to LDAPS or plain LDAP to get around the one that’s missing. Restrict LDAP on 389/TCP where you can. The bypass ran over 389/TCP. If 389/TCP is blocked then this technique fails. Reduce NTLM wherever possible. Every NTLM authentication you remove is one less thing an attacker can relay. The last two recommendations are more complicated and may be aspirational goals for some organizations, because legacy applications often depend on plain LDAP and NTLM. Elad Shamir: You can’t write an NTLM relay blog without Elad. As always, Elad’s guidance is what pushed me to go after LDAP after finding the SMB signing bypass. It is an NTLM relay technique that worked against domain controllers even when LDAP signing was required. An attacker opens a signed LDAP connection with a session key they know, relays a victim’s NTLM authentication over that connection, and slips a malicious LDAP operation into the same signed message. The domain controller checks the signature with the attacker’s key, then runs the operation with the victim’s privileges. Is LDAP signing enough to stop NTLM relay attacks? Not on its own. Before the October 2026 update, every Windows Server 2022 and Windows Server 2025 domain controller we tested accepted relayed NTLM authentication with LDAP signing required. Install the update, enforce LDAP signing and channel binding together, and reduce NTLM wherever you can. Does the LDAP signing bypass work against LDAPS? The technique targets LDAP on 389/TCP. If 389/TCP is blocked then this technique will not work against LDAPS (636/TCP). Which Windows Server versions were vulnerable? We tested against Server 2016 domain controller and above, and it was vulnerable until the October 2026 cumulative update. Does the attacker need domain credentials? Not necessarily. The attacker needs a signed LDAP session with a session key they know. That can come from valid domain account credentials or, where the domain controller accepts it, an anonymous LDAP connection. The attacker also needs to coerce a victim into authenticating to them. What can an attacker do with the LDAP signing bypass? The attacker can make a domain controller authenticate to the attacker and relay the authentication to another domain controller to compromise the domain instantly. In our example, we relayed a server’s computer account and wrote msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on that server to set up resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD). Has Microsoft patched the LDAP signing bypass? Yes. We reported it to Microsoft on October 6, 2026, and Microsoft independently shipped a fix on October 13, 2026 (KB5126646). The patch tracks each LDAP connection’s identity with a counter. If the identity changes partway through a signed SASL record, the domain controller discards the rest of that SASL record, so the stacked operation never runs. Microsoft fixed the related SMB issue in September 2026. First and foremost, to better understand NTLM and relay attacks in detail please read the following blogs as this blog post will not cover the basics of it: The Renaissance of NTLM Relay Attacks: Everything You Need to Know NTLM Relay We independently identified the similar vulnerability in SMB as well. That vulnerability was patched in September 2026. Another researcher also identified this silent patch and published a blog here: Defeating Enforced SMB Signing
items.summary_html:
For years, we thought LDAP and SMB signing protected us from NTLM relay attacks. However, we found that both protocols could be relay targets through re-authentication on a connection the attacker already owned. Signing was still enforced, just with the attacker known session key. Microsoft fixed SMB quietly in September 2026 and LDAP in October 2026. Every Windows Server from 2016 to 2025 was vulnerable to NTLM relay attacks, even with signing enforced in both protocols.

Introduction

Traditionally, LDAP signing was considered one of the “effective mitigations” against NTLM relay attacks. So, naturally, we had to ruin it. To circumvent LDAP signing, we first establish a signed LDAP connection to the DC using valid credentials or an anonymous security context and keep the session key. We then coerce a victim and relay their NTLM authentication over that existing LDAP connection, slipping our malicious LDAP operation into the same signed SASL record as the victim’s NTLM AUTHENTICATE message. The DC verifies the signature using our session key, switches authorization to the victim’s identity, and executes the malicious LDAP operation with the victim’s privileges. Microsoft patched this in October of 2026, but every Windows Server was vulnerable until then.

You’re probably thinking: “So what, Raj? Why should I care?” This bypass enables machine account NTLM authentication from a domain controller over SMB to be relayed to LDAP on another domain controller, from an unauthenticated or unprivileged context.  Relay to LDAP enables the total compromise of the victim domain controller via computer takeover primitives such as Kerberos resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD)  and shadow credentials, which then leads to DCSync and complete domain and forest compromise.

To better understand NTLM and relay attacks in detail, please read the following blogs, as this blog post will not cover the basics:

  • The Renaissance of NTLM Relay Attacks: Everything You Need to Know
  • NTLM Relay
Note to readers

SpecterOps partners with OpenAI as part of the Daybreak Trusted Access for Cyber Program. We used OpenAI’s Daybreak Red model to assist in this research. Specifically, the model excelled at reverse engineering the DLLs under guidance and pinpointing the exact bug, which significantly reduced the research time. We reported this vulnerability to Microsoft on October 6, 2026 but we never received a response to that MSRC report. The fix shipped on October 13, 2026 update, so we can’t say whether our report had anything to do with it.

We independently identified a similar vulnerability in SMB, and Microsoft patched it quietly in September 2026. Another researcher also noticed that silent patch and published a blog, Defeating Enforced SMB Signing. This blog post describes an LDAP variant that we found in September 2026.

Background: Why Signing Was Supposed to Stop NTLM Relay

NTLM relay attacks used to be straightforward: an attacker positioned between a client and server could relay the NTLM authentication exchange and authenticate to the server as the client. 

Microsoft introduced NTLMv2 to strengthen NTLMv1’s authentication and session security. NTLMv2 supports signing to protect message integrity and sealing to encrypt messages. Later, Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) added channel and service binding to help prevent relay attacks. 

Since then NTLM relay attacks have become more complicated, especially cross-protocol relaying. Windows Server 2025 raises the baseline further. SMB signing is now required by default for outbound connections, and new Active Directory deployments require LDAP signing by default. Relaying from SMB to LDAP is still harder because the two protocols handle signing differently. SMB negotiates signing on its own, but the Windows SMB client still sets the signing flag in its NTLM messages. LDAP has no separate negotiation, so it relies on NTLM to decide whether signing is used. When we relay that SMB authentication to LDAP, the DC honors the flag and expects every message after the bind to be signed.

The ordinary relay was blocked when SMB or LDAP required signing because we did not know the victim’s exported session key. LDAP over TLS was blocked when channel binding was required. This is where relaying from HTTP became easier because HTTP does not provide per-message signing and it doesn’t even negotiate a session key; when HTTPS is used, TLS provides transport integrity instead. As a result, coercing a victim through WebClient generally produces an NTLM exchange that is easier to relay and never negotiates signing. WebDAV also allows us to capture that authentication on an external host and route it back into the target environment through attacker-controlled infrastructure. Elad Shamir calls this technique “There and Back Again,” and Logan Goins demonstrates the complete workflow in this blog post.

NTLMv2 Basics: Session Keys, Signing, and the MIC

We will briefly cover NTLMv2 terms so we are all on the same page when these terms come up later. During normal NTLMv2 authentication, the client uses its NT hash, uppercased username and domain name to derive the ResponseKeyNT through the NTOWFv2 function. It then builds the NTLMv2_CLIENT_CHALLENGE structure, which contains a timestamp, a client challenge, and AV pairs. The client then computes the NTProofStr by running HMAC-MD5 over the server challenge and the NTLMv2_CLIENT_CHALLENGE structure using the ResponseKeyNT as the key. The final NTLMv2 response is the concatenation of the NTProofStr and the NTLMv2_CLIENT_CHALLENGE structure. So the AV pairs are protected by the NTProofStr, and changing them would invalidate that proof. 

For NTLMv2, the client computes a SessionBaseKey by running HMAC-MD5 over the NTProofStr using the ResponseKeyNT as the key. The KeyExchangeKey is the same as SessionBaseKey and we will refer to it as the SessionBaseKey in this blog post. When key exchange is negotiated for signing or sealing (encryption), the client generates a random 16-byte ExportedSessionKey and encrypts it with RC4 using the SessionBaseKey. That encrypted key is included in the AUTHENTICATE message. The ExportedSessionKey is used as input to derive signing and sealing keys by both LDAP and SMB protocols, but each protocol derives its own signing and sealing keys differently. 

Another important concept is the Message Integrity Code (MIC). The MIC protects the entire NTLM exchange from tampering. The MsvAvFlags AV pair in the AUTHENTICATE message tells the server that a MIC is present. The client computes the MIC over all three NTLM messages using the ExportedSessionKey, so any modification to any of those messages invalidates the MIC, resulting in the server rejecting authentication.

Typically, if a target DC requires LDAP signing, we cannot perform NTLM relay against LDAP because we don’t know the victim’s (client’s) session key. The signing requirement is negotiated during the SASL bind and protects the LDAP messages sent after authentication, not just subsequent Bind requests. Without the session key, we cannot generate valid signatures for LDAP messages.

The problem arises when the LDAP server honors that request even though the DC does not require signing for LDAP. So we can’t relay SMB to LDAP because LDAP enforces the signing the victim requested. This applies to typical NTLMv2 exchanges, with exceptions such as legacy NTLMv1 or vulnerable implementations.

LDAP also supports channel binding when authentication happens over LDAPS (with TLS). Signing protects the LDAP messages, while channel binding ties the authentication to the TLS channel. Channel binding only applies to LDAPS, and it doesn’t apply to LDAP.

Traditionally, we could bypass LDAP signing and channel binding if only one protection is enforced. If LDAP signing is enforced but channel binding is not, we can target LDAPS, and since TLS traffic is signed, it satisfies the DC’s signing requirements. If channel binding is enforced but LDAP signing is not required, we can instead target LDAP, where there is no TLS channel to bind the authentication to. After authentication, we may upgrade that connection with StartTLS because TLS is established after the bind, and channel binding was not checked during that authentication exchange. The benefit of using StartTLS is that it allows performing sensitive operations such as password changes or resets, assuming the relayed account has the necessary permissions.

With LDAP signing required and channel binding set to Always, NTLM relay to LDAP should be impossible. However, as we’ll see, the word itself says “I’m possible”.

So the signing flag that used to be the problem is what makes this technique work.

Before going further, we need to explain SASL. SASL (Simple Authentication and Security Layer) is a framework that lets a protocol like LDAP plug in an authentication mechanism, such as NTLM or Kerberos, and optionally add a layer that signs and encrypts every message after the bind. Once that layer is on, LDAP sends a SASL record, which is a length-prefixed block that is signed (and optionally sealed) as one unit and can hold more than one LDAP message. This does not give us the victim’s session key (Y). If we send another SASL record signed with X, the DC rejects it because the connection now requires Y’s session key. The issue is what happens inside the SASL record we already sent. Its contents pass the signature check under our original security context (X), but the modification runs under Y’s identity after the bind completes.

This technique bypasses LDAP signing, not channel binding. Channel binding only applies to LDAPS, because it ties authentication to the TLS channel, and LDAP (389/TCP) has no TLS channel to bind to. The domain controller we tested against had both LDAP signing and channel binding enforced, and the attack still worked over 389/TCP. The attack sequence follows:

  1. The attacker coerces the victim into authenticating over SMB
  2. The victim’s SMB client connects to the attacker and begins session setup
  3. The attacker establishes a signed LDAP session through GSS-SPNEGO using either valid domain credentials or, where accepted, anonymous NTLM SASL authentication, with a session key known to the attacker
  4. The victim’s SMB client sends an NTLM NEGOTIATE message
  5. The attacker carries that message in a GSS-SPNEGO SASL BindRequest over the existing protected LDAP connection
  6. The target returns an NTLM CHALLENGE message through GSS-SPNEGO, protected by the existing LDAP session
  7. The attacker forwards the NTLM CHALLENGE message to the victim’s SMB client
  8. The victim’s SMB client returns the final SPNEGO response carrying the NTLM AUTHENTICATE message
  9. The attacker sends a GSS-SPNEGO BindRequest carrying that response, followed by a separate LDAP ModifyRequest, together in one SASL record signed using the attacker’s original LDAP session key

Walkthrough: Relaying SMB to LDAP With Signing Required

Now let’s dive deeper into this vulnerability and analyze how it works and what made it possible.

In this example, we have three hosts. The domain controller is LYS-DC (10.4.10.47), the attacker is a Kali host (10.4.10.233), and the victim is LYS-SRV22 (10.4.10.48). The DC was running build 26100.33451 (KB5129235, the September 2026 cumulative update) before the October 2026 update (KB5126646, build 26100.33648) introduced the fix.

First, we coerce the victim into connecting to the attacker host. The victim opens an SMB connection and sends an SMB NEGOTIATE request, which agrees on the SMB dialect and lists the security mechanisms it supports. We don’t respond yet. The TCP layer acknowledges the packet, but the relay holds the victim at this point until our LDAP connection is ready.

In frame 12, we bind to the DC over LDAP as LYS\LYS.LOW and keep the session key from that authentication. Every LDAP message after the bind has to be signed with this key, and since we authenticated as LYS.LOW we know it.

The session key shown above is in encrypted format so we can’t directly use it.

In frame 28, we resume the victim’s SMB connection and the victim (LYS\LYS-SRV22$) sends us its NTLM NEGOTIATE message. As with any Windows SMB client, the NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_SIGN flag is set, as you can see in the screenshot below. 

In frame 29, we relay that NTLM NEGOTIATE message to the DC inside a Bind request. Because the connection is already signed, the Bind travels as a SASL-protected message signed and sealed with LYS.LOW’s session key. That is why the payload looks encrypted in the screenshot. We wrote a small Wireshark plugin that decrypts these messages with the LYS.LOW key so we can see what is being sent, which we will show later.

In frames 30 to 33, we finish the NTLM exchange. The DC sends a NTLM CHALLENGE message to us, we forward it to Y (LYS\LYS-SRV22$) over SMB, and Y answers with its NTLM AUTHENTICATE message. We only pass the messages between Y and the DC. We never learn Y’s password or session key.

Frame 34 is where the attack happens. Instead of sending Y’s AUTHENTICATE message on its own, we put two LDAP messages into one SASL record and sign it with X’s session key. The first is a BindRequest carrying Y’s AUTHENTICATE message. The second is a ModifyRequest that writes msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on LYS-SRV22$, with a security descriptor that grants an account we control (HXRBOX2$). The DC verifies the signature on the SASL record once, using X’s key. It then completes the bind as Y and processes the ModifyRequest as Y too. So the whole resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD) attack happens in one signed SASL record.

Root Cause: Inside LDAP_CONN::ProcessRequestEx

To uncover what happens on the domain controller side, the core of the vulnerability lives inside the LDAP_CONN::ProcessRequestEx function. This function runs for every LDAP request received on a connection. It first checks whether signing was negotiated on the connection, and if it was, it expects the message to be signed with the negotiated signing key. It verifies this by calling LDAP_REQUEST::DecryptSignedOrSealedMessage, which checks the SASL record against the key of the connection’s current security context. One thing to note here is that signing only starts after the NTLM authentication exchange is completed. Since we were the ones who authenticated on this connection, we already possess the session key at this point. So when we perform the reauthentication, we continue the open SMB connection with the victim and relay the NTLM messages back and forth with the DC. Once we have the victim’s final NTLM AUTHENTICATE message, we relay it in a Bind request together with our own LDAP operation, both in the same SASL record signed with our key.

Next, ProcessRequestEx calls the LDAP_CONN::BindRequest function, where the victim’s identity is validated. Within that function, it later calls LDAP_CONN::MoveSecurityContext, LDAP_CONN::InstallNewSecurityContext, and LDAP_CONN::SetSecurityContextAtts,  which switch the connection’s authorization to the victim’s.

After LDAP_CONN::BindRequest returns, there is still data left in the SASL record, so ProcessRequestEx processes the next message and calls the LDAP_CONN::ModifyRequest function. This is where our stacked LDAP operation goes, the one we wanted to perform with the victim’s authorization. Since the authorization context was already switched to the victim during the Bind, the Modify executes as the victim. So basically there is no check that notices the identity changed partway through the SASL record, or that anything after the reauthentication should be verified with the new signing key, which only the victim holds. The SASL record gets verified just once, with the session key that we control, and never again after that.

How Microsoft Patched the LDAP Signing Bypass

Microsoft fixed this issue by giving every LDAP connection a counter that tracks its identity. So first it captures a baseline. Whenever new client data arrives, LDAP_REQUEST::ReceivedClientData reads the connection’s current identity counter and saves a copy of it inside the request itself. This is like a snapshot of which identity the connection was authenticated as when that data came in. Nothing is validated or blocked at this point – it’s just recorded.

That counter only increments when the connection’s identity actually changes, and that is exactly what our relayed Bind does. When the Bind completes, LDAP_CONN::SetSecurityContextAtts installs the victim’s security context and increments the same counter, which leaves a trace that the switch happened.

Later, after the Bind in that request has switched the connection over to the victim, the counter on the connection has increased, but the copy saved in the request hasn’t. So when ProcessRequestEx compares the two, and they don’t match, it knows the identity changed partway through the SASL record. It then throws away the rest of the SASL record, which means our stacked Modify never runs.

Proof of Concept: Running the Attack With ntlmrelayx

To test out the above described attack, we are releasing “The LDAP Switcheroo” that wraps ntlmrelayx.py with our custom modifications to make this attack work.

https://github.com/grayhatkiller/switcheroo  

How to Defend Against NTLM Relay to LDAP

Signing alone was never a complete defense against NTLM relay. To close the gap this research exposed:

  • Patch domain controllers first. Install the October 2026 cumulative update (KB5126646) on every domain controller. This fixes the LDAP signing bypass.
  • Patch for the SMB fix. Install the September 2026 update (KB5122882) on every server to close the SMB signing bypass.
  • Enforce LDAP signing and channel binding together. Either one on its own leaves a path open. With both enforced, an attacker can’t switch to LDAPS or plain LDAP to get around the one that’s missing.
  • Restrict LDAP on 389/TCP where you can. The bypass ran over 389/TCP. If 389/TCP is blocked then this technique fails.
  • Reduce NTLM wherever possible. Every NTLM authentication you remove is one less thing an attacker can relay.

The last two recommendations are more complicated and may be aspirational goals for some organizations, because legacy applications often depend on plain LDAP and NTLM.

Acknowledgements, Prior Work, and References
  • Duane Michael: For helping me along the way and supporting this side quest from my original research. At this point, he was the co-author of this blog.
  • Elad Shamir: You can’t write an NTLM relay blog without Elad. As always, Elad’s guidance is what pushed me to go after LDAP after finding the SMB signing bypass.
  • Lydéric Lefebvre: For publishing the SMB signing bypass: https://blackfield.ch/blog/defeating-enforced-smb-signing/
  • Elad Shamir, The Renaissance of NTLM Relay Attacks, https://specterops.io/blog/2025/04/08/the-renaissance-of-ntlm-relay-attacks-everything-you-need-to-know/
  • Hackndo, NTLM Relay, https://en.hackndo.com/ntlm-relay/
  • MS-NLMP (NTLM), Microsoft, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/openspecs/windows_protocols/ms-nlmp/b38c36ed-2804-4868-a9ff-8dd3182128e4
  • RFC-4422 (SASL), https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4422/
  • LDAP Signing, Microsoft, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/ldap-signing
  • LDAP Channel Binding, Microsoft, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/ldap-channel-binding
  • ntlmrelayx, Fortra, https://github.com/fortra/impacket/blob/master/examples/ntlmrelayx.py
Frequently Asked Questions What is the LDAP signing bypass? 

It is an NTLM relay technique that worked against domain controllers even when LDAP signing was required. An attacker opens a signed LDAP connection with a session key they know, relays a victim’s NTLM authentication over that connection, and slips a malicious LDAP operation into the same signed message. The domain controller checks the signature with the attacker’s key, then runs the operation with the victim’s privileges.

Is LDAP signing enough to stop NTLM relay attacks? 

Not on its own. Before the October 2026 update, every Windows Server 2022 and Windows Server 2025 domain controller we tested accepted relayed NTLM authentication with LDAP signing required. Install the update, enforce LDAP signing and channel binding together, and reduce NTLM wherever you can.

Does the LDAP signing bypass work against LDAPS? 

The technique targets LDAP on 389/TCP. If 389/TCP is blocked then this technique will not work against LDAPS (636/TCP).

Which Windows Server versions were vulnerable? 

We tested against Server 2016 domain controller and above, and it was vulnerable until the October 2026 cumulative update.

Does the attacker need domain credentials? 

Not necessarily. The attacker needs a signed LDAP session with a session key they know. That can come from valid domain account credentials or, where the domain controller accepts it, an anonymous LDAP connection. The attacker also needs to coerce a victim into authenticating to them.

What can an attacker do with the LDAP signing bypass? 

The attacker can make a domain controller authenticate to the attacker and relay the authentication to another domain controller to compromise the domain instantly. In our example, we relayed a server’s computer account and wrote msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on that server to set up resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD).

Has Microsoft patched the LDAP signing bypass? 

Yes. We reported it to Microsoft on October 6, 2026, and Microsoft independently shipped a fix on October 13, 2026 (KB5126646). The patch tracks each LDAP connection’s identity with a counter. If the identity changes partway through a signed SASL record, the domain controller discards the rest of that SASL record, so the stacked operation never runs. Microsoft fixed the related SMB issue in September 2026.

First and foremost, to better understand NTLM and relay attacks in detail please read the following blogs as this blog post will not cover the basics of it:

  • The Renaissance of NTLM Relay Attacks: Everything You Need to Know
  • NTLM Relay

We independently identified the similar vulnerability in SMB as well. That vulnerability was patched in September 2026. Another researcher also identified this silent patch and published a blog here:

  • Defeating Enforced SMB Signing

items.title: WhatsApp May Stop Working Without Registered SIM Under New Rules
items.summary: WhatsApp users in India may face access issues without a registered SIM under new government rules expected to take effect on January 1, 2027. Messaging platforms reportedly have until December 31, 2026, to comply. The change could affect people using accounts on secondary phones, tablets, and devices without an active registered SIM. The requirement, known as SIM-binding , means an account must remain connected to the active SIM associated with its registered mobile number. Unlike a one-time text verification code, this creates an ongoing link between the messaging service and the SIM installed in the device. WhatsApp Stops Working Without SIM The Department of Telecommunications issued its original directions on November 28, 2025, under the Telecom Cyber Security Rules, 2024, as amended. Its official explanation names WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, Snapchat, Arattai, ShareChat, Josh and JioChat among the covered services. Messaging accounts can still work after the associated SIM is removed or deactivated. DoT says criminals exploit this gap to operate accounts remotely, including from outside India, while using Indian numbers for phishing , investment fraud and fake government calls. The government cited cyber-fraud losses exceeding ₹22,800 crore in 2024. The directions aim to make those accounts easier to trace by requiring continued access to the registered SIM. However, the policy should not be mistaken for a guarantee that it will prevent every scam or account takeover. The original order required web sessions to log out at least every six hours. However, recent reporting says this blanket requirement has been replaced with risk-based logouts. According to CNBC-TV18 , WhatsApp sessions may end when suspicious activity is detected, potentially disrupting users who remove, deactivate, or switch their registered SIM cards while traveling. Rules for tablets, companion phones and other linked devices will depend on each platform’s implementation. DoT’s original explanation says roaming is unaffected when the registered SIM remains in the handset. SIM binding addresses number misuse, but device-linking scams remain a separate concern. Cybersecurity News previously reported on WhatsApp GhostPairing attacks , where victims approve an attacker’s linked device. Russian-linked phishing campaigns that abuse legitimate WhatsApp linking requests. These attacks show why controlling a phone number alone doesn’t eliminate every account-security risk. Users should review WhatsApp’s Linked Devices section and remove unfamiliar sessions. January 1 should be treated as the expected rollout date, not proof that every unsupported setup will stop working simultaneously. Actual disruption will depend on platform readiness and the final changes each service introduces. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: Critical Okta Access Gateway Flaw Lets Attackers With Admin Access Execute System Commands
items.summary: Okta has disclosed a critical security flaw in Okta Access Gateway that lets an authenticated administrator run system commands through the appliance’s Admin Console. Tracked as CVE-2026-115547, the vulnerability affects versions before 2026.10.2 and has a CVSS v3.1 score of 9.1, according to the October 22, 2026 advisory. The issue involves weak input validation when the Admin Console processes specially formatted configuration values. An attacker with administrative access can use those values to trigger command execution under the OAG service account. The disclosure does not describe an unauthenticated attack. The flaw sits where administrative configuration input reaches processing functions inside the gateway. Instead of treating the supplied values strictly as configuration data, the affected software can allow crafted input to lead to system command execution. Okta Access Gateway Flaw Okta classifies the issue under CWE-94, improper control of code generation, and CWE-20, improper input validation. The required access is an important limit. An attacker must first gain administrative access to the OAG Admin Console. A regular application account alone does not meet the stated conditions, and the advisory does not identify an authentication bypass that removes this requirement. Successful exploitation runs commands with the permissions of the OAG service account. That is not the same as confirmed root access. The potential damage depends on what that account can read, change, or run, making its actual permissions important when assessing exposure. The supplied CVSS v3.1 vector describes a network attack with low complexity, high required privileges, and no user interaction. It also assigns high impact to confidentiality, integrity, and availability, with changed scope. Organizations running Okta Access Gateway versions before 2026.10.2 should upgrade to version 2026.10.2 or later. The supplied disclosure identifies that release as the fix and does not provide a separate workaround. The patch follows earlier Okta Access Gateway and Auth0 security fixes covering authorization bypass, SQL injection, and stored cross-site scripting. Those September issues had different requirements and fixes, so the earlier Access Gateway 2026.9.1 update does not meet this advisory’s minimum patched version. Administrators should also review who can reach the management console and investigate unexpected configuration changes. Previous reporting on Okta administrator session abuse at 1Password shows why protecting privileged sessions matters, although that incident is separate from this vulnerability. The supplied advisory does not report active exploitation, publish attack payloads, or identify the affected configuration field. Those gaps do not prove exploitation is impossible. Teams should prioritize the appliance upgrade and check Okta’s security advisory portal for further guidance as details become available. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: HPE Warns Critical Aruba Networking Flaws Could Let Hackers Take Complete Control of Devices
items.summary: Hewlett Packard Enterprise has released security patches for multiple vulnerabilities in Aruba Networking wireless software that could let attackers take complete control of affected devices. The flaws affect AOS-8 and AOS-10 deployments across Mobility Conductors, Controllers, Gateways, and access points. Several allow attacks without a valid login, making prompt patching a priority for network administrators. HPE Warns Aruba Networking Flaws HPE’s October 22 security bulletin, HPESBNW05162, describes authentication bypass, command injection, SQL injection, and buffer overflow flaws. Eight CVE entries carry the maximum CVSS severity score of 10.0. Successful attacks could expose sensitive data, change device settings, or run commands with high system privileges. Among the most serious issues, CVE-2026-79850 lets an attacker bypass AOS-8 authentication without credentials and execute commands as root, giving them full control of the underlying operating system. CVE-2026-79855 separately affects the AOS-8 SSH service and can grant unauthenticated administrative access. AOS-10 also contains critical weaknesses. CVE-2026-79845 affects PAPI, Aruba’s access point management protocol, and could let attackers bypass login checks, change configurations, and access sensitive information. CVE-2026-79847 and CVE-2026-79851 involve buffer overflows that could allow malicious code to run with privileged permissions. Other flaws expose services reached through PAPI traffic. Attackers can trigger CVE-2026-79860 by sending specially crafted packets to UDP port 8211 on affected AOS-8 systems. HPE also lists SQL injection flaws that could extend beyond database access and allow command execution on the operating system. The attack conditions vary. Some vulnerabilities can be reached remotely, while others require an attacker on an adjacent network or physical access. Certain command execution flaws also depend on conditions outside the attacker’s control. Not every listed issue provides the same route to device takeover. Cybersecurity News previously reported on Aruba access point command injection vulnerabilities and AOS controller and gateway security flaws . Those earlier reports concern separate disclosures, not the newly released fixes. The affected releases include AOS-10.8.1.1, AOS-10.7.2.6, and AOS-10.4.1.13 and earlier versions within their respective branches. AOS-8.13.3.0 and AOS-8.10.0.23 and earlier releases in those branches are also affected. Compatible hardware and virtual deployments fall within scope, even when individual models are absent from the bulletin’s example list. HPE recommends upgrading to AOS-10.8.1.2, AOS-10.7.2.7, AOS-10.4.1.14, AOS-8.13.3.1, or AOS-8.10.0.24, depending on the installed branch. Later releases in those branches also contain the fixes. Updates are available through the HPE Networking Support Portal. Until updates are deployed, HPE recommends restricting command line and web management interfaces to a dedicated network segment or VLAN, backed by firewall rules. Administrators should also enable controls that track and log user activity. These measures reduce exposure but do not replace installing the patches. HPE said it knew of no public discussion or exploit code targeting these vulnerabilities when the advisory was released. That statement does not establish whether attacks have occurred. Older software beyond maintenance or support should not be assumed safe, and HPE urges customers to move to supported releases. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: PHP2Shell Operational Guidance
items.summary: First published on 22 October 2026, last updated on 23 October 2026 at 16:45 CEST. This public operational guidance is provided to customers and published for the benefit of the wider community. TLP:AMBER information is disclosed through regular channels. TL;DR What: Two critical PHP vulnerabilities where disclosed, CVE-2026-109618 (RCE via OOM corruption) and CVE-2026-109619 (RCE via stale global state), collectively PHP2Shell . Both rated CVSS v4.0 9.2 (Critical). A third, lower-risk CVE (CVE-2026-115560) was disclosed on 23 October and will ship in the regular release cycle. Who’s affected: Any PHP installation serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. Particular attention for Apache mod_php, where unauthenticated exploitation has been demonstrated. Exploitation status: Active exploitation attempts observed by Amazon, Cloudflare, WatchTowr, and NVISO. No confirmed successful compromises or reliable public exploit yet, but PoC claims are circulating. What to do: Patch to PHP 8.5.12 / 8.4.27 / 8.3.36 / 8.2.35 immediately, prioritising internet-facing systems. Where patching is delayed, apply PHP’s vulnerability-specific mitigations (full details below). Verify that web-server processes are actually using the patched runtime. What happened? On 20 October 2026, information about two critical vulnerabilities in PHP surfaced publicly ahead of their planned coordinated disclosure. The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, have each received a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 (Critical). In response, the PHP security team announced an emergency security release scheduled for 21 October 2026 at 14:00 UTC (16:00 CEST), with the possibility of an earlier release if technical details become public or active exploitation is detected. Both vulnerabilities are reported to potentially allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Successful exploitation could enable a remote attacker to execute malicious code on a vulnerable server, potentially compromising the applications and data hosted on it. On 21 October 2026 at 13:30 UTC (15:30 CEST), the PHP security team released emergency patches addressing both vulnerabilities. The following are the minimum fixed upstream PHP versions: PHP branch Fixed version PHP 8.5 8.5.12 PHP 8.4 8.4.27 PHP 8.3 8.3.36 PHP 8.2 8.2.35 PHP 8.1 and older No standard upstream release; vendor backports or migration required On 23 October 2026, the PHP security team released an informational advisory about another vulnerability: CVE-2026-115560. This vulnerability requires specific combinations of configuration and application code. Because the PHP security team assesses the exploitation of this vulnerability as unlikely, the patch will be released in the regular release cycle, rather than an emergency patch like CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Why should organisations be concerned? PHP is one of the most widely used server-side programming languages for web development. It underpins many websites, content management systems (CMS), e-commerce platforms, customer portals, and business applications. Popular platforms such as WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento rely on PHP to execute application logic. Data theft: Sensitive information, application secrets, credentials, or customer data accessible to that process could be exposed. Website compromise: Attackers can modify application content, deploy malicious scripts, or establish persistence through webshells. Operational disruption: Compromised applications could be taken offline, manipulated, or used to facilitate further attacks. Lateral movement: A compromised server could provide an initial foothold for attacks against other connected systems. What do we know about these vulnerabilities? This removes the controllable PHP memory limit failure, but an underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path. Set a low post_max_size . For applications that do not require file uploads, set post_max_size = 8M . If file uploads are necessary, set post_max_size = 32M . Keep upload_max_filesize below post_max_size . Consider enforcing limits at the web server or proxy level for decoded request size, input field count, multipart part count, header count, and nesting depth. These limits must also cover requests without a usable Content-Length . Use a container or cgroup limit as an availability boundary, preferably with a policy that kills only the affected worker. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA , as these can cause the vulnerable allocation failure. RCE via stale global state (CVE-2026-109619): Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker. Use php.ini , an FPM pool or server configuration that applies before request parsing. Do not rely on ini_set() or FPM .user.ini . This blocks the confirmed session paths but not other variants. On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed fatal backtrace path only. Remove invalid or deprecated settings applied per request that emit diagnostics before initialization. Hiding diagnostics with error_reporting , display_errors or @ does not help. Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and execution timeouts, including failures in callbacks, upload or import processing and cleanup. RCE (CVE-2026-115560) Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker. As a general recommendation, the PHP team advises updating PHP instances to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35. Developing a reliable exploit is difficult, as it requires bypassing Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) while simultaneously exploiting the vulnerability to achieve stable code execution. Organisations should inventory internet-facing websites, internal applications, hosting environments, containers, and third-party products relying on PHP. For each installation, identify the PHP version, hosting platform, application owner, business criticality, and external accessibility. Do not overlook legacy applications or PHP runtimes bundled with vendor-managed software. Depending on business requirements, this may involve: Restricting access through VPNs, network allowlists, or authenticated gateways. Temporarily disabling non-essential internet-facing PHP services. Segmenting web servers from sensitive internal environments. Reviewing outbound connectivity and limiting unnecessary network access. Applying validated vendor-provided protections or Web Application Firewall rules where available. A Web Application Firewall is not a replacement for patching, especially when the vulnerabilities’ technical characteristics have not been fully established. CERT-EU has recommended considering isolation of internet-facing applications where immediate patching cannot be performed. Prepare for emergency patch deployment The PHP security team released emergency security updates on 21 October 2026 at 13:30 UTC. Organisations should deploy them promptly by identifying responsible system owners, following standard update procedures, arranging maintenance windows, and establishing appropriate rollback plans. When applying the releases: Confirm the affected and fixed PHP versions. Apply the relevant security updates, prioritising externally accessible systems. Coordinate with managed hosting providers and software vendors where PHP is not directly administered. Validate application functionality after updating. Verify that production web-server processes are using the patched PHP runtime. It is important to note that updating a content management system or web application does not necessarily update the underlying PHP installation. Organisations using end-of-life PHP branches should evaluate migration to supported versions or obtain confirmation of vendor-maintained security backports. Strengthen detection and monitoring Security Operations Centres should increase monitoring of PHP-based infrastructure, particularly for unexpected behaviour originating from web-server processes. Useful detection opportunities include: Suspicious process execution : Monitor for PHP or web-server processes such as php-fpm , php-cgi , apache2 , or httpd launching unexpected command interpreters, including sh , bash , or PowerShell . Potential payload retrieval: Investigate unexpected execution of download utilities such as curl or wget by web-server processes, especially when followed by script execution. Suspicious web activity : Review HTTP access logs, reverse-proxy telemetry, and WAF events for unusual request patterns, unexpected requests to PHP endpoints, or significant increases in server errors. Security teams should confirm that affected systems have been successfully updated, necessary services have restarted, and no vulnerable runtime instances remain active. Additional attention should be given to load-balanced environments, containers, staging environments, and systems maintained by third-party providers.
