items.summary_html:
First published on 22 October 2026, last updated on 23 October 2026 at 16:45 CEST. This public operational guidance is provided to customers and published for the benefit of the wider community. TLP:AMBER information is disclosed through regular channels.

TL;DR

  • What: Two critical PHP vulnerabilities where disclosed, CVE-2026-109618 (RCE via OOM corruption) and CVE-2026-109619 (RCE via stale global state), collectively PHP2Shell. Both rated CVSS v4.0 9.2 (Critical). A third, lower-risk CVE (CVE-2026-115560) was disclosed on 23 October and will ship in the regular release cycle.
  • Who’s affected: Any PHP installation serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. Particular attention for Apache mod_php, where unauthenticated exploitation has been demonstrated.
  • Exploitation status: Active exploitation attempts observed by Amazon, Cloudflare, WatchTowr, and NVISO. No confirmed successful compromises or reliable public exploit yet, but PoC claims are circulating.
  • What to do: Patch to PHP 8.5.12 / 8.4.27 / 8.3.36 / 8.2.35 immediately, prioritising internet-facing systems. Where patching is delayed, apply PHP’s vulnerability-specific mitigations (full details below). Verify that web-server processes are actually using the patched runtime.
What happened?

On 20 October 2026, information about two critical vulnerabilities in PHP surfaced publicly ahead of their planned coordinated disclosure. The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, have each received a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 (Critical).

In response, the PHP security team announced an emergency security release scheduled for 21 October 2026 at 14:00 UTC (16:00 CEST), with the possibility of an earlier release if technical details become public or active exploitation is detected.

Both vulnerabilities are reported to potentially allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Successful exploitation could enable a remote attacker to execute malicious code on a vulnerable server, potentially compromising the applications and data hosted on it.

On 21 October 2026 at 13:30 UTC (15:30 CEST), the PHP security team released emergency patches addressing both vulnerabilities.

The following are the minimum fixed upstream PHP versions:

PHP branchFixed versionPHP 8.58.5.12PHP 8.48.4.27PHP 8.38.3.36PHP 8.28.2.35PHP 8.1 and olderNo standard upstream release; vendor backports or migration required

On 23 October 2026, the PHP security team released an informational advisory about another vulnerability: CVE-2026-115560. This vulnerability requires specific combinations of configuration and application code. Because the PHP security team assesses the exploitation of this vulnerability as unlikely, the patch will be released in the regular release cycle, rather than an emergency patch like CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

Why should organisations be concerned?

PHP is one of the most widely used server-side programming languages for web development. It underpins many websites, content management systems (CMS), e-commerce platforms, customer portals, and business applications.

Popular platforms such as WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento rely on PHP to execute application logic. Unlike a vulnerability affecting a specific plugin or individual web application, a vulnerability in PHP
itself may affect multiple applications that rely on the same underlying runtime. This makes the potential attack surface particularly broad.

Organisations may also be running PHP without necessarily being aware of it. PHP runtimes can be embedded in legacy applications, hosting environments, internal management portals, containers, and third-party software.

The potential consequences of successful remote code execution include:

  • Unauthorised server access: Attackers may execute commands within the security context of the affected PHP process.
  • Data theft: Sensitive information, application secrets, credentials, or customer data accessible to that process could be exposed.
  • Website compromise: Attackers can modify application content, deploy malicious scripts, or establish persistence through webshells.
  • Operational disruption: Compromised applications could be taken offline, manipulated, or used to facilitate further attacks.
  • Lateral movement: A compromised server could provide an initial foothold for attacks against other connected systems.
What do we know about these vulnerabilities?

Three vulnerabilities have been associated with the PHP2Shell disclosure:

IdentifierSeverityImpactCVE-2026-109618CVSS v4.0 9.2 – CriticalRCE via OOM corruptionCVE-2026-109619CVSS v4.0 9.2 – CriticalRCE via stale global stateCVE-2026-115560UnknownRCE

The PHP team provided the following mitigation steps:

If you cannot update immediately: while only an update is a complete solution, the following
measures reduce exposure to specific attack paths but do not make an installation safe.

  • RCE via OOM corruption (CVE-2026-109618):
    • Set memory_limit=-1, preferably in a way applications cannot override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration, and check that no pool, directory or application setting puts a finite limit back. This removes the controllable PHP memory limit failure, but an underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable
      path.
    • Set a low post_max_size. For applications that do not require file uploads, set post_max_size = 8M. If file uploads are necessary, set post_max_size = 32M. Keep upload_max_filesize below post_max_size. Consider enforcing limits at the web server or proxy level for decoded request size, input field count, multipart part count, header count, and nesting depth. These limits must also cover requests without a usable Content-Length.
    • Use a container or cgroup limit as an availability boundary, preferably with a policy that kills only the affected worker. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, as these can cause the vulnerable allocation failure.
  • RCE via stale global state (CVE-2026-109619):
    • Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker. Use php.ini, an FPM pool or server configuration that applies before request parsing. Do not rely on ini_set() or FPM .user.ini. This blocks the confirmed session paths but not other variants.
    • On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed fatal backtrace path only.
    • Remove invalid or deprecated settings applied per request that emit diagnostics before initialization. Hiding diagnostics with error_reporting, display_errors or @ does not help.
    • Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and execution timeouts, including failures in callbacks,
      upload or import processing and cleanup.
  • RCE (CVE-2026-115560)
    • Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker.

As a general recommendation, the PHP team advises updating PHP instances to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27,
8.3.36 or 8.2.35.

Understanding the risk

Remote code execution vulnerabilities allow an attacker, under certain conditions, to cause a vulnerable application or software component to execute code that the attacker controls. Successful remote code execution can result in defacement, database exfiltration, deployment of webshells or malware, and full compromise of the hosted application.

Has PHP2Shell been exploited in the wild?

As of 23 October 2026, there are active PHP2Shell exploitation attempts without evidence of successful compromise.

On 21 October 2026, Amazon’s security team reported detecting PHP2Shell exploitation attempts in its MadPot honeypot infrastructure and explicitly stated “PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild”.

Amazon reported on:

  • 17 October 2026: First identified exploitation attempt, four days before public disclosure.
  • 21 October, 02:00–08:00 UTC: Additional exploitation attempts from multiple anonymised sources.
  • 21 October, after patch publication: Additional PoCs appeared and were used against AWS sensors almost immediately.

Cloudflare confirms that it observed malicious traffic targeting its customers but did not provide proof that customer systems were compromised.

NVISO confirms network-wide attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities, without success so far and partially aligning with Sophos observations. We have also observed some attempts that crash the server.

WatchTowr also confirms exploitation attempts of both vulnerabilities in the wild.

The company VulnCheck claims to have a working exploit for CVE-2026-109618, but we have not been able to confirm it.

There are currently at least 748 public GitHub repositories related to PHP2Shell, some with more than a thousand stars. However, no publicly available exploit has yet been confirmed to reliably achieve full exploitation of the vulnerabilities.

Developing a reliable exploit is difficult, as it requires bypassing Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) while simultaneously exploiting the vulnerability to achieve stable code execution. Over time, crafting an exploit and sharing it publicly for free demands a growing investment of time and money, reducing the incentive to do so.

The absence of a publicly available exploit does not mean no working exploit exists. Researchers involved in the coordinated disclosure of the vulnerabilities have one, and it is plausible that threat actors have developed their own, even though no successful compromise has been reported so far.

How can organisations protect themselves?

NVISO recommends a risk-based response, starting with internet-facing and business-critical PHP deployments.

Identify potentially affected systems

The priority is understanding where PHP is deployed. Organisations should inventory internet-facing websites, internal applications, hosting environments, containers, and third-party products relying on PHP. For each installation, identify the PHP version, hosting platform, application owner, business criticality, and external accessibility. Do not overlook legacy applications or PHP runtimes bundled with vendor-managed software.

Reduce exposure until patches are deployed

Where immediate remediation is not possible, organisations should consider restricting access to high risk PHP applications. Depending on business requirements, this may involve:

  • Restricting access through VPNs, network allowlists, or authenticated gateways.
  • Temporarily disabling non-essential internet-facing PHP services.
  • Segmenting web servers from sensitive internal environments.
  • Reviewing outbound connectivity and limiting unnecessary network access.
  • Applying validated vendor-provided protections or Web Application Firewall rules where
    available.
  • A Web Application Firewall is not a replacement for patching, especially when the vulnerabilities’ technical characteristics have not been fully established.

CERT-EU has recommended considering isolation of internet-facing applications where immediate patching cannot be performed.

Prepare for emergency patch deployment

The PHP security team released emergency security updates on 21 October 2026 at 13:30 UTC. Organisations should deploy them promptly by identifying responsible system owners, following standard update procedures, arranging maintenance windows, and establishing appropriate rollback plans. When applying the releases:

  • Confirm the affected and fixed PHP versions.
  • Apply the relevant security updates, prioritising externally accessible systems.
  • Coordinate with managed hosting providers and software vendors where PHP is not directly
    administered.
  • Validate application functionality after updating.
  • Verify that production web-server processes are using the patched PHP runtime.

It is important to note that updating a content management system or web application does not
necessarily update the underlying PHP installation.
Organisations using end-of-life PHP branches should evaluate migration to supported versions or obtain
confirmation of vendor-maintained security backports.

Strengthen detection and monitoring

Security Operations Centres should increase monitoring of PHP-based infrastructure, particularly for unexpected behaviour originating from web-server processes. Useful detection opportunities include:

  • Suspicious process execution: Monitor for PHP or web-server processes such as php-fpm, php-cgi, apache2, or httpd launching unexpected command interpreters, including sh, bash, or PowerShell.
  • Potential payload retrieval: Investigate unexpected execution of download utilities such as curl or wget by web-server processes, especially when followed by script execution.
  • Suspicious web activity: Review HTTP access logs, reverse-proxy telemetry, and WAF events for unusual request patterns, unexpected requests to PHP endpoints, or significant increases in server errors.
  • Signs of post-exploitation: Monitor newly created PHP files in web-accessible directories, unexpected outbound connections, suspicious scheduled tasks, modified services, or unauthorised user-account
    changes. These are general behavioural detection opportunities associated with web-server compromise. They should not be interpreted as validated PHP2Shell-specific detection signatures. Where suspicious activity is identified, organisations should preserve relevant evidence and investigate whether compromise occurred before patch deployment.
Verify remediation and continue monitoring

Patching should be followed by verification. Security teams should confirm that affected systems have been successfully updated, necessary services have restarted, and no vulnerable runtime instances remain active.

Additional attention should be given to load-balanced environments, containers, staging environments, and systems maintained by third-party providers.

Because exploitation could occur before remediation, organisations should also review relevant historical telemetry and investigate signs of compromise.

What happens next?

With the patches now public, attackers are actively reverse-engineering them to produce reliable exploits. Exploitation attempts are already being observed in the wild (see above) and are expected to intensify in the coming days as public PoCs mature. Organisations should treat patching as time-critical and continue monitoring official PHP security announcements and trusted security advisories for further updates.

NVISO recommendations

Our immediate recommendations are to identify PHP deployments, prioritise exposed assets, reduce
attack surface, prepare emergency patching, and strengthen security monitoring. Given the critical severity and potential reach of these vulnerabilities, organisations should not wait
for confirmed widespread exploitation before taking preventive action.

NVISO’s Threat Intelligence and CSIRT teams continue to monitor this developing situation. If your organisation requires assistance assessing exposure, responding to potential exploitation, or
investigating suspicious activity, contact NVISO CSIRT.

  • php2shell Researcher Disclosure Site

items.title: Japanese Game Maker Capcom Has Confirmed – 11,774,247 Customer Records Exposed
items.summary: Capcom has announced plans to notify customers after unauthorized access to its CAPCOM ID service affected 11,774,247 records worldwide. The Japanese game publisher disclosed the incident on October 22, 2026, saying the exposed information included email addresses and details of account activity. Attackers also changed passwords on 196 accounts without permission. Capcom has reset those passwords, while its games and online services remain available. Capcom Confirms Records Exposed According to the company’s official security notice, CAPCOM ID is a shared account service used across its websites and required for online access to certain games. The company apologized to customers and said it had completed emergency response measures. Its investigation into the full impact remains ongoing. The affected records contained registered email addresses, account creation dates and times, last login dates and times, login counts, and the IP address used during the most recent login. These details reveal account activity, although the notice does not establish that every exposed record represents a separate person. A smaller group of 43 records also included dates of birth, gender, country or region, and nicknames. These records are part of the overall total, not a separate set of affected accounts. The affected data did not include credit card information. Capcom has not confirmed any compromise of customers’ originally chosen passwords. However, unauthorized password changes affecting 196 accounts show the incident involved changes to some accounts, not just access to stored information. The company has not publicly explained how it made those changes. Capcom detected suspicious activity on October 19 and immediately began blocking access while investigating. It confirmed unauthorized access that day and introduced emergency measures. On October 20, the company established an internal incident response headquarters and confirmed that customer information had been affected. Capcom reported the incident to the Osaka Prefectural Police and Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission on October 21. It says investigators identified and addressed the attack method, but the public notice does not name a vulnerability, describe the entry point, or identify an attacker. That leaves important technical questions unanswered. The disclosure doesn’t say whether attackers used stolen credentials, exploited a software flaw, or reached the service another way. Capcom warned that affected information could support fraudulent emails or messages pretending to come from the company or related parties. Customers should avoid links and attachments in suspicious messages. The warning describes a possible follow-up threat, not a confirmed phishing campaign linked to this breach. Related reporting on malware affecting Japanese cloud servers highlights similar warnings about fake support messages. Coverage of QR-code phishing emails also shows how criminals use deceptive messages to steal login details. Neither report links to Capcom. Capcom says registered email addresses can still be used. Affected customers will receive notifications, and dedicated regional support channels are available. The company plans further security improvements based on its findings and will publish additional information through official channels as required. items.title: Multiple Waves of DDoS Attacks Caused This Week’s Outage in North Korea
items.summary: Multiple waves of DDoS attacks disrupted North Korea’s public internet services this week, knocking major state websites offline. Kentik’s internet analysis director Doug Madory linked the outages to sudden traffic floods from Vietnam, the Philippines, Venezuela, and other countries. The traffic began at 02:01 UTC on October 20, making the country’s websites unreachable. The disruption affected more than 40 websites using North Korea’s .kp domain, including the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Korean Central News Agency. Access remained unstable for roughly 32 hours. South Korean reporting indicated that services returned around 7 p.m. local time on October 21, after repeated downtime and brief recoveries. North Korea Hit by Multiple DDoS Attacks In Doug Madory public findings , Madory said aggregate traffic data showed several waves of incoming traffic rather than one continuous surge. That timing helped connect the website failures to a distributed denial-of-service attack, which overwhelms a target with traffic and prevents normal users from reaching it. “This traffic all started at the same time, and it is coming from Vietnam and Venezuela. That’s definitely a DDoS attack,” Madory told Reuters, according to its report published by AsiaOne. Kentik cautioned that its analysis covered only part of the traffic heading toward North Korea. The countries in the traffic records do not identify who ordered the attacks. Kentik has not identified the people responsible. Although compromised devices can generate traffic from many locations, no specific botnet has been publicly linked to this incident. Looks like the North Koreans changed how 175.45.176.0/24 was transited in the past few hours going via Cenbong (AS134544) to Transtelecom (AS20485) in Russia. pic.twitter.com/9jtL9bQfUw — Doug Madory (also on Bluesky) (@DougMadory) October 21, 2026 Madory’s accompanying observations identified repeated downtime affecting 175.45.176.0/24, a network block containing name servers for .kp domains. These servers help translate website names into internet addresses. Their loss can leave multiple sites unreachable, even when individual web servers remain online. His route observations also described changes involving North Korea’s AS131279 network. The 175.45.176.0/24 block moved from Cenbong to Russia’s TTK, while 175.45.178.0/24 switched to TTK before returning to Cenbong. The other two listed blocks retained their respective providers. Those observations describe how traffic paths changed during the incident. They do not establish whether operators deliberately changed routes to reduce the attack’s impact. Early coverage considered power problems or telecommunications faults as possible explanations. Kentik’s later findings added direct traffic evidence supporting a DDoS explanation. However, the available reports do not identify the attack method, peak traffic volume, or tools used. Related reporting on the Dysphoria botnet explains how compromised routers and cameras can generate coordinated traffic floods. For now, the strongest evidence is the close match between incoming traffic spikes and service failures. The incident shows why outage investigations need traffic measurements alongside website checks, while the attacker’s identity and the operation’s full scale remain unresolved. items.summary_html:
Multiple waves of DDoS attacks disrupted North Korea’s public internet services this week, knocking major state websites offline.

Kentik’s internet analysis director Doug Madory linked the outages to sudden traffic floods from Vietnam, the Philippines, Venezuela, and other countries. The traffic began at 02:01 UTC on October 20, making the country’s websites unreachable.

The disruption affected more than 40 websites using North Korea’s .kp domain, including the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Korean Central News Agency.

Access remained unstable for roughly 32 hours. South Korean reporting indicated that services returned around 7 p.m. local time on October 21, after repeated downtime and brief recoveries.

North Korea Hit by Multiple DDoS Attacks

In Doug Madory public findings, Madory said aggregate traffic data showed several waves of incoming traffic rather than one continuous surge. That timing helped connect the website failures to a distributed denial-of-service attack, which overwhelms a target with traffic and prevents normal users from reaching it.

“This traffic all started at the same time, and it is coming from Vietnam and Venezuela. That’s definitely a DDoS attack,” Madory told Reuters, according to its report published by AsiaOne. Kentik cautioned that its analysis covered only part of the traffic heading toward North Korea.

The countries in the traffic records do not identify who ordered the attacks. Kentik has not identified the people responsible. Although compromised devices can generate traffic from many locations, no specific botnet has been publicly linked to this incident.

Looks like the North Koreans changed how 175.45.176.0/24 was transited in the past few hours going via Cenbong (AS134544) to Transtelecom (AS20485) in Russia. pic.twitter.com/9jtL9bQfUw

— Doug Madory (also on Bluesky) (@DougMadory) October 21, 2026

Madory’s accompanying observations identified repeated downtime affecting 175.45.176.0/24, a network block containing name servers for .kp domains.

These servers help translate website names into internet addresses. Their loss can leave multiple sites unreachable, even when individual web servers remain online.

His route observations also described changes involving North Korea’s AS131279 network. The 175.45.176.0/24 block moved from Cenbong to Russia’s TTK, while 175.45.178.0/24 switched to TTK before returning to Cenbong. The other two listed blocks retained their respective providers.

Those observations describe how traffic paths changed during the incident. They do not establish whether operators deliberately changed routes to reduce the attack’s impact.

Early coverage considered power problems or telecommunications faults as possible explanations. Kentik’s later findings added direct traffic evidence supporting a DDoS explanation.

However, the available reports do not identify the attack method, peak traffic volume, or tools used. Related reporting on the Dysphoria botnet explains how compromised routers and cameras can generate coordinated traffic floods.

For now, the strongest evidence is the close match between incoming traffic spikes and service failures. The incident shows why outage investigations need traffic measurements alongside website checks, while the attacker’s identity and the operation’s full scale remain unresolved.

items.title: New Node2Shell Node.js RCE Exploit Let Attackers Execute Malicious Code Through Brotli-Compressed Data
items.summary: Researchers has demonstrated Node2Shell, a working exploit that lets an attacker run code inside a Node.js application through specially crafted, Brotli-compressed data. The research targets CVE-2026-111497 , a high-severity memory flaw in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. The Node.js security advisory, published on October 21, 2026, confirms that the flaw can allow remote code execution and affects the 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x release lines. Fixes are available across all three branches. New Node2Shell Node.js RCE Exploit According to the supplied Imperva research , its standalone proof of concept worked against the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image without a debugger or modified binary. The code delivered with the compressed data created a marker file that the test application was not instructed to produce. Execution required multiple attempts in the tested setup. The results establish exploitation on that specific build and application configuration, not reliable execution across every Node.js platform. The flaw appears when the decoder encounters an invalid transition between block types within a Brotli stream. Instead of rejecting the broken stream, the vulnerable code treats the condition as a need for more input and continues processing with an invalid internal state. Imperva’s separate memory-sanitizer test showed that this behavior could write beyond an intended buffer. That out-of-bounds write provides the underlying memory corruption behind the demonstrated code execution. The patched decoder returns a format error for the invalid transition. Node.js 24.22.1 release notes confirm the inclusion of the Brotli security fix. In Imperva’s application tests, that release rejected the same malicious inputs without creating the marker file. Imperva tested compressed HTTP responses consumed through Node.js’s built-in fetch() function and incoming request bodies decoded by configured Express and body-parser middleware. The tested setups included Express 5.0.0 with body-parser 2.0.1, Express 5.3.0 with body-parser 2.3.0, and standalone body-parser 2.0.0. Both raw() and json() parser paths allowed execution in the tested vulnerable environments. These packages provide routes into the affected decoder rather than containing the underlying flaw. A bare Node.js HTTP server does not automatically decompress incoming Brotli bodies. Cybersecurity News previously covered the affected branches in its report on Node.js security updates. Its October 21 security roundup also highlights the need to rebuild container images with the updated runtime. Administrators should deploy Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1, or newer fixed versions in those branches. The official advisory lists these releases as the security updates addressing the flaw. Two tested routes into the native decoder (source : imperva ) Teams should check the actual Node.js binary inside deployed containers and hosts, then review where services decode untrusted compressed requests or responses. Imperva says it added WAF rules covering reproduced exploitation attempts. Those controls provide temporary protection, but replacing the vulnerable runtime remains essential. Decoder errors and unexpected process exits may support investigation, but neither alone proves successful exploitation. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: Hackers Actively Exploiting Critical VeloCloud Orchestrator Flaw to Gain Superuser Access
items.summary: Hackers are actively exploiting a critical SQL injection flaw in VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO) that allows logged-in users to gain superuser operator access. Arista Networks disclosed the vulnerability on October 22, 2026, warning that successful attacks could compromise the orchestrator, its host, and the data it manages. Arista has already patched hosted deployments, including Dedicated instances. Tracked as CVE-2026-114625, the vulnerability carries a CVSS v3.1 score of 9.9 and a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.4. Arista discovered the issue and confirmed active exploitation. Security Advisory 0199 identifies the weakness as CWE-89 (SQL injection) and tracks it internally as BUG2043622. Exploitation requires network access to the VCO web interface and a valid authenticated portal session. However, attackers do not need an administrator account. Enterprise Read Only, the lowest built-in tenant role, provides enough access to exploit the flaw. The attack requires no user interaction and is low complexity. A successful attacker can gain operator privileges and impersonate a local “superuser operator” account. This opens access to internal functions that should not be available remotely. Arista warns that exploitation can affect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of both the orchestrator and its managed data. The login requirement is important. This is not an unauthenticated attack , but a limited account can become a route to much broader control. Hackers Exploiting VeloCloud Orchestrator Flaw Arista says VCO is exposed by default and no product configuration removes the exposure. Restricting network access is a temporary safeguard, not a fix. The disclosure follows earlier VeloCloud Orchestrator exploitation involving a separate command injection vulnerability. Another related report covered SonicWall SQL injection flaws that could turn read-only access into administrator control. Those cases involve different vulnerabilities and should not be confused with this issue. Affected on-premises deployments include VCO 5.2.x releases before 5.2.3.18, VCO 6.1.x releases before 6.1.3.10, and VCO 6.4.x releases before 6.4.2.12. Administrators should upgrade to the fixed version in their release train or a later release. Arista has not assessed software that has reached end of support. VeloCloud Gateway and VeloCloud Edge are not affected. Arista also lists its EOS-based products and other named platforms as unaffected. Operators should check the affected software list first instead of assuming that every Arista or VeloCloud product needs the same update. Arista identified 74.82.197.86 and 38.54.50.151 as source IP addresses observed conducting attacks. Security teams should block these addresses and search historical logs for related activity. Investigators should also examine unusual URL-like paths, encoded characters, references to local or internal services, and unusually high request rates. Where feasible, teams should preserve web access, backend application, system, and database logs, along with relevant file timestamps, before remediation. Arista also recommends restricting web access to trusted administrative networks, checking unexpected outbound connections, reviewing administrator changes, and monitoring for backdoor services or webshells . Customers outside supported release trains should contact Arista Technical Assistance Center about upgrade options. These interim controls reduce exposure, but installing a fixed release remains the recommended resolution. Because exploitation is already confirmed, affected organizations should prioritize patching alongside a review for signs of compromise rather than treating the upgrade as routine maintenance. items.title: StealC Malware Returns as New Stadia RAT to Steal Passwords and Secretly Control Windows PCs
items.summary: The seller behind StealC has returned with Stadia, a Windows remote access trojan that combines password theft with hidden desktop control. Advertised on October 16, 2026, the malware expands beyond stealing data, allowing criminals to run commands, browse files, manage processes, and load more malicious software. The return follows June’s Operation Endgame disruption. Authorities seized 326 servers and 142 domains, according to Varonis. Although the earlier StealC infrastructure takedown disrupted the criminal service, its surviving code gave the seller a foundation for rebuilding under a new name. Researchers from Varonis Threat Labs identified Stadia’s connection to StealC after obtaining a build, examining its code, and testing its web panel against their own Windows machine. Their technical analysis of Stadia found an embedded browser encryption helper shared byte for byte with StealC 3.5, providing direct evidence of code reuse. StealC Malware Returns as New Stadia RAT Stadia brings together six modules: a stealer, hidden desktop access, a remote command shell, a loader, a file explorer, and a process manager. Hidden Virtual Network Computing, or HVNC, lets an operator work inside a separate desktop that the victim cannot see. The file tools support uploads, downloads, and execution. Forum post (Source – Varonis) The seller advertises collection from more than 50 browsers, 120 cryptocurrency extensions, and 50 desktop wallets. Targets also include messaging apps, gaming sessions, email clients, and VPN software. Similar combinations appear in Dolphin X credential theft coverage, where stolen browser data and remote access create risks beyond individual account losses. Monthly subscriptions cost $300 for Basic, $550 for Team, and $900 for Pro. Only Pro includes all six modules. Former StealC customers receive a free Pro month, helping the seller attract buyers whose previous infrastructure disappeared. The tested panel and agent both reported version 1.1.2. How Stadia Hides and Communicates The examined sample is an unsigned, 560,128-byte, 32-bit Windows executable built with Microsoft Visual C++. It hides important strings using RC4 encryption and Base64 encoding, while resolving most Windows functions during execution. It also exits when certain Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Kazakh, or Uzbek language settings are detected. Installation creates a random folder beneath Windows’ shared application-data directory and uses a filename resembling legitimate software. A hidden scheduled task runs at logon and every 15 minutes. With elevated permissions, Stadia also adds its installation folder to Microsoft Defender exclusions through PowerShell. For browser theft, an unsigned process starts Chrome, Edge, or Brave in a suspended state and injects roughly 26 KB of code. A temporary text file briefly holds the recovered browser encryption key before deletion. Related ChonkyChicken browser credential attacks show why protected browser storage remains an important monitoring target. Stadia contacts three hard-coded servers over HTTP. Its requests claim to contain JSON, but actually carry RC4-encrypted, Base64-encoded data. Defenders should investigate this mismatch alongside suspicious browser injection, hidden tasks, and new antivirus exclusions. Varonis warns that server addresses and keys change between builds, making behavior-based detection more durable than static blocking alone. The report does not establish an initial delivery method or independently verified infection count. items.title: How to Export AWS CloudTrail Logs
items.summary: For the last 90 days of management events, use the CloudTrail console ( Event history → Download events → JSON ) or aws cloudtrail lookup-events. For anything older, or for data events like S3 object reads, read your trail’s log files in S3. They sit under s3:// /AWSLogs/ /CloudTrail/ /YYYY/MM/DD/. CloudTrail is the audit log of your AWS control plane: every console login, every API call, every role assumption. In a cloud incident, it’s the first thing everyone asks for. Prime Core has 262 detection rules for CloudTrail, mapped to 177 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Among them: misuse of cloud accounts (T1078.004), attackers switching off cloud logging (T1562.008) and data theft from cloud storage (T1530). Before you start Event history and trails are different things. Event history is always on and free. It keeps 90 days of management events, per region. A trail is something you configure: it writes to S3, keeps logs as long as you like, and can include data events. Check what you have: aws cloudtrail describe-trails aws cloudtrail get-trail-status --name IsLogging: false on a trail that should be running is a finding in itself. Regions matter. Event history is per region, and events from global services like IAM usually land in us-east-1. If you’re looking for a CreateUser call in eu-west-1, you won’t find it. Permissions. cloudtrail:LookupEvents for event history. For trail files, s3:ListBucket and s3:GetObject on the bucket, plus kms:Decrypt if the trail is encrypted with a KMS key. Option 1: Console download Open CloudTrail, go to Event history , set the time range and any filters (event name, user, resource), then choose Download events → JSON . The download respects your filters, so check them first. It covers the current region only. Option 2: lookup-events from the CLI aws cloudtrail lookup-events --region us-east-1 \ --start-time 2026-10-19T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-10-20T00:00:00Z \ --output json > ct_use1_1019.json Two things to know. First, each result wraps the actual event as a JSON string in CloudTrailEvent. Unwrap it into one clean event per line: jq -c '.Events[].CloudTrailEvent | fromjson' ct_use1_1019.json > ct_use1_1019.jsonl Second, lookup-events is rate limited per account and region, and it accepts only one –lookup-attributes filter per call. Wide time windows take a while, so narrow them where you can. To cover every region, loop over aws ec2 describe-regions –query ‘Regions[].RegionName’ –output text. Option 3: Trail files from S3 This is the route for history beyond 90 days and for data events: aws s3 cp s3://my-trail-bucket/AWSLogs/123456789012/CloudTrail/eu-west-1/2026/10/19/ ./ct/ --recursive gunzip ./ct/*.json.gz jq -c '.Records[]' ./ct/*.json > ct_euw1_1019.jsonl Each file holds a Records array, and the jq line flattens all of them into one event per line. Organization trails add the organization ID to the path: AWSLogs/ / /CloudTrail/…. If you use CloudTrail Lake, you can run SQL over your events and save the results instead. What to look for Event Why it matters ConsoleLogin Check additionalEventData.MFAUsed, failures, and source IPs you don’t recognize CreateUser, CreateAccessKey, AttachUserPolicy New identities and keys: classic persistence and privilege escalation StopLogging, DeleteTrail, PutEventSelectors Someone reducing what CloudTrail sees AssumeRole from odd sources Lateral movement between roles and accounts Bursts of errorCode: AccessDenied Reconnaissance with stolen credentials GetSecretValue, GetObject bursts Data access; GetObject appears only if S3 data events are on Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl (or .json file). Sanitize. [what gets masked: account IDs, ARNs, IPs, access key IDs, usernames]. Look it over before you continue. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix lookup-events returns nothing Wrong region; IAM events usually live in us-east-1 Query us-east-1, or loop over all regions Nothing older than 90 days Event history retention Use the trail files in S3 No GetObject events S3 data events aren’t enabled on the trail Expected; enable them for the future AccessDenied reading trail files Missing kms:Decrypt, or the bucket policy Fix IAM or the bucket policy ThrottlingException lookup-events rate limit Smaller windows; let the CLI retry FAQ Does event history include data events? No. Only management events. Data events exist only if a trail or event data store was set up to record them. How quickly do events show up? Usually within minutes of the API call. items.summary_html:
For the last 90 days of management events, use the CloudTrail console (Event history → Download events → JSON) or aws cloudtrail lookup-events. For anything older, or for data events like S3 object reads, read your trail’s log files in S3. They sit under s3:///AWSLogs//CloudTrail//YYYY/MM/DD/.

CloudTrail is the audit log of your AWS control plane: every console login, every API call, every role assumption. In a cloud incident, it’s the first thing everyone asks for. Prime Core has 262 detection rules for CloudTrail, mapped to 177 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Among them: misuse of cloud accounts (T1078.004), attackers switching off cloud logging (T1562.008) and data theft from cloud storage (T1530).

Before you start

Event history and trails are different things. Event history is always on and free. It keeps 90 days of management events, per region. A trail is something you configure: it writes to S3, keeps logs as long as you like, and can include data events. Check what you have:

aws cloudtrail describe-trails

aws cloudtrail get-trail-status --name

IsLogging: false on a trail that should be running is a finding in itself.

Regions matter. Event history is per region, and events from global services like IAM usually land in us-east-1. If you’re looking for a CreateUser call in eu-west-1, you won’t find it.

Permissions. cloudtrail:LookupEvents for event history. For trail files, s3:ListBucket and s3:GetObject on the bucket, plus kms:Decrypt if the trail is encrypted with a KMS key.

Option 1: Console download

Open CloudTrail, go to Event history, set the time range and any filters (event name, user, resource), then choose Download events → JSON. The download respects your filters, so check them first. It covers the current region only.

Option 2: lookup-events from the CLI 
aws cloudtrail lookup-events --region us-east-1 \

  --start-time 2026-10-19T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-10-20T00:00:00Z \

  --output json > ct_use1_1019.json

Two things to know. First, each result wraps the actual event as a JSON string in CloudTrailEvent. Unwrap it into one clean event per line:

jq -c '.Events[].CloudTrailEvent | fromjson' ct_use1_1019.json > ct_use1_1019.jsonl

Second, lookup-events is rate limited per account and region, and it accepts only one –lookup-attributes filter per call. Wide time windows take a while, so narrow them where you can. To cover every region, loop over aws ec2 describe-regions –query ‘Regions[].RegionName’ –output text.

Option 3: Trail files from S3

This is the route for history beyond 90 days and for data events:

aws s3 cp s3://my-trail-bucket/AWSLogs/123456789012/CloudTrail/eu-west-1/2026/10/19/ ./ct/ --recursive

gunzip ./ct/*.json.gz

jq -c '.Records[]' ./ct/*.json > ct_euw1_1019.jsonl

Each file holds a Records array, and the jq line flattens all of them into one event per line. Organization trails add the organization ID to the path: AWSLogs///CloudTrail/…. If you use CloudTrail Lake, you can run SQL over your events and save the results instead.

  1. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl (or .json file). 
  2. Sanitize. [what gets masked: account IDs, ARNs, IPs, access key IDs, usernames]. Look it over before you continue.
  3. Review.

items.title: How to Export Microsoft Entra ID Sign-in Logs
items.summary: In the Microsoft Entra admin center, open Identity → Monitoring & health → Sign-in logs , set your filters, and choose Download → JSON . For bigger or scripted pulls, use Microsoft Graph: GET /auditLogs/signIns. Either way, you only get what’s still retained: 7 days on Entra ID Free, 30 days with P1 or P2. Sign-in logs show who authenticated, from where, to which app, and whether MFA and Conditional Access held. In identity-driven attacks, that’s most of the story. Prime Core has 170 detection rules for Entra ID sign-in data, mapped to 113 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Among them: password spraying (T1110.003), MFA fatigue (T1621) and logins with stolen cloud credentials (T1078.004). Get Started for Free Before you start Retention is short. If the activity you’re after is older than 7 or 30 days, the portal and Graph won’t have it. The only place it might still exist is wherever your diagnostic settings send sign-in logs: a Log Analytics workspace, Microsoft Sentinel or a storage account. See our [Microsoft Sentinel export guide] for that route. Roles. Reports Reader is the least-privileged role that can read sign-in logs. Security Reader and Global Reader work too. There are four kinds of sign-ins. Interactive user, non-interactive user, service principal and managed identity each have their own tab in the portal. Token replay and abuse of refresh tokens tend to show up under non-interactive , which people forget to export. Option 1: Download from the portal Go to Sign-in logs and pick the tab (start with interactive, then non-interactive). Set Date and any filters (user, application, status). Choose Download , then JSON . The portal limits how many records a single download includes. [PROOF: confirm the current limit.] For large ranges, split by day or use Graph. Option 2: Microsoft Graph PowerShell This pulls raw API JSON, follows paging, and writes one sign-in per line: Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "AuditLog.Read.All" $uri = "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/auditLogs/signIns?`$filter=createdDateTime ge 2026-10-19T00:00:00Z and createdDateTime lt 2026-10-20T00:00:00Z" do { $page = Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET -Uri $uri -OutputType Json | ConvertFrom-Json $page.value | ForEach-Object { $_ | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress } | Add-Content signins_1019.jsonl $uri = $page.'@odata.nextLink' } while ($uri) The v1.0 endpoint returns interactive sign-ins. Non-interactive and service principal sign-ins need the beta endpoint with a signInEventTypes filter. Reading sign-ins through the API also depends on your tenant’s license tier. Timestamps are UTC throughout. What to look for Field or value What it tells you status.errorCode 50126 Wrong username or password. Many of these across many users means spraying status.errorCode 50053 Account locked by smart lockout status.errorCode 500121 MFA failed or was denied; a burst of these is MFA fatigue clientAppUsed = IMAP, POP, SMTP, “Other clients” Legacy authentication that skips MFA conditionalAccessStatus Whether CA applied, passed or failed riskLevelDuringSignIn, location, ipAddress Risky or unfamiliar origins The pattern worth stopping for: a string of 50126 failures across many accounts from one IP range, then a success for one of them. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the JSON file. Sanitize. [what gets masked: UPNs, display names, IPs, device names, tenant and object IDs]. Look it over before you continue. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix Nothing older than a week or a month Retention for your license tier Check Log Analytics, Sentinel or storage if diagnostic settings were on Graph returns 403 Missing AuditLog.Read.All consent, role or license Grant consent; check your role and tenant license Export has only interactive sign-ins Other types live in separate tabs, or in beta Graph Export each tab; use the beta endpoint Download contains fewer records than the portal shows Portal download limit Split by day, or use Graph FAQ What about Entra audit logs? Those are a different log: directory changes like new users, role assignments and app consents. Same portal area, Audit logs. In Graph it’s /auditLogs/directoryAudits. In an incident, you usually want both. Can I get sign-ins from Sentinel instead? Yes, if the Entra ID connector is on: they’re in the SigninLogs and AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs tables, with whatever retention your workspace has.

items.title: Critical PHP2Shell Exploit Code Goes Public as Hackers Attempt to Deploy Botnet Malware
items.summary: Public proof-of-concept code for two critical PHP vulnerabilities is now available, and attackers have tried to use the flaws to deploy botnet malware. Known together as PHP2Shell, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 both carry a CVSS severity score of 9.2 and can allow attackers to run code without logging in. However, attempted exploitation must not be confused with a confirmed breach. In its latest correction, issued on October 22 at 21:21 UTC, Sophos said its customer data showed scanning and a small number of failed exploit attempts. It found no evidence of a successful compromise through these vulnerabilities. Researchers from Sophos identified the intended payload as Potassium, a likely Mirai botnet variant. Security controls blocked the attempt, so the malware was not delivered. Analysis of the sample nevertheless showed a larger, updated version of the Mirai-derived threat seen earlier in 2026, with download and network disruption features. The activity follows earlier PHP2Shell targeting before patches became public. Reporting on PHP attacks before patching describes Amazon observations dating to October 17, four days before the fixes. Those findings underline why defenders should review older logs, while keeping attempted attacks separate from proven code execution on real servers. Critical PHP2Shell Exploit Code Goes Public PHP released security updates on October 21. The affected software includes PHP installations serving web requests through PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The Dutch National Cyber Security Centre notes that Apache mod_php carries the highest risk because exploitation can occur before application code starts running. The flaws involve different failures in how PHP handles memory and request data. CVE-2026-109618 can corrupt memory during request cleanup after an out-of-memory condition. CVE-2026-109619 concerns old request data left in shared internal state, which a later request handled by the same worker can reuse. These weaknesses can expose more than a single website. Products that bundle PHP, including management interfaces and network appliances, may also need updates from their suppliers. Administrators should therefore check the runtime used by each service, rather than relying only on the PHP version shown by a command-line check. Public exploit code does not mean every vulnerable server can be compromised reliably. Sophos said its own research team found working exploitation difficult, even with AI support. Earlier Cloudflare PHP attack coverage also shows why web application firewall rules are a temporary safeguard, not a replacement for updates. Potassium Botnet Payload Examined The blocked traffic included a scanning-related User-Agent, a multipart boundary, and a distinct POST request pattern. Sophos published a temporary file path and an execution command as related indicators. Since its earlier success claim was withdrawn, those details should not be presented as proof that customer systems ran the payload. Sample analysis showed that Potassium resolves an encrypted command-and-control address and makes an HTTP request. It checks for a successful HTTP 200 response and verifies that the returned file begins with Linux ELF magic bytes. That check shows the downloader expects another Linux executable, rather than ordinary web content. The sample also supports hostname lookup and fallback resolution through public DNS services. Those public services are not malicious indicators by themselves. Like other Mirai-based malware, Potassium can launch distributed denial-of-service attacks, using compromised machines to flood targets with traffic. Separate RondoDoX botnet exploit activity illustrates similar interest in turning exposed application servers into botnet resources. Organizations should update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, or install an approved vendor backport. Restarting affected services and checking the active workers helps ensure the patched code is actually in use. Bundled runtimes, containers, and appliances need separate checks because updating one host package may leave other copies unchanged. Sophos has added firewall and endpoint intrusion prevention signatures alongside existing detection rules. Defenders should keep these protections current, but assess alerts against process and network evidence. A blocked request alone cannot show whether another request succeeded. Equally, a public exploit demonstration does not prove that the same code works against a production system with different settings, dependencies, or worker process behavior. Where patching cannot happen immediately, Sophos recommends considering removal of exposed PHP systems from the internet or placing them behind network-level authentication. Teams should monitor unusual processes, unexpected outbound connections, and suspicious web requests. Temporary settings and firewall signatures can reduce exposure, but they do not fully fix both flaws. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Type Indicator Source context Source IP 45[.]198[.]224[.]169 PHP2Shell exploit attempt Payload-hosting IP 92[.]118[.]112[.]100 Related payload infrastructure Payload URL hxxp://92[.]118[.]112[.]100/nfs Related malware download location Command-and-control IP 134[.]199[.]154[.]64 Potassium C2 server Command-and-control IP 117[.]55[.]202[.]115 Potassium C2 server Domain thunder[.]godofthunder[.]st Contacted during sandbox analysis Domain hackattackkaboom[.]botlesscucks[.]st Related malware staging server Domain hik[.]gettingheadfromduckysmom[.]st Potassium infrastructure embedded in payload MD5 b61a098fc62a2c2696e196dca78da71a Related likely Mirai-variant sample SHA-1 c472dab4ff7c16782a8037f988d4daa6d4bdb343 Related likely Mirai-variant sample SHA-256 0c5486f06620e26e316f4b33f318b0d646d5e1133789331aa2fed012360d1486 Related likely Mirai-variant sample File path /tmp/nfs Published payload-path indicator Command ./nfs php Published payload-execution indicator User-Agent php2shell-scan/109618 Observed exploit traffic Multipart boundary B7kQpoc618 Observed exploit-request string Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally defanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. That check shows the downloader expects another Linux executable, rather than ordinary web content. The sample also supports hostname lookup and fallback resolution through public DNS services.

Those public services are not malicious indicators by themselves. Like other Mirai-based malware, Potassium can launch distributed denial-of-service attacks, using compromised machines to flood targets with traffic.

Separate RondoDoX botnet exploit activity illustrates similar interest in turning exposed application servers into botnet resources.

Organizations should update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, or install an approved vendor backport. Restarting affected services and checking the active workers helps ensure the patched code is actually in use.

Bundled runtimes, containers, and appliances need separate checks because updating one host package may leave other copies unchanged.

Sophos has added firewall and endpoint intrusion prevention signatures alongside existing detection rules. Defenders should keep these protections current, but assess alerts against process and network evidence.

A blocked request alone cannot show whether another request succeeded. Equally, a public exploit demonstration does not prove that the same code works against a production system with different settings, dependencies, or worker process behavior.

Where patching cannot happen immediately, Sophos recommends considering removal of exposed PHP systems from the internet or placing them behind network-level authentication.

Teams should monitor unusual processes, unexpected outbound connections, and suspicious web requests. Temporary settings and firewall signatures can reduce exposure, but they do not fully fix both flaws.

items.summary: Executive Summary On October 21, 2026, Node.js released fixes for 10 vulnerabilities across its three supported release lines: 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x. Four are rated High. The most severe, CVE-2026-111497, is an out-of-bounds write in the bundled Brotli decoder that Node.js says permits remote code execution. These flaws live in the Node.js runtime itself, not in application packages, so dependency checks will not surface them. Qualys customers can find affected runtimes across hosts, containers, and cloud workloads, including copies outside standard install paths, prioritize those exposed to the internet, and confirm each fix after patching. Why This Release Needs Attention Now The four high-severity vulnerabilities impact two areas that nearly every Node.js service interacts with: compressed data and outbound connections. CVE-2026-111497 is a vulnerability found in the code responsible for decompressing Brotli data. Any service that unpacks Brotli content it did not create is affected by this issue. Additionally, there are three other high-severity vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-105482, CVE-2026-105483, and CVE-2026-106069. These vulnerabilities compromise Node.js’s ability to verify hostnames and certificates, which is especially important for services that connect to hosts on behalf of users. Three additional points apply to every team: No workarounds are available. Node.js has not published any for these ten CVEs. Upgrading the runtime is the solution. No CVSS scores are available. Currently, the CVE records are reserved and do not have CVSS scores. No updates are available for unsupported lines. Only versions 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x have received fixes. All other versions, including 25.x and 20.x, remain vulnerable and must be upgraded to a supported release. Why Updating Application Dependencies Is Not Enough Updating application dependencies alone will not resolve these issues. The vulnerable code is included in the Node.js runtime, which encompasses runtimes embedded in container images and single-executable applications (SEAs). Node.js also often runs from nonstandard locations: Version managers such as nvm Application folders Bundled runtimes SEAs Container images, running containers, and serverless functions such as AWS Lambda Node.js runtimes What the Vulnerabilities Affect The vulnerabilities span zlib, DNS, TLS, HTTP, crypto, and the Permission Model. Three of the four high-severity issues weaken hostname or certificate validation, which matters for any service that makes outbound TLS or DNS calls on behalf of users. CVE Severity Module Description Affected lines CVE-2026-111497 High zlib (Brotli) Brotli decoder out-of-bounds write; potential remote code execution 22.x, 24.x, 26.x CVE-2026-105482 High DNS DNS resolution truncation involving embedded NUL characters 22.x, 24.x, 26.x CVE-2026-105483 High TLS TLS hostname validation bypass using fullwidth IP digits 24.x, 26.x CVE-2026-106069 High TLS TLS hostname validation bypass with noncanonical IP addresses 22.x, 24.x, 26.x CVE-2026-105481 Medium HTTP HTTP keep-alive response handling issue 22.x, 24.x, 26.x CVE-2026-106072 Medium TLS Improper certificate validation for unusual IPv4 representations 22.x, 24.x, 26.x CVE-2026-106074 Medium crypto Repeated random values across startup snapshots 22.x, 24.x, 26.x CVE-2026-106070 Low zlib (ZipFile) ZIP validation exposes attacker-controlled bytes 26.x CVE-2026-106071 Low Permission Model Permission Model filesystem over-grant 26.x CVE-2026-106073 Low fs / Permission Model Permission Model bypass using fs.realpathSync 22.x, 24.x, 26.x High-Severity Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-111497 (Brotli) . A crafted Brotli stream can cause the decoder to write outside its allocated memory bounds. Node.js classifies this outcome as a remote code execution vulnerability. Services that decompress Brotli data from untrusted sources, such as HTTP clients and proxies that accept the Content-Encoding: br , or services that handle uploaded compressed files, are particularly at risk. CVE-2026-105482 (DNS) . The functions dns.resolve* , dns.reverse , and the Resolver class send names to c-ares as C strings. Therefore, if an embedded NUL character is present, it will truncate the name. An application has the ability to validate one hostname against an allowlist while querying a different name. The dns.lookup function remains unaffected by this issue. CVE-2026-106069 (TLS) . The `tls.checkServerIdentity` function can verify a non-canonical IP address, such as one in octal or shortened form, against a certificate for one address while the connection is directed to a different one. This vulnerability allows an attacker to present a certificate that is valid for an endpoint that does not actually belong to them. CVE-2026-105483 (TLS) . Hostnames using Unicode fullwidth digits normalize to an IP address and can match a certificate issued for that IP. This issue only affects the 24.x and 26.x lines. Medium- and Low-Severity Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-105481 (Medium, HTTP): With http.Agent keep-alive, a server can send a response through an idle reused socket before the next request, which Node.js will interpret as the response to that request. CVE-2026-106072 (Medium, TLS): Certificates with DNS names were accepted for non-canonical IPv4 endpoints. This issue has been resolved in the same commit as CVE-2026-106069. CVE-2026-106074 (Medium, crypto): Cached values for crypto.randomUUID and crypto.randomInt were stored in startup snapshots, causing processes that initiated from the same snapshot to produce identical initial values. Only SEAs using useSnapshot or user-land snapshots are affected. CVE-2026-106070 (Low, zlib): In the experimental zlib.ZipFile API (added in 26.8.0), a read after a failed header check could return bytes from the wrong file position. CVE-2026-106071 (Low, Permission Model): Using Wildcard paths in the --allow-fs-read or --allow-fs-write options may provide access to more files paths than originally intended. CVE-2026-106073 (Low, fs): fs.realpathSync bypassed the Permission Model check that its sibling functions perform, allowing calls on ungranted paths. Fixed Versions and Upgrade Guidance Each supported line has a fixed release, and any subsequent release in the same line also includes the fixes. Node.js version 26 will become LTS on October 28, 2026. Teams using version 26.x should upgrade to version 26.12.1 before this transition. To build the inventory in step 1, run one CSAM or VMDR query per release line, so patched assets on other lines are not counted: Run the following queries in CSAM > Inventory > Assets . Step Action All assets with Node.js installed (software: ((name: “Node.js”))) Assets running end-of-life Node.js (21.x and earlier, 23.x, 25.x) ((software: (((name: “Node.js”) AND (version: (*..22.0.0)))))) Node.js on your most critical assets ((asset.criticalityScore: [4..*)) AND (software: ((name: “Node.js”)))) Reduce Exposure Before You Patch Upgrading the runtime is the only complete fix. Teams on 22.x should upgrade the runtime manually until a patch is available. For the 24.x and 26.x patches: Patch reliability: High for 24.22.1, Low for 26.12.1. These flaws live in the Node.js runtime itself, not in application packages, so dependency checks will not surface them. Qualys customers can find affected runtimes across hosts, containers, and cloud workloads, including copies outside standard install paths, prioritize those exposed to the internet, and confirm each fix after patching.

Why This Release Needs Attention Now

The four high-severity vulnerabilities impact two areas that nearly every Node.js service interacts with: compressed data and outbound connections.

CVE-2026-111497 is a vulnerability found in the code responsible for decompressing Brotli data. Any service that unpacks Brotli content it did not create is affected by this issue. Additionally, there are three other high-severity vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-105482, CVE-2026-105483, and CVE-2026-106069. These vulnerabilities compromise Node.js’s ability to verify hostnames and certificates, which is especially important for services that connect to hosts on behalf of users.

Three additional points apply to every team:

  • No workarounds are available. Node.js has not published any for these ten CVEs. Upgrading the runtime is the solution.
  • No CVSS scores are available. Currently, the CVE records are reserved and do not have CVSS scores.
  • No updates are available for unsupported lines. Only versions 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x have received fixes. All other versions, including 25.x and 20.x, remain vulnerable and must be upgraded to a supported release.
Why Updating Application Dependencies Is Not Enough

Updating application dependencies alone will not resolve these issues. The vulnerable code is included in the Node.js runtime, which encompasses runtimes embedded in container images and single-executable applications (SEAs).

Node.js also often runs from nonstandard locations:

  • Version managers such as nvm
  • Application folders
  • Bundled runtimes
  • SEAs
  • Container images, running containers, and serverless functions such as AWS Lambda Node.js runtimes
What the Vulnerabilities Affect

The vulnerabilities span zlib, DNS, TLS, HTTP, crypto, and the Permission Model. Three of the four high-severity issues weaken hostname or certificate validation, which matters for any service that makes outbound TLS or DNS calls on behalf of users.

Services that decompress Brotli data from untrusted sources, such as HTTP clients and proxies that accept the Content-Encoding: br, or services that handle uploaded compressed files, are particularly at risk.

CVE-2026-105482 (DNS). The functions dns.resolve*, dns.reverse, and the Resolver class send names to c-ares as C strings. Therefore, if an embedded NUL character is present, it will truncate the name. An application has the ability to validate one hostname against an allowlist while querying a different name. The dns.lookup function remains unaffected by this issue.

CVE-2026-106069 (TLS). The `tls.checkServerIdentity` function can verify a non-canonical IP address, such as one in octal or shortened form, against a certificate for one address while the connection is directed to a different one. This vulnerability allows an attacker to present a certificate that is valid for an endpoint that does not actually belong to them.

CVE-2026-105483 (TLS). Hostnames using Unicode fullwidth digits normalize to an IP address and can match a certificate issued for that IP. This issue only affects the 24.x and 26.x lines.

Each supported line has a fixed release, and any subsequent release in the same line also includes the fixes.

items.title: How to Export the Microsoft 365 Unified Audit Log
items.summary: The Purview portal ( Audit → Search ) lets you search the Unified Audit Log and export the results to CSV. The full event sits in one column, AuditData, as a JSON blob. To get clean JSON, one event per line, use Exchange Online PowerShell and Search-UnifiedAuditLog. The script is below. Standard audit retention is 180 days; Audit (Premium) keeps a year by default. The Unified Audit Log covers Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams and admin activity in one place. In a business email compromise, it’s where the inbox rules, forwarding and mass downloads show up. Prime Core has 79 detection rules for Microsoft 365 audit data, mapped to 33 MITRE ATT&CK techniques.
