items.title: Multi-tenant GPU Kubernetes on simulated hardware with Kamaji and HAMi
items.summary: GPU teams usually face a bad trade-off. Give every team its own Kubernetes cluster and you pay for a control plane per team. Put everyone in one shared cluster and you get weak isolation. Either way, Kubernetes hands out GPUs as whole cards, so a pod that needs 4 GB of an 80 GB GPU still blocks the entire card. This post shows a way out by combining two open-source projects: Kamaji runs each tenant’s Kubernetes control plane as pods inside one management cluster. HAMi lets pods request a slice of a GPU (memory in MB, compute in %) and packs several pods onto one card. I built the whole thing on a single machine with no physical GPU, using HAMi’s mock device plugin to simulate the cards. The result: two fully isolated tenant clusters, each scheduling fractional-GPU workloads through HAMi, with all eight tests passing. Everything below is reproducible: the exact versions, the commands that worked, the errors I hit and how I fixed them. Architecture One kind cluster hosts Kamaji and both tenant control planes; each tenant’s worker is a separate container that joins over the kind network and runs HAMi. Tenants never share a node or an API server. The only shared pieces are the management cluster and the kamaji-etcd datastore, where each tenant’s data is kept separate. Why Kamaji + HAMi Kamaji solves the cluster problem and HAMi solves the GPU problem; they work at different layers, so they don’t overlap. The interesting part is where they meet. A tenant’s API server lives in the management cluster, but HAMi’s webhook lives on the tenant’s worker nodes. Every GPU pod creation therefore depends on the API server reaching back into the tenant through Kamaji’s Konnectivity tunnel. Proving that path works was the main goal of this lab. Lab setup Everything runs as Docker containers on one Linux host; 4 CPU cores, 8 GB of free RAM and 20 GB of disk are enough. How do you test GPU sharing without a GPU? HAMi’s real device plugin talks to the NVIDIA driver, so it can’t start without hardware. The mock device plugin skips hardware discovery. You describe fake cards in a node annotation, and it registers gpumem and gpucores capacity from that. HAMi’s webhook, scheduler and quota logic then run exactly as they would on real nodes. Two simulated setups make the tenants easy to tell apart: tenant-a: 1 × NVIDIA A100 80 GB (81,920 MB, 100 cores) tenant-b: 2 × NVIDIA L4 24 GB (49,152 MB, 200 cores) Step-by-step build The build has five steps; step 3 creates both tenants at once, and steps 4 and 5 are repeated per tenant. Plain kubectl talks to the management cluster; --kubeconfig tenant-a.kubeconfig talks to a tenant. Step 1: Management cluster, cert-manager and MetalLB kind create cluster --name kamaji kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.21.2/cert-manager.yaml kubectl -n cert-manager wait pod --all --for=condition=Ready --timeout=180s kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/metallb/metallb/v0.16.1/config/manifests/metallb-frr-k8s.yaml kubectl -n metallb-system wait pod --all --for=condition=Ready --timeout=180s Find your kind network’s IPv4 subnet, then give MetalLB a range at the top of it: docker network inspect kind | grep Subnet cat < Step 2: Install Kamaji helm repo add clastix https://clastix.github.io/charts helm upgrade --install kamaji clastix/kamaji \ --namespace kamaji-system --create-namespace \ --set 'resources=null' --version 0.0.0+latest kubectl -n kamaji-system get pods Step 3: Create the Tenant Control Planes This creates both tenants, tenant-a and tenant-b : export TENANT_VERSION=v1.36.4 kubectl create namespace tenants for t in tenant-a tenant-b; do cat < Once both tenant control plane pods are Running, save a kubeconfig for each tenant: for t in tenant-a tenant-b; do kubectl -n tenants get secret ${t}-admin-kubeconfig -o jsonpath='{.data.admin\.conf}' | base64 -d > ${t}.kubeconfig kubectl --kubeconfig ${t}.kubeconfig cluster-info Done Each tenant control plane is a single pod in the tenants namespace of the management cluster, running on the kamaji-control-plane node. The 4/4 in the READY column are its four containers: kube-apiserver : the tenant’s API server, exposed through the MetalLB IP kube-scheduler : the tenant’s default scheduler kube-controller-manager : runs the tenant’s built-in controllers konnectivity-server : the management-cluster end of the tunnel that lets the API server reach the tenant’s worker nodes Step 4: Join a worker node Kamaji has no kind helper for workers, so the worker is a kindest/node container on the kind network, joined with standard kubeadm. Its version must match the tenant. docker run -d --name tenant-a-worker --hostname tenant-a-worker \ --network kind --privileged \ --security-opt seccomp=unconfined --security-opt apparmor=unconfined \ --tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /run -v /var -v /lib/modules:/lib/modules:ro \ kindest/node:v1.36.4@sha256:099e049362a1526b2db71494e1947aae99bd16290d7c895f2b7ea312e3cbfaed sleep 15 docker exec -i tenant-a-worker sh -c 'cat > /root/tenant-a.kubeconfig' < tenant-a.kubeconfig JOIN_CMD=$(docker exec tenant-a-worker kubeadm token create --print-join-command \ --kubeconfig /root/tenant-a.kubeconfig) echo "$JOIN_CMD" docker exec tenant-a-worker bash -c "${JOIN_CMD} --ignore-preflight-errors=all" Install Calico in the tenant (not the management cluster), with its pool set to the tenant podCidr : curl -sLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.31.2/manifests/calico.yaml sed -i 's|# - name: CALICO_IPV4POOL_CIDR|- name: CALICO_IPV4POOL_CIDR|; s|# value: "192.168.0.0/16"| value: "10.244.0.0/16"|' calico.yaml kubectl --kubeconfig tenant-a.kubeconfig apply -f calico.yaml kubectl --kubeconfig tenant-a.kubeconfig get nodes Step 5: HAMi and mock GPUs in the tenant # Don’t label the worker gpu=on; that starts HAMi’s real NVIDIA device plugin, which fails without a driver. export KUBECONFIG=$PWD/tenant-a.kubeconfig helm repo add hami-charts https://project-hami.github.io/HAMi/ helm install hami hami-charts/hami -n kube-system # wait for hami-scheduler Running, and the hami-scheduler-device ConfigMap to exist kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Project-HAMi/mock-device-plugin/master/k8s-mock-rbac.yaml kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Project-HAMi/mock-device-plugin/master/k8s-mock-plugin.yaml # Simulate 1 x A100 80 GB NODE=tenant-a-worker kubectl patch node $NODE --subresource=status --type=json \ -p '[{"op":"add","path":"/status/capacity/nvidia.com~1gpu","value":"10"}]' kubectl annotate node $NODE \ 'hami.io/node-nvidia-register=[{"id":"GPU-MOCK-0","count":10,"devmem":81920,"devcore":100,"type":"NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-80GB","health":true,"numa":0,"mode":"hami-core"}]' About 30 seconds later the node advertises the fake card: { "nvidia.com/gpu": "10", "nvidia.com/gpucores": "100", "nvidia.com/gpumem": "81920", "nvidia.com/gpumem-percentage": "100" } For tenant-b , repeat steps 4 and 5 with tenant-b names. Its annotation describes two cards ( GPU-MOCK-B0 and GPU-MOCK-B1 , 24,576 MB and 100 cores each), with nvidia.com/gpu capacity set to 20. How a GPU pod gets scheduled A GPU pod crosses from the management cluster into the tenant and back before it lands on a node, and that round trip is what makes the two projects work together. The dashed hop is the key integration point. The API server runs inside the management cluster, but HAMi’s webhook runs on the tenant worker, so the admission call travels through Kamaji’s Konnectivity tunnel. If that hop failed, GPU pods would fall back to the default scheduler and HAMi would never see them. Test results All eight tests passed. TC-03 and TC-05: three pods share one card Each pod asks for 20,000 MB and 30% of a GPU. This loop creates all three. After each pod is scheduled, it releases HAMi’s node lock by hand, because the mock plugin never does (see gotcha 2 ): export KUBECONFIG=$PWD/tenant-a.kubeconfig for i in 1 2 3; do cat < The webhook routed the pod to HAMi, and HAMi placed it on the mock card: $ kubectl get pod gpu-share-1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.schedulerName}' Hami-scheduler Annotations: hami.io/vgpu-devices-allocated: GPU-MOCK-0,NVIDIA,20000,30:; hami.io/vgpu-node: tenant-a-worker Events: Normal FilteringSucceed hami-scheduler find fit node(tenant-a-worker), 0 nodes not fit, 1 nodes fit Normal BindingSucceed hami-scheduler Successfully binding node [tenant-a-worker] to default/gpu-share-1 Three such pods ended up running on the same card: 60,000 MB and 90% of compute in use. NAME READY STATUS NODE gpu-share-1 1/1 Running tenant-a-worker gpu-share-2 1/1 Running tenant-a-worker gpu-share-3 1/1 Running tenant-a-worker TC-06 and TC-07: HAMi refuses to over-commit A fourth 30% pod would need 120 of 100 cores: cat < It stays Pending, and HAMi names the reason: $ kubectl describe pod gpu-share-4 | sed -n '/Events/,$p' Events: Type Reason Age From Message ---- ------ ---- ---- ------- Warning FailedScheduling 15s hami-scheduler 0/1 nodes are available: 1 1/1 CardInsufficientCore. no new claims to deallocate, preemption: 0/1 nodes are available: 1 No preemption victims found for incoming pod. Warning FilteringFailed 15s (x2 over 15s) hami-scheduler 1 nodes CardInsufficientCore(tenant-a-worker) Warning FilteringFailed 15s (x2 over 15s) hami-scheduler no available node, 1 nodes do not meet A pod asking for 90,000 MB exceeds the 81,920 MB card: cat < It stays Pending, this time with CardInsufficientMemory. TC-08: tenants can’t see each other Run the same queries against each tenant’s API server and compare what comes back: for t in a b; do echo "===== tenant-$t =====" kubectl --kubeconfig tenant-$t.kubeconfig get nodes kubectl --kubeconfig tenant-$t.kubeconfig get pods -A | grep -E 'gpu-|NAME' kubectl --kubeconfig tenant-$t.kubeconfig get nodes -o json \ | jq '.items[].status.allocatable | with_entries(select(.key|test("gpumem|gpucores")))' done ===== tenant-a ===== NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION tenant-a-worker Ready 29m v1.36.4 NAMESPACE NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE default gpu-share-1 1/1 Running 0 14m default gpu-share-2 1/1 Running 0 12m default gpu-share-3 1/1 Running 0 12m { "nvidia.com/gpucores": "100", "nvidia.com/gpumem": "81920", "nvidia.com/gpumem-percentage": "100" } ===== tenant-b ===== NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION tenant-b-worker Ready 5m28s v1.36.4 NAMESPACE NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE { "nvidia.com/gpucores": "200", "nvidia.com/gpumem": "49152", "nvidia.com/gpumem-percentage": "200" } Each tenant sees only its own worker, its own pods and its own GPU capacity: Both control planes run in the same management cluster, yet neither tenant’s API returns anything belonging to the other. Gotchas and fixes Few things broke along the way; each has a one-line fix. 1. IPv6 on the kind network broke the MetalLB pool. The gateway lookup from the Kamaji guide printed fc00:f853:ccd:e793::1172.18.0.1 , with the IPv6 and IPv4 gateways glued together. Fix: read the IPv4 subnet with docker network inspect kind | grep Subnet and write the range (172.18.255.200-172.18.255.250) directly. 2. GPU pods stuck on “node lock contention”. After the first GPU pod, the next ones stayed Pending with: Warning BindingFailed hami-scheduler node tenant-a-worker has been locked within 5m0s: node lock contention HAMi locks a node while binding a pod and marks it hami.io/bind-phase : allocating . On real nodes, HAMi’s device plugin completes the allocation and releases the lock. The mock plugin doesn’t, so the lock only expires after 5 minutes. Fix for the lab: do the device plugin’s job by hand. kubectl annotate pod gpu-share-1 hami.io/bind-phase=success --overwrite kubectl annotate node tenant-a-worker hami.io/mutex.lock- The next pod bound within seconds. This is a mock-only artifact, not a Kamaji or HAMi bug. What this lab does not prove The lab proves the wiring and the scheduling decisions, not runtime GPU isolation. No real memory or compute limits. HAMi-core enforces GPU limits inside the container through the NVIDIA driver. A mock card has nothing to enforce. No performance data. No CUDA workloads ran, so throughput and noisy-neighbour effects are untested. Hand-made device data. On real nodes, HAMi’s device plugin writes the node annotation and completes each allocation; here I did both by hand. Unofficial worker path. Joining kindest/node containers works, but Kamaji’s supported route for workers is kubeadm on real machines or Cluster API. Conclusion Kamaji and HAMi fit together without any glue code. Kamaji gives each team its own Kubernetes API without a control plane machine per team, and HAMi turns each GPU into a pool of slices inside those clusters. The one real integration risk, the hosted API server calling HAMi’s webhook back through Konnectivity, worked on the first try. If you have no GPU, the mock device plugin is enough to build and test the whole platform before you buy one.

For tenant-b, repeat steps 4 and 5 with tenant-b names. Its annotation describes two cards (GPU-MOCK-B0 and GPU-MOCK-B1, 24,576 MB and 100 cores each), with nvidia.com/gpu capacity set to 20.

How a GPU pod gets scheduled

A GPU pod crosses from the management cluster into the tenant and back before it lands on a node, and that round trip is what makes the two projects work together.

The dashed hop is the key integration point. The API server runs inside the management cluster, but HAMi’s webhook runs on the tenant worker, so the admission call travels through Kamaji’s Konnectivity tunnel. If that hop failed, GPU pods would fall back to the default scheduler and HAMi would never see them.

Test results

All eight tests passed.

TC-03 and TC-05: three pods share one card

Each pod asks for 20,000 MB and 30% of a GPU. This loop creates all three. After each pod is scheduled, it releases HAMi’s node lock by hand, because the mock plugin never does (see gotcha 2):

export KUBECONFIG=$PWD/tenant-a.kubeconfig

for i in 1 2 3; do
cat <

The webhook routed the pod to HAMi, and HAMi placed it on the mock card:

$ kubectl get pod gpu-share-1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.schedulerName}'

Hami-scheduler

Annotations:  hami.io/vgpu-devices-allocated: GPU-MOCK-0,NVIDIA,20000,30:;

             hami.io/vgpu-node: tenant-a-worker

Events:

 Normal  FilteringSucceed  hami-scheduler  find fit node(tenant-a-worker), 0 nodes not fit, 1 nodes fit

 Normal  BindingSucceed    hami-scheduler  Successfully binding node [tenant-a-worker] to default/gpu-share-1

Three such pods ended up running on the same card: 60,000 MB and 90% of compute in use.

NAME          READY   STATUS    NODE
gpu-share-1   1/1     Running   tenant-a-worker
gpu-share-2   1/1     Running   tenant-a-worker
gpu-share-3   1/1     Running   tenant-a-worker

TC-06 and TC-07: HAMi refuses to over-commit

A fourth 30% pod would need 120 of 100 cores:

cat <

It stays Pending, and HAMi names the reason:

$ kubectl describe pod gpu-share-4 | sed -n '/Events/,$p'
Events:
 Type     Reason            Age                From            Message
 ----     ------            ----               ----            -------
 Warning  FailedScheduling  15s                hami-scheduler  0/1 nodes are available: 1 1/1 CardInsufficientCore. no new claims to deallocate, preemption: 0/1 nodes are available: 1 No preemption victims found for incoming pod.

 Warning  FilteringFailed   15s (x2 over 15s)  hami-scheduler  1 nodes CardInsufficientCore(tenant-a-worker)
 Warning  FilteringFailed   15s (x2 over 15s)  hami-scheduler  no available node, 1 nodes do not meet

A pod asking for 90,000 MB exceeds the 81,920 MB card:

cat <

It stays Pending, this time with CardInsufficientMemory.

TC-08: tenants can’t see each other

Run the same queries against each tenant’s API server and compare what comes back:

for t in a b; do
 echo "===== tenant-$t ====="

 kubectl --kubeconfig tenant-$t.kubeconfig get nodes
 kubectl --kubeconfig tenant-$t.kubeconfig get pods -A | grep -E 'gpu-|NAME'
 kubectl --kubeconfig tenant-$t.kubeconfig get nodes -o json \
   | jq '.items[].status.allocatable | with_entries(select(.key|test("gpumem|gpucores")))'
done

===== tenant-a =====
NAME              STATUS   ROLES    AGE   VERSION
tenant-a-worker   Ready       29m   v1.36.4
NAMESPACE     NAME          READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
default       gpu-share-1   1/1     Running   0          14m
default       gpu-share-2   1/1     Running   0          12m
default       gpu-share-3   1/1     Running   0          12m
{
 "nvidia.com/gpucores": "100",
 "nvidia.com/gpumem": "81920",

}
===== tenant-b =====

tenant-b-worker   Ready       5m28s   v1.36.4
NAMESPACE     NAME          READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
{
 "nvidia.com/gpucores": "200",
 "nvidia.com/gpumem": "49152",

}

Each tenant sees only its own worker, its own pods and its own GPU capacity:

Both control planes run in the same management cluster, yet neither tenant’s API returns anything belonging to the other.

Gotchas and fixes

Few things broke along the way; each has a one-line fix.

1. IPv6 on the kind network broke the MetalLB pool. The gateway lookup from the Kamaji guide printed fc00:f853:ccd:e793::1172.18.0.1, with the IPv6 and IPv4 gateways glued together. Fix: read the IPv4 subnet with docker network inspect kind | grep Subnet and write the range (172.18.255.200-172.18.255.250) directly.

2. GPU pods stuck on “node lock contention”. After the first GPU pod, the next ones stayed Pending with:

Warning  BindingFailed  hami-scheduler  node tenant-a-worker has been locked within 5m0s: node lock contention

HAMi locks a node while binding a pod and marks it hami.io/bind-phase: allocating. On real nodes, HAMi’s device plugin completes the allocation and releases the lock. The mock plugin doesn’t, so the lock only expires after 5 minutes. Fix for the lab: do the device plugin’s job by hand.

kubectl annotate pod gpu-share-1 hami.io/bind-phase=success --overwrite
kubectl annotate node tenant-a-worker hami.io/mutex.lock-

The next pod bound within seconds. This is a mock-only artifact, not a Kamaji or HAMi bug.

What this lab does not prove

The lab proves the wiring and the scheduling decisions, not runtime GPU isolation.

  • No real memory or compute limits. HAMi-core enforces GPU limits inside the container through the NVIDIA driver. A mock card has nothing to enforce.
  • No performance data. No CUDA workloads ran, so throughput and noisy-neighbour effects are untested.
  • Hand-made device data. On real nodes, HAMi’s device plugin writes the node annotation and completes each allocation; here I did both by hand.
  • Unofficial worker path. Joining kindest/node containers works, but Kamaji’s supported route for workers is kubeadm on real machines or Cluster API.
Conclusion

Kamaji and HAMi fit together without any glue code. Kamaji gives each team its own Kubernetes API without a control plane machine per team, and HAMi turns each GPU into a pool of slices inside those clusters. The one real integration risk, the hosted API server calling HAMi’s webhook back through Konnectivity, worked on the first try. If you have no GPU, the mock device plugin is enough to build and test the whole platform before you buy one.

items.title: Hackers Use New BlackX Bootkit to Bypass Windows Secure Boot on Fully Patched Systems
items.summary: A new UEFI bootkit called BlackX has been used in cyberespionage attacks against diplomatic organizations in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan. The malware targets Secure Boot, a feature designed to help stop untrusted software from running before Windows starts. Researchers say the infected computers had received Windows updates, but a key Secure Boot protection had not been fully applied. Securelist analysts reported the findings on October 22, 2026. They say BlackX uses Baton Drop, a vulnerability tracked as CVE-2022-21894, and shares parts of its design with the BlackLotus bootkit. The findings show why an installed update does not always mean that the protection it is meant to provide has been fully activated. Securelist’s BlackX report describes the malware and the campaign in detail. BlackX is installed after attackers have already gained access to a victim’s network and administrator-level rights. Its installer, inst.exe , works with an encrypted file named PVMDIJGKAX2 , which contains components needed to install the malware. Securelist says this design can make it harder for incident responders to recover all the bootkit’s parts from the installer alone. The bootkit uses Baton Drop to load attacker-controlled EFI files and interfere with Secure Boot. EFI files run during the computer’s startup process, before Windows loads. By gaining a place in that early sequence, a bootkit can give malicious code a chance to run before many operating-system security tools are active. Hackers Use New BlackX Bootkit Readers can learn more about related boot-time risks in this Cybersecurity News report on managing UEFI Secure Boot settings . Securelist says the campaign’s kernel driver attempts to weaken security tools by disrupting process, thread, and registry callbacks, and by interfering with Event Tracing for Windows (ETW), which software can use to collect system activity. It also tries to hide its files: when certain file requests are made, the driver reportedly returns a handle to the legitimate calc.exe process instead of to the requested malicious file. BlackLotus advertisement (Source – Securelist) The bootkit also delivers user-mode malware for espionage. One payload is a remote-access Trojan that can load additional .NET code and use Google Drive, OneDrive, or Yandex.Disk for command-and-control communication. Another, named OxiDLLRunner by the researchers, decrypts a file called v8_context_snapshot.bin and runs a Rust payload that contacts a reported command-and-control domain. The report links the activity to APT41 with medium confidence, based on overlaps with previously reported activity and shared technical details. That assessment is not definitive attribution. Why patched systems were still at risk The issue was not simply that the targeted computers lacked Windows updates. Securelist says the protection against Baton Drop depends on revoking trust in the “Windows Production PCA 2011” certificate used to sign vulnerable UEFI components. Installing an update and applying that revocation are separate steps in the process described by the researchers. Microsoft’s guidance for CVE-2023-24932 also describes multiple steps for deploying Secure Boot protections, including updating certificates, boot managers, and the UEFI revocation list. Its instructions warn that blocking older boot components can affect recovery media and other boot options, so administrators should test changes and prepare recovery options before applying them broadly. See Microsoft’s Secure Boot revocation guidance . The distinction matters because Windows may report that updates are installed even when the firmware’s forbidden-signature list has not yet been updated as intended. Securelist reported that the certificate’s expiration on October 19, 2026, did not by itself stop vulnerable binaries from loading; the certificate must be blocked by the relevant revocation mechanism. Administrators should therefore verify their devices’ Secure Boot configuration and revocation status, following Microsoft’s current instructions and accounting for their organization’s boot and recovery needs. BlackX is not the first bootkit story to raise questions about trust in old boot components. Cybersecurity News has previously covered BlackLotus and how a downgrade technique could leave a Windows device exposed despite an up-to-date status. That background helps explain why Secure Boot protection depends on more than the visible update state of Windows. The main lesson for defenders is to confirm that Secure Boot protections are active in firmware, not only that Windows updates have been installed. Organizations should review Microsoft’s deployment guidance, verify that the necessary revocations have taken effect, and check boot and recovery media for compatibility. Since BlackX was installed after attackers obtained administrator access, teams should also investigate suspicious administrative activity and boot-related changes, and review endpoint alerts for signs that security monitoring has been tampered with. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Type Indicator Installer file inst.exe Encrypted file PVMDIJGKAX2 Installer path and command line C:\ProgramData\Intel\inst.exe PVMDIJGKAX2 Q46F6MDLI3RX2KV1 Delivered executable name googleupdate.exe Original filename jcef_helper.exe MD5 AF8A983B9ADA07EAE1259BF2953ABD40 Related payload file v8_context_snapshot.bin Reported command-and-control domain www[.]archivetj[.]com Driver certificate serial number 0bcdf5e0da32d68900b8b7638459d072 Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally defanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: Compromised TLS Certificates
items.summary: The Indian CA eMudhra Limited has eight TLS certificates with laughably weak private keys : The compromised eMudhra keys were defective at a level that’s challenging the imagination of many of the engineers studying the incident. A normal size for a NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private key contains roughly 384 bits of entropy, a size allowing almost 2 384 , or a number with 116 digits, different possibilities. The private key sizes of the compromised keys ranged from 3 to 8 bits. Astonishingly, the private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237. “That is extremely in the ‘this should not be possible’ category,” Valdorda said. “Maybe some horribly dangerous key generation interface has a ‘size’ parameter and they set it to 1 by mistake???” Ben Cartwright-Cox, director of BGP.tools, said: “My guess is that it’s example code that accidentally leaked to production, but hard to know. But it’s bonkers that no one noticed.” At this early stage, the most immediate threat appears to be for those using VPNs, especially in countries with governments likely to maliciously intercept traffic. There are likely many other cases for concern. End users largely have no recourse other than to hold off using many non-browser forms of TLS communication until they receive assurances updates are in place. The whole certificate regime has long been a mess: The incident is the latest to expose a fatal flaw in the TLS regimen. It’s only as strong as its weakest link, which in this case was eMudhra. Fortunately, transparency logs account for much of that failure, but this measure requires parties to actively monitor massive feeds and works only after unauthorized certificates have been issued. eMudhra representatives weren’t immediately available to answer questions. One caveat: exploiting compromised certificates requires an active adversary-in-the-middle attack, meaning the attacker must act as a proxy between two TLS parties and receive encrypted traffic, decrypt it, reencrypt it, and send it to the other party. Such capabilities, in some cases, are usually limited to only the most well-resourced attackers. People with control of a local network­at a coffee shop, university, or other organization­face much less of a challenge. Cleanup of this is going to be another mess—and it’s right on top of the PHP vulnerabilities. Some more information .

The Indian CA eMudhra Limited has eight TLS certificates with laughably weak private keys:

The compromised eMudhra keys were defective at a level that’s challenging the imagination of many of the engineers studying the incident. A normal size for a NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private key contains roughly 384 bits of entropy, a size allowing almost 2384, or a number with 116 digits, different possibilities. The private key sizes of the compromised keys ranged from 3 to 8 bits. Astonishingly, the private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237.

“That is extremely in the ‘this should not be possible’ category,” Valdorda said. “Maybe some horribly dangerous key generation interface has a ‘size’ parameter and they set it to 1 by mistake???”

Ben Cartwright-Cox, director of BGP.tools, said: “My guess is that it’s example code that accidentally leaked to production, but hard to know. But it’s bonkers that no one noticed.”

At this early stage, the most immediate threat appears to be for those using VPNs, especially in countries with governments likely to maliciously intercept traffic. There are likely many other cases for concern. End users largely have no recourse other than to hold off using many non-browser forms of TLS communication until they receive assurances updates are in place.

The whole certificate regime has long been a mess:

The incident is the latest to expose a fatal flaw in the TLS regimen. It’s only as strong as its weakest link, which in this case was eMudhra. Fortunately, transparency logs account for much of that failure, but this measure requires parties to actively monitor massive feeds and works only after unauthorized certificates have been issued. eMudhra representatives weren’t immediately available to answer questions.

One caveat: exploiting compromised certificates requires an active adversary-in-the-middle attack, meaning the attacker must act as a proxy between two TLS parties and receive encrypted traffic, decrypt it, reencrypt it, and send it to the other party. Such capabilities, in some cases, are usually limited to only the most well-resourced attackers. People with control of a local network­at a coffee shop, university, or other organization­face much less of a challenge.

Cleanup of this is going to be another mess—and it’s right on top of the PHP vulnerabilities.

items.title: CVE-2026-111497: Node.js Brotli Decoder Flaw Enables Remote Code Execution
items.summary: Node.js has released security updates addressing CVE-2026-111497, a high-severity vulnerability in its bundled Brotli decompression code that can potentially enable remote code execution. The flaw is an out-of-bounds write triggered when a vulnerable decoder processes specially crafted Brotli-compressed data. The issue affects all currently supported Node.js branches—22.x, 24.x, and 26.x. Node.js addressed the vulnerability in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1 as part of the October 21, 2026 security release, which fixed ten vulnerabilities in total. The risk is particularly relevant because Brotli compression is commonly used for HTTP traffic. Node.js applications can invoke the vulnerable decoder directly through node:zlib or automatically when fetch() receives a response using Content-Encoding: br. An application may therefore be exposed whenever attacker-controlled Brotli content reaches the decoder through an inbound request, remote response, proxy workflow, or other data-processing path. For CVE-2026-111497 detection, security teams should prioritize Node.js applications that process untrusted compressed content and monitor them for crashes, abnormal memory behavior, unusual child processes, and suspicious activity immediately following Brotli decompression. SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform enables security teams to strengthen visibility into emerging vulnerability exploitation and associated post-compromise behavior with detection content deployable across SIEM, EDR, and Data Lake technologies. Click Explore Detections to access relevant detection content and hunting logic. To Detect CVE-2026-111497, defenders should correlate Node.js application telemetry with endpoint, proxy, web, and network activity to identify suspicious behavior surrounding compressed HTTP traffic. Security teams can also leverage Prime Architect to transform fresh vulnerability intelligence into Sigma rules and hunting queries, validate detection logic, and translate relevant detection content across supported security platforms. Contact Sales CVE-2026-111497 analysis The vulnerability resides in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. Brotli is a compression algorithm widely used to reduce web content size, and Node.js includes its own copy of the library. A malformed compressed stream can trigger an out-of-bounds write, causing the decoder to write outside the memory buffer allocated for decompressed data. The upstream fix changes the decoder so that invalid input is rejected earlier instead of allowing execution to continue into the unsafe memory-write condition. CVE-2026-111497 affects Node.js 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x before the October 21 security releases. The patched versions are: Node.js 22.23.4 Node.js 24.22.1 Node.js 26.12.1 Node.js 20.x and earlier releases have reached end of life and do not receive the security update, so organizations using those versions should migrate to a supported branch. The underlying problem is not limited to Node.js. The vulnerable code comes from the Brotli project itself, and the corresponding fixes were released in Brotli 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1. Other applications that embed vulnerable Brotli versions may therefore need separate updates even if they do not use Node.js. The attack surface depends on how compressed data reaches the application. Direct use of Brotli decompression APIs is one obvious route. However, Node.js can also automatically process Brotli-compressed HTTP responses when applications use fetch(). This makes applications that retrieve attacker-controlled content especially relevant. Examples include URL preview services, crawlers, webhook processors, proxy platforms, content scanners, conversion services, and applications that allow users to submit remote URLs. Inbound traffic can create another path where a web application or middleware accepts Brotli-compressed request bodies. Security teams should therefore examine actual application data flows rather than limiting exposure assessment to explicit Brotli calls in source code. The details for CVE-2026-111497 show why the issue can have consequences beyond a simple service crash. Memory corruption can potentially affect nearby process state and, depending on platform protections and runtime conditions, lead to memory disclosure or arbitrary code execution. Node.js explicitly describes the vulnerability as capable of remote code execution, but its practical exploitability deserves nuance. The flaw is rated High by the Node.js Project rather than Critical. A public CVE-2026-111497 PoC released after disclosure achieved code execution against a deliberately weakened test build. Against a standard Node.js build, the researcher reported a crash and limited process-memory disclosure but did not achieve reliable code execution. This means the memory-corruption primitive is demonstrated, while successful RCE against normal production builds depends on additional exploit conditions. Patched Node.js versions reject the malformed content used in the demonstration. As of October 22, no exploitation in the wild had been reported. Accordingly, campaign-specific CVE-2026-111497 IOCs such as malicious IP addresses, domains, payload hashes, or confirmed exploit request signatures have not been published in the cited research. Security teams should instead focus on behavioral indicators such as: Unexpected crashes of Node.js services handling compressed traffic Segmentation faults or native decoder failures Abnormal memory-protection or exploit-prevention alerts Node.js spawning shells or command interpreters Unusual outbound connections immediately after Brotli processing Suspicious compressed requests from unfamiliar sources Server-side fetch() activity reaching untrusted infrastructure Unexpected file or process changes originating from a Node.js service account The October 21 Node.js release also fixed additional high-severity issues involving TLS hostname validation and DNS processing. CybersecurityNews notes that organizations should treat the release as a broader runtime security update rather than focusing exclusively on the Brotli flaw. The same release also refreshed certificate trust information following the eMudhra certificate authority compromise, further increasing the value of upgrading rather than attempting to backport only one fix. CVE-2026-111497 Mitigation The primary CVE-2026-111497 mitigation is to upgrade all supported Node.js installations to a patched version: 22.x → 22.23.4 or later 24.x → 24.22.1 or later 26.x → 26.12.1 or later The Node.js Project provides no equivalent temporary runtime workaround for the Brotli vulnerability, making upgrading the reliable remediation path. After updating the runtime, administrators should restart all affected Node.js services. Long-running processes continue using the old runtime until restarted. Containerized workloads require additional attention. CybersecurityNews specifically recommends rebuilding container images so deployed applications contain the patched Node.js runtime. Updating Node.js on the underlying host does not replace a vulnerable runtime already embedded inside a container image. Organizations using Brotli independently should also update vulnerable library versions. Software inventories and SBOMs can help identify embedded copies in native applications, appliances, development tools, and third-party packages. Where immediate upgrading is not possible, organizations can temporarily reduce attack surface by: Rejecting Brotli-compressed request bodies where compression is unnecessary Restricting server-side HTTP requests to trusted destinations Preventing users from supplying arbitrary remote URLs Limiting outbound connectivity from vulnerable workloads Disabling optional Brotli processing where operationally feasible Monitoring application crashes and memory-related errors closely Inspecting unusual child processes launched by Node.js Vercel introduced firewall protections to block malicious Brotli data arriving through inbound requests. However, The Hacker News notes that those rules do not protect applications that independently fetch malicious Brotli responses from external servers, illustrating why WAF filtering cannot replace the runtime upgrade. Administrators should also confirm the runtime actually used by production workloads after patching. Package-manager output alone is insufficient when older Node.js binaries remain inside containers, serverless bundles, packaged applications, or manually installed runtime directories. If exploitation is suspected, responders should isolate the affected workload and preserve application, endpoint, proxy, and network telemetry. Crash dumps may be especially valuable because the vulnerability directly affects process memory. Security teams should investigate: Unexpected Node.js child processes Newly created files or persistence mechanisms Unusual outbound connections Changes to application or deployment configuration Credentials and secrets available in environment variables API keys, tokens, and cloud credentials accessible to the Node.js process Backend data stores reachable using the application’s service identity Because limited process-memory disclosure has been demonstrated, secrets resident in the vulnerable application’s memory should be considered potentially exposed when suspicious exploitation activity is identified, even if arbitrary code execution cannot be conclusively proven. Organizations should also review the privileges assigned to affected services. Successful exploitation of a minimally privileged container has different consequences from exploitation of a Node.js process holding cloud credentials, database administrative access, CI/CD tokens, or deployment permissions. SOC Prime customers can leverage behavior-based detection content to identify vulnerability exploitation and related attacker activity while vulnerable systems are discovered and remediated. Disclaimer: Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added. FAQ What is CVE-2026-111497 and how does it work? CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the Brotli decoder included with Node.js. A maliciously constructed Brotli stream can cause the decoder to write beyond its intended memory buffer. Depending on the environment and exploitation conditions, this can lead to a process crash, disclosure of process memory, or potentially execution of attacker-controlled code. The vulnerable decoder may be reached through direct decompression APIs or automatically when Node.js processes Brotli-compressed HTTP responses. When was CVE-2026-111497 first discovered? The Node.js Project publicly disclosed and patched the vulnerability on October 21, 2026. OpenAI Codex Security researchers Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer are credited with reporting the issue to Node.js. The Hacker News reports that the corresponding Brotli source-code change was first made upstream in February 2026 but was distributed as a security fix in October. What is the impact of CVE-2026-111497 on systems? Successful exploitation can corrupt memory within a vulnerable Node.js process. Possible consequences include denial of service through application crashes, exposure of process memory, and potentially remote code execution. The actual impact depends on whether attacker-controlled Brotli content reaches the decoder and whether the memory-corruption primitive can bypass protections in the target runtime and operating system. If code execution is achieved, the attacker would generally inherit the permissions and access available to the compromised Node.js process, potentially exposing application data, credentials, cloud resources, or connected backend systems. Can CVE-2026-111497 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Node.js 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x installations remain vulnerable if they have not been updated to the October 21 patched releases. Organizations running Node.js 20.x or older should migrate to a supported release because end-of-life branches do not receive this fix. Rebuild container images, update independently bundled Brotli libraries, and verify that production services are actually running the patched binaries. Until patching is complete, reduce exposure to untrusted Brotli input and restrict server-side requests to approved destinations. Monitor vulnerable services for crashes, unusual child processes, unexpected network activity, and other signs of memory exploitation. Node.js has released security updates addressing CVE-2026-111497, a high-severity vulnerability in its bundled Brotli decompression code that can potentially enable remote code execution. The flaw is an out-of-bounds write triggered when a vulnerable decoder processes specially crafted Brotli-compressed data.

The issue affects all currently supported Node.js branches—22.x, 24.x, and 26.x. Node.js addressed the vulnerability in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1 as part of the October 21, 2026 security release, which fixed ten vulnerabilities in total.

The risk is particularly relevant because Brotli compression is commonly used for HTTP traffic. Node.js applications can invoke the vulnerable decoder directly through node:zlib or automatically when fetch() receives a response using Content-Encoding: br. An application may therefore be exposed whenever attacker-controlled Brotli content reaches the decoder through an inbound request, remote response, proxy workflow, or other data-processing path.

For CVE-2026-111497 detection, security teams should prioritize Node.js applications that process untrusted compressed content and monitor them for crashes, abnormal memory behavior, unusual child processes, and suspicious activity immediately following Brotli decompression.

Click Explore Detections to access relevant detection content and hunting logic. To Detect CVE-2026-111497, defenders should correlate Node.js application telemetry with endpoint, proxy, web, and network activity to identify suspicious behavior surrounding compressed HTTP traffic.

Security teams can also leverage Prime Architect to transform fresh vulnerability intelligence into Sigma rules and hunting queries, validate detection logic, and translate relevant detection content across supported security platforms.

Contact Sales

CVE-2026-111497 analysis

The vulnerability resides in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. Brotli is a compression algorithm widely used to reduce web content size, and Node.js includes its own copy of the library.

A malformed compressed stream can trigger an out-of-bounds write, causing the decoder to write outside the memory buffer allocated for decompressed data. The upstream fix changes the decoder so that invalid input is rejected earlier instead of allowing execution to continue into the unsafe memory-write condition.

CVE-2026-111497 affects Node.js 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x before the October 21 security releases. The patched versions are:

  • Node.js 22.23.4
  • Node.js 24.22.1
  • Node.js 26.12.1

Node.js 20.x and earlier releases have reached end of life and do not receive the security update, so organizations using those versions should migrate to a supported branch.

The underlying problem is not limited to Node.js. The vulnerable code comes from the Brotli project itself, and the corresponding fixes were released in Brotli 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1. Other applications that embed vulnerable Brotli versions may therefore need separate updates even if they do not use Node.js.

The attack surface depends on how compressed data reaches the application. Direct use of Brotli decompression APIs is one obvious route. However, Node.js can also automatically process Brotli-compressed HTTP responses when applications use fetch().

This makes applications that retrieve attacker-controlled content especially relevant. Examples include URL preview services, crawlers, webhook processors, proxy platforms, content scanners, conversion services, and applications that allow users to submit remote URLs.

Inbound traffic can create another path where a web application or middleware accepts Brotli-compressed request bodies. Security teams should therefore examine actual application data flows rather than limiting exposure assessment to explicit Brotli calls in source code.

The details for CVE-2026-111497 show why the issue can have consequences beyond a simple service crash. Memory corruption can potentially affect nearby process state and, depending on platform protections and runtime conditions, lead to memory disclosure or arbitrary code execution.

Node.js explicitly describes the vulnerability as capable of remote code execution, but its practical exploitability deserves nuance. The flaw is rated High by the Node.js Project rather than Critical.

A public CVE-2026-111497 PoC released after disclosure achieved code execution against a deliberately weakened test build. Against a standard Node.js build, the researcher reported a crash and limited process-memory disclosure but did not achieve reliable code execution. This means the memory-corruption primitive is demonstrated, while successful RCE against normal production builds depends on additional exploit conditions.

Patched Node.js versions reject the malformed content used in the demonstration. As of October 22, no exploitation in the wild had been reported.

Accordingly, campaign-specific CVE-2026-111497 IOCs such as malicious IP addresses, domains, payload hashes, or confirmed exploit request signatures have not been published in the cited research.

Security teams should instead focus on behavioral indicators such as:

  • Unexpected crashes of Node.js services handling compressed traffic
  • Segmentation faults or native decoder failures
  • Abnormal memory-protection or exploit-prevention alerts
  • Node.js spawning shells or command interpreters
  • Unusual outbound connections immediately after Brotli processing
  • Suspicious compressed requests from unfamiliar sources
  • Server-side fetch() activity reaching untrusted infrastructure
  • Unexpected file or process changes originating from a Node.js service account

The October 21 Node.js release also fixed additional high-severity issues involving TLS hostname validation and DNS processing. CybersecurityNews notes that organizations should treat the release as a broader runtime security update rather than focusing exclusively on the Brotli flaw.

The same release also refreshed certificate trust information following the eMudhra certificate authority compromise, further increasing the value of upgrading rather than attempting to backport only one fix.

CVE-2026-111497 Mitigation

The primary CVE-2026-111497 mitigation is to upgrade all supported Node.js installations to a patched version:

  • 22.x → 22.23.4 or later
  • 24.x → 24.22.1 or later
  • 26.x → 26.12.1 or later

The Node.js Project provides no equivalent temporary runtime workaround for the Brotli vulnerability, making upgrading the reliable remediation path.

After updating the runtime, administrators should restart all affected Node.js services. Long-running processes continue using the old runtime until restarted.

Containerized workloads require additional attention. CybersecurityNews specifically recommends rebuilding container images so deployed applications contain the patched Node.js runtime. Updating Node.js on the underlying host does not replace a vulnerable runtime already embedded inside a container image.

Organizations using Brotli independently should also update vulnerable library versions. Software inventories and SBOMs can help identify embedded copies in native applications, appliances, development tools, and third-party packages.

Where immediate upgrading is not possible, organizations can temporarily reduce attack surface by:

  • Rejecting Brotli-compressed request bodies where compression is unnecessary
  • Restricting server-side HTTP requests to trusted destinations
  • Preventing users from supplying arbitrary remote URLs
  • Limiting outbound connectivity from vulnerable workloads
  • Disabling optional Brotli processing where operationally feasible
  • Monitoring application crashes and memory-related errors closely
  • Inspecting unusual child processes launched by Node.js

Vercel introduced firewall protections to block malicious Brotli data arriving through inbound requests. However, The Hacker News notes that those rules do not protect applications that independently fetch malicious Brotli responses from external servers, illustrating why WAF filtering cannot replace the runtime upgrade.

Administrators should also confirm the runtime actually used by production workloads after patching. Package-manager output alone is insufficient when older Node.js binaries remain inside containers, serverless bundles, packaged applications, or manually installed runtime directories.

If exploitation is suspected, responders should isolate the affected workload and preserve application, endpoint, proxy, and network telemetry. Crash dumps may be especially valuable because the vulnerability directly affects process memory.

Security teams should investigate:

  • Unexpected Node.js child processes
  • Newly created files or persistence mechanisms
  • Unusual outbound connections
  • Changes to application or deployment configuration
  • Credentials and secrets available in environment variables
  • API keys, tokens, and cloud credentials accessible to the Node.js process
  • Backend data stores reachable using the application’s service identity

Because limited process-memory disclosure has been demonstrated, secrets resident in the vulnerable application’s memory should be considered potentially exposed when suspicious exploitation activity is identified, even if arbitrary code execution cannot be conclusively proven.

Organizations should also review the privileges assigned to affected services. Successful exploitation of a minimally privileged container has different consequences from exploitation of a Node.js process holding cloud credentials, database administrative access, CI/CD tokens, or deployment permissions.

FAQ

What is CVE-2026-111497 and how does it work?

CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the Brotli decoder included with Node.js. A maliciously constructed Brotli stream can cause the decoder to write beyond its intended memory buffer. Depending on the environment and exploitation conditions, this can lead to a process crash, disclosure of process memory, or potentially execution of attacker-controlled code. The vulnerable decoder may be reached through direct decompression APIs or automatically when Node.js processes Brotli-compressed HTTP responses.

When was CVE-2026-111497 first discovered?

The Node.js Project publicly disclosed and patched the vulnerability on October 21, 2026. OpenAI Codex Security researchers Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer are credited with reporting the issue to Node.js. The Hacker News reports that the corresponding Brotli source-code change was first made upstream in February 2026 but was distributed as a security fix in October.

What is the impact of CVE-2026-111497 on systems?

Successful exploitation can corrupt memory within a vulnerable Node.js process. Possible consequences include denial of service through application crashes, exposure of process memory, and potentially remote code execution. The actual impact depends on whether attacker-controlled Brotli content reaches the decoder and whether the memory-corruption primitive can bypass protections in the target runtime and operating system. If code execution is achieved, the attacker would generally inherit the permissions and access available to the compromised Node.js process, potentially exposing application data, credentials, cloud resources, or connected backend systems.

Can CVE-2026-111497 still affect me in 2026?

Yes. Node.js 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x installations remain vulnerable if they have not been updated to the October 21 patched releases. Organizations running Node.js 20.x or older should migrate to a supported release because end-of-life branches do not receive this fix. Applications that embed vulnerable Brotli libraries independently may also remain exposed even if Node.js itself has been updated.

How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-111497?

Upgrade Node.js to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, 26.12.1, or a newer supported release and restart affected workloads. Rebuild container images, update independently bundled Brotli libraries, and verify that production services are actually running the patched binaries. Until patching is complete, reduce exposure to untrusted Brotli input and restrict server-side requests to approved destinations. Monitor vulnerable services for crashes, unusual child processes, unexpected network activity, and other signs of memory exploitation. If suspicious activity is discovered, isolate the workload, preserve forensic evidence, and rotate sensitive credentials available to the affected Node.js process.

items.title: Crime Stoppers chapter freezes tips after breach breaks anonymity promise
items.summary: A breach exposed personal information in supposedly anonymous crime reports. Now one Crime Stoppers chapter has stopped accepting tips because it cannot guarantee anonymity. Toronto Crime Stoppers, which works with the community, police, and media to help solve crimes, has paused phone, website, and app submissions while it seeks a safer system. The breach occurred in March and involved P3 Global Intel, the Texas-based tip-management platform owned by Navigate360. Its software is used by Crime Stoppers programs and other organizations in the US and elsewhere. An October CBC investigation revealed the Canadian impact: More than 1.5 million tips spanning 25 years were exposed, with over 850,000 containing personal information. That included addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and some banking details associated with rewards. The exposed details belonged to tipsters, people named in allegations, and others, including police and Crime Stoppers staff. Following CBC’s reporting, Toronto Crime Stoppers acknowledged that its promise of anonymity had been broken for some users. The organization stopped accepting tips, saying it could no longer guarantee users’ anonymity. In an October 21 statement , the organization says identifying details are normally removed before tips reach investigators, but some original submissions containing potentially identifying information were stolen from P3. For affected tipsters, exposure could create a risk of retaliation, intimidation, or extortion. Scammers could also use details of a genuine tip to make an approach more convincing. Unfortunately, the pause removes a reporting option for people afraid to approach police. Toronto police still accept reports directly, but warn that those channels are not anonymous. How to stay safe Toronto Crime Stoppers warned people worried about exposure to watch for impersonators. It says it will never contact them first to request a tip number, password, or other information. The statement did not describe an individual notification process or offer a way to check whether a particular tip was affected. For anyone wanting to submit a new tip, the organization’s message was clear: “Until we have a safer way to protect you, please do not send us tips by phone, online, or through the app.” Anyone in immediate danger should call 911. During the pause, non-emergency reports in Toronto should go directly to Toronto police, with the understanding that those channels are not anonymous. If you use a different Crime Stoppers program, check its official website for updates and advice about its reporting system. For more general advice if your information may have been exposed, read our blog “ Involved in a data breach? Here’s what you need to know .” What do cybercriminals know about you? items.title: SBI Notifies Customers Impacted by the Recent Cyber Incident
items.summary: State Bank of India (SBI) has individually notified customers whose information was identified in a recent cyber incident, sending alerts through email and WhatsApp. In its latest advisory on October 23 , the bank said customer account balances and funds remain safe while investigators examine the suspected exposure of personal information found on the dark web. The update shifts the bank’s response from an initial public disclosure to direct communication with customers. According to The Economic Times, SBI said it had informed all customers whose data was identified as involved. The bank also warned users to stay alert for suspicious calls, messages, and emails, and never share passwords, PINs, or one-time passwords. SBI’s preliminary review examined approximately 375,000 records available on the dark web and identified 3,897 customer records containing personally identifiable information. These figures represent different measures. The larger number describes the records reviewed, not a confirmed count of affected SBI customers or compromised bank accounts. SBI Notifies Customers Impacted By Cyber Incident The information reportedly included names, registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, email addresses and home addresses. Other fields included gender, branch details, Customer Information File identifiers, and information linked to loan inquiries and lead records. These details can identify customers and provide context about their banking relationships. pic.twitter.com/lrIZtM5nnQ — State Bank of India (@TheOfficialSBI) October 23, 2026 As covered in Cybersecurity News’ earlier report on the SBI data loss incident , the disclosure did not establish how the information was obtained. It also did not confirm that attackers had entered SBI’s core banking systems. No publicly identified entry point, exploited software flaw, or malware family explained the incident. SBI received alerts on October 16 from its threat intelligence service provider, the Defense Cyber Agency, and the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, known as CERT-In. The bank activated its incident response and containment procedures and appointed an independent cybersecurity agency impaneled with CERT-In to investigate. Investigators are examining the authenticity, source and extent of the exposed information. SBI has said the incident caused no material impact on its core operations, financial performance or business continuity. Banking services continued without disruption, according to the bank’s disclosure. An earlier unverified claim about an SBI data breach alleged that customer records and banking documents had been posted online. Those allegations should remain separate from SBI’s confirmed findings while the investigation continues. Personal data exposure does not automatically mean an account has been taken over. Available reporting does not establish that passwords, PINs, OTPs, or transaction credentials were compromised. However, exposed contact and loan details could help criminals create convincing messages that appear to come from the bank. Customers should verify unexpected notifications through official banking channels rather than trust a message because it contains accurate personal details. They should avoid unfamiliar links and check statements for unauthorized transactions. SBI’s official cybersecurity guidance lists report.phishing@sbi.co.in for reporting cyber incidents and directs users to India’s cybercrime helpline, 1930. The bank’s latest warning stresses that customers must never disclose authentication codes or banking passwords to anyone. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Email encryption has a usability paradox: the strongest cryptography loses to the recipient who gives up at the portal login and asks for the file “some other way.”

The 2026 winners solve for both ends sender-side automation (policies, DLP triggers, one-click protect) and recipient experiences that don’t require a manual.

We scored ten services on exactly that trade, plus control depth (expiry, revoke, audit) and compliance evidence.

Virtru takes 1; Microsoft Purview and Proofpoint complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Virtru the lowest-friction path to encrypted mail recipients actually open.

• Healthcare lane: Paubox’s no-portal delivery is the HIPAA-workflow standout.

Research-based evaluation: recipient friction (no-portal/no-account paths), policy automation (DLP-triggered, content-aware encryption), sender controls (expiry, revoke, disable-forward, audit), compliance evidence (HIPAA/GDPR-class), platform fit, and pricing structure.

Pros: Suite consolidation; policy automation; familiar at scale.

Cons: Portal experience; deepest value only inside the suite.

Bottom line: The suite shop’s encryption checkbox, competently done.

In 2026 you evaluate an MFT vendor’s security engineering exposure architecture, patch velocity, hardening posture before its scheduler. How We Scored (Methodology) Research-based evaluation: security architecture and track record (internet-exposure design, hardening guidance, disclosure/patch velocity), automation and orchestration depth, B2B protocol breadth (SFTP/AS2/AS4/APIs), compliance evidence, operational scale, and pricing structure. No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Weights: security posture 30% , automation depth 25%, protocol/B2B breadth 20%, operational scale 15%, pricing clarity 10%. Pros: Governance at scale; API/MFT convergence; enterprise references. Cons: Enterprise weight; quote-only economics. Bottom line: The backbone-grade incumbent still earning the position. 2. Cons: Breach history requires explicit diligence; internet-exposure discipline mandatory. Bottom line: Strong product make the rebuilt posture prove itself in writing. 4. Fortra (GoAnywhere + Globalscape EFT) — Broadest Portfolio, One Vendor Fortra (GoAnywhere + Globalscape EFT) — Broadest Portfolio, One Vendor Snapshot: Licensed/quote | Two MFT lines under one roof | Sheet listed both; we count one vendor Why it earns 4: Fortra owns two of the market’s best-known products GoAnywhere’s automation-rich platform and Globalscape EFT’s Windows-centric depth so our ten-row sheet yields nine vendors. Its own 2024 exploitation episode requires the same posture diligence as its peers. Pros: Transaction-level visibility; EDI/API convergence; supply-chain fit. Cons: Posture diligence applies here too. Bottom line: MFT that understands the business document inside the file. 6. SEEBURGER — Best Integration-Suite MFT SEEBURGER — Best Integration-Suite MFT Snapshot: Quote | BIS platform | MFT as one engine of a B2B/EDI/API suite Why it earns 6: SEEBURGER delivers MFT inside its Business Integration Suite one platform spanning EDI, API, and IoT flows with German-engineering governance compelling where the enterprise wants a single integration estate rather than a standalone transfer tool. Pros: True suite consolidation; strong European/manufacturing base. Cons: Suite commitment is the price of entry. Bottom line: For estates consolidating all integration, not just transfers. 7. Pros: Deployment flexibility; protocol breadth; automation-ecosystem ties. Cons: Brand transition diligence. Bottom line: Flexible, sensible, and now part of an automation house. 9. Pros: Right-sized; strong PGP automation; transparent pricing. Cons: Not aiming at partner-community scale. Bottom line: The focused tool that does transfers well and stops there. First, exposure architecture: no MFT admin interface internet-facing, ever demand the vendor’s zero-exposure reference design (gateway/proxy tier) and deploy it from day one. Second, posture evidence: exploitation history handled, patch SLAs, time-to-patch track record for the last three CVEs, bounty program, hardening guide quality in writing, scored like a feature. Third, operational resilience: can you patch within 24 hours of an advisory without breaking flows (staging environment, rollback plan)? Then and only then compare schedulers, protocol breadth, and partner onboarding. Why it earns 1: Axway runs the transfer backbones of banks and logistics giants with central governance over thousands of flows, strong identity integration, and an API-management adjacency that modernizes B2B patterns instead of embalming them while keeping a security-architecture reputation that survived the category’s worst years intact.

Pros: Governance at scale; API/MFT convergence; enterprise references.

Cons: Enterprise weight; quote-only economics.

Bottom line: The backbone-grade incumbent still earning the position.

2. IBM (Sterling) — Best B2B Backbone Scale IBM (Sterling) — Best B2B Backbone Scale

Snapshot: Quote | Sterling File Gateway/Connect:Direct | Decades of mission-critical transfer

Why it earns 2: When the requirement is millions of files across thousands of partners with mainframe-to-cloud reach, Sterling’s File Gateway and Connect:Direct lineage remains the reference: high-assurance point-to-point transfer, deep partner-community management, and the operational hardening of forty years in production.

Pros: Unmatched scale pedigree; Connect:Direct assurance; partner-management depth.

Cons: Modernization effort and cost; skills scarcity.

Bottom line: The heavyweight for estates where failure isn’t survivable.

3. Progress (MOVEit) — Hardened Survivor, Rebuilt Posture Progress (MOVEit) — Hardened Survivor, Rebuilt Posture

Snapshot: Licensed/quote | MOVEit Transfer/Automation | Post-2023 security overhaul

Why it earns 3: MOVEit is the category’s cautionary tale and its stress test: the 2023 mass exploitation forced a security rebuild expanded testing, hardening guidance, bounty and disclosure investment that buyers should verify rather than assume, but the product’s automation depth and compliance toolkit remain first-rank. We rank it on capability plus demonstrated remediation, with the diligence burden stated plainly.

Pros: Automation and reporting depth; large install base; visible post-incident investment.

Cons: Breach history requires explicit diligence; internet-exposure discipline mandatory.

Bottom line: Strong product make the rebuilt posture prove itself in writing.

Why it earns 4: Fortra owns two of the market’s best-known products GoAnywhere’s automation-rich platform and Globalscape EFT’s Windows-centric depth so our ten-row sheet yields nine vendors.

GoAnywhere’s own 2023 exploitation means the same diligence standard as MOVEit applies: demand patch-velocity evidence and the zero-exposure reference architecture. Portfolio overlap also makes roadmap questions fair game at renewal.

Pros: Two mature products; strong automation (GoAnywhere); portfolio flexibility.

Cons: Exploitation history (GoAnywhere) and two-product roadmap clarity.

Bottom line: One vendor, two products — pick the line, and get the roadmap in writing.

5. Cleo — Best Ecosystem-Integration MFT Cleo — Best Ecosystem-Integration MFT

Snapshot: Subscription/quote | Cleo Integration Cloud | MFT fused with EDI/API integration

Why it earns 5: Cleo’s bet is that transfers are integrations: its Integration Cloud unifies MFT, EDI, and API flows with end-to-end visibility into the business transaction, not just the file hop the right shape for supply-chain estates where a late file is a late shipment.

Its own 2024 exploitation episode requires the same posture diligence as its peers.

Pros: Transaction-level visibility; EDI/API convergence; supply-chain fit.

Cons: Brand transition diligence.

Cons: Not aiming at partner-community scale.

The category’s breach history writes your evaluation script. First, exposure architecture: no MFT admin interface internet-facing, ever demand the vendor’s zero-exposure reference design (gateway/proxy tier) and deploy it from day one.

Second, posture evidence: exploitation history handled, patch SLAs, time-to-patch track record for the last three CVEs, bounty program, hardening guide quality in writing, scored like a feature.

Third, operational resilience: can you patch within 24 hours of an advisory without breaking flows (staging environment, rollback plan)? Then and only then compare schedulers, protocol breadth, and partner onboarding.

Inventory your flows before shortlisting ten SFTP jobs point to Coviant/JSCAPE-class value; thousands of partner flows point to Axway/Sterling; EDI-entangled supply chains to Cleo/SEEBURGER; audit-plane governance to Kiteworks.

FAQs

What is the best managed file transfer solution in 2026? Axway ranks 1 for enterprise depth with posture intact, IBM Sterling for backbone scale, and Progress MOVEit as the hardened survivor whose rebuilt security buyers should verify with Coviant and JSCAPE leading the value lanes.

Why only 9 vendors? Our source sheet listed GoAnywhere and Globalscape separately, but both are Fortra products one vendor, ranked once with both lines noted.

Is MOVEit safe to buy after 2023? The product remains capable and Progress has invested visibly in security since. Buy it the modern way: zero-exposure deployment, contractual patch SLAs, and your own 24-hour-patch capability.

MFT vs secure file sharing which do we need? MFT moves files between systems on schedules and triggers; sharing platforms serve humans collaborating. Most enterprises need both see our secure file sharing ranking for the human side.

What’s the single most important MFT security control? Architecture: no directly internet-exposed admin surface, a gateway tier in the DMZ, and SOC monitoring of the MFT estate itself. Most category breaches exploited exposed services.

Axway and Sterling carry the backbones, MOVEit and GoAnywhere carry lessons the whole category paid for, and Cleo and SEEBURGER fold transfers into the integrations they really are buy the security architecture first, the scheduler second, and treat every MFT server as the crown-jewel target attackers already proved it is.

items.title: Hackers Exploit Critical Citrix NetScaler RCE Flaw to Deploy Web Shells and Malware
items.summary: A critical vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway is being exploited to run commands on exposed appliances, install web shells and deliver malware. Tracked as CVE-2026-88771, the flaw allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute commands remotely. Citrix disclosed it on September 27, 2026, and confirmed exploitation of appliances that had not been protected by an update. The vulnerability is rated 9.8 under CVSS v3.1 and 9.5 under CVSS v4.0, according to the Zscaler ThreatLabz report. The activity is concerning because NetScaler devices often sit at the edge of company networks and handle remote access or application traffic. A web shell can provide a way back into a compromised appliance, while a separate malware implant can give attackers another foothold. The campaign also shows why applying a patch alone may not be enough: organizations need to check whether attackers already changed files, settings or system logs. Researchers from Zscaler ThreatLabz identified a staged exploitation chain that used log poisoning, command execution, attempts to place web shells and delivery of a FreeBSD malware implant. Their technical analysis of CVE-2026-88771 says the attackers first placed encoded content in web access logs, then sent crafted authentication requests designed to trigger a vulnerable diagnostic process. Hackers Exploit Critical Citrix NetScaler RCE Flaw In the observed activity, requests to common NetScaler web paths carried a distinctive “INDEX:” marker and encoded content in the User-Agent field. These requests were intended to get attacker-controlled data written to access logs; the initial request did not itself run the full payload. Attackers then sent authentication requests containing text made to resemble a Packet Processing Engine failure message. The vulnerable process, a Perl diagnostic script, later handled matching log entries. According to Zscaler, the script did not safely handle attacker-controlled characters in the forged message. When the script processed a poisoned entry, appended commands could run with its privileges. This delayed method helps explain why a request that appears to be ordinary web or login traffic may be part of a larger attempt to compromise an appliance. Attack chain (Source – Zscaler) The observed payloads attempted to create web-accessible files, enable PHP or Perl handling in the web server, and install files named Nx_7508.php and Nx_7508.pl . Researchers also saw attempts to download and run a 64-bit FreeBSD binary named kw2-freebsd-x64-s11 . Zscaler reported that the download infrastructure had also appeared in activity targeting Magento and Adobe Commerce with CVE-2026-75650, known as StyleSmuggler. That overlap is an investigative lead, not proof that the same threat actor carried out both campaigns. This is not the first time attackers have used NetScaler flaws to leave behind web shells. Cyber Security News previously reported on web shells on hacked Citrix NetScalers and a separate campaign involving Citrix NetScaler zero-days and malware . These earlier reports are useful context, but they concern different incidents and should not be treated as evidence that the same operators are responsible. What organizations should do Citrix’s fixed builds listed in the Zscaler report are NetScaler ADC and Gateway 14.1-73.46 or later, and 13.1-64.29 or later. The report also lists 14.1-73.46 FIPS or later for 14.1-FIPS, and 13.1.37.283 or later for 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP. Administrators should verify the correct build for their product and upgrade promptly. Before updating, preserve relevant evidence where possible, including remote syslog data, technical support bundles and available core dumps. Then review authentication and web access logs for suspicious “INDEX:” User-Agent values, forged “pitboss PPE” failure messages, unexpected requests to the paths listed below, and appliance-initiated connections to unfamiliar hosts. Also inspect for unapproved web files, changed web-server settings and suspicious processes. If compromise is suspected, isolate the appliance while preserving evidence and rotate credentials, tokens and certificates it could access. Patching prevents further exploitation of the flaw, but does not by itself remove an existing web shell or implant. Related coverage of another critical NetScaler flaw and previous NetScaler exploitation can help teams compare the current activity with earlier disclosures. The weaknesses and campaigns differ, so responders should use the indicators below for this incident and check the relevant vendor guidance for each flaw.
