items.title: Hacker With Limited Skills Used DeepSeek AI to Breach Indian University and Steal Over 5,200 Records
items.summary: A cybercriminal using the online handle BUGSTER used artificial intelligence tools to support attacks on Indian organizations, including two universities. In one confirmed intrusion, the attacker stole a MongoDB database containing more than 5,200 records, including personal information about students and staff, according to Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42. The researchers did not name the universities. The actor’s setup combined Hermes Agent, an AI assistant framework, with DeepSeek V4 as its reasoning model and Cursor as a coding tool. Unit 42 said the attacker turned off safety controls and relied on AI-written scripts and reports. The case shows how AI can help a person with limited skills take on tasks that once demanded more experience, though it does not mean the model carried out the activity on its own. Analysts from Unit 42 identified and investigated the activity by examining the operator’s environment, tools and records. They found evidence of activity beyond the university intrusions, including credential theft, Wi-Fi password cracking, cryptocurrency research, and plans for phone-service fraud. Hacker With Limited Skills Used DeepSeek AI At one university, the actor used AI-assisted research to map an online education platform and its related services. The report described a WordPress site, a learning platform, a student portal and an administration dashboard. The actor then used the information to try account passwords, and the tool identified one working login. Unit 42 did not say that this activity led to the theft of the 5,200 records; that database came from a separate university intrusion. Example of a WordPress REST API enumeration report from the activity (Source – Unit42) In the second case, the actor accessed a public university’s database with an administrator account protected by a weak password. The stolen MongoDB data included student records from diploma, undergraduate and postgraduate programs, as well as faculty information. The actor’s records also showed details about parts of the university’s cloud and database setup. These incidents show why an exposed service or weak account can have serious effects, even without a newly discovered software flaw. The activity described by Unit 42 relied on basic tools, information gathered about the targets and access to an administrator account. Readers following DeepSeek-powered Hermes Agent attacks can compare this case with another report on AI-assisted activity involving the same tools. AI supported work across several schemes Unit 42 said the actor used AI-generated reports to organize research and produce scripts. Investigators also found a large credential-scanning toolkit designed to look for exposed secrets, such as cloud keys and private keys in files or logs. This kind of information can give criminals access to services if an organization has left it unprotected. The actor also built AI profiles for separate tasks. One profile was used to seek advice about VoIP fraud, while another researched phone carriers. Unit 42 found planning material but no call records or signs that the phone operation had become active. This distinction matters: the report documents preparation and research, not proof that the planned fraud was carried out. Other activity included an automated process for trying to crack Wi-Fi passwords. Unit 42 said it required a device near the target networks to collect authentication data, suggesting the actor had local access to the locations. The actor also collected information about large cryptocurrency holders, but researchers did not find evidence of follow-up activity against them. Using the pandarouter profile to investigate a carrier (Source – Unit42) Related reporting on DeepSeek safety research findings covers concerns about AI models producing harmful guidance. Unit 42’s findings add a different point: an attacker can combine an AI model with ordinary tools and weak account security to pursue several types of crime. Universities and other organizations should review administrator accounts, remove weak or reused passwords, and require multi-factor authentication where possible. They should also limit database access to approved systems and users, check internet-facing portals for unnecessary exposure, and monitor account activity for unusual login attempts or access to large sets of records. Organizations should protect secrets such as API keys and cloud credentials by keeping them out of public files and logs. If a credential may have been exposed, teams should revoke or rotate it, then review access records for signs of misuse. These steps address the security gaps described in the report; they do not depend on identifying a particular AI model. The activity also highlights the value of monitoring what AI agents can access. If AI tools are used for legitimate work, organizations should limit their permissions, keep safety and approval controls enabled, and review their actions. The case is part of a wider set of reported concerns about AI-enabled cybercrime, including DeepSeek-powered credential theft activity . Universities and other organizations should review administrator accounts, remove weak or reused passwords, and require multi-factor authentication where possible.

They should also limit database access to approved systems and users, check internet-facing portals for unnecessary exposure, and monitor account activity for unusual login attempts or access to large sets of records.

Organizations should protect secrets such as API keys and cloud credentials by keeping them out of public files and logs. If a credential may have been exposed, teams should revoke or rotate it, then review access records for signs of misuse.

These steps address the security gaps described in the report; they do not depend on identifying a particular AI model. The activity also highlights the value of monitoring what AI agents can access.

If AI tools are used for legitimate work, organizations should limit their permissions, keep safety and approval controls enabled, and review their actions. The case is part of a wider set of reported concerns about AI-enabled cybercrime, including DeepSeek-powered credential theft activity.

items.title: Oracle Issues Emergency Java Update for Critical 9.1 HTTPS Trust Vulnerability
items.summary: Oracle has released an emergency Java security update to address CVE-2026-91403, a critical vulnerability affecting how Java applications trust digital certificates. Published on October 21, 2026, the alert assigns the flaw a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.1 and covers Oracle Java SE and GraalVM. The update blocks affected intermediate certificate authority certificates linked to eMudhra. According to Oracle’s security advisory, the issue affects the Java Secure Socket Extension, or JSSE, component. Oracle rates exploitation as low complexity, with no authentication or user interaction required. Successful attacks can expose or change sensitive data, although the risk matrix lists no availability impact. The problem involves certificate chains that Java uses to decide whether a remote service is trusted. Red Hat explains that eMudhra issued intermediate certificates with weak private keys. An attacker positioned between a Java client and a server could use those weak keys to create certificates for arbitrary hostnames, making a malicious site appear trusted. This undermines the identity checks behind HTTPS. Encryption alone cannot protect a connection when the client accepts an attacker’s certificate as valid. The fix therefore changes which certificates Java accepts, rather than removing HTTPS support or replacing the entire certificate system. Oracle’s update specifically distrusts the impacted intermediate certificates. Affected Java and GraalVM Versions Oracle lists Java SE 8u511, 8u511-perf, 11.0.33, 17.0.21, 21.0.13, 25.0.5, and 27.0.1 as affected. GraalVM for JDK 17.0.21 and 21.0.13, alongside GraalVM Enterprise Edition 21.3.20, are also included. Earlier releases may be vulnerable, but unsupported versions were not tested. Oracle notes that affected APIs can be reached through services supplying data to JSSE. Its advisory also covers certain sandboxed Java Web Start applications and applets that load untrusted code. The announcement does not report confirmed attacks exploiting this vulnerability. Oracle recommends installing the latest Java update or following its eMudhra mitigation instructions . Teams unable to update immediately can replace the local blocked.certs file with Oracle’s supplied version, preserving existing custom entries. Java 8 requires the replacement file to be named blacklisted.certs . Alternatively, Oracle advises enabling TLS revocation checks using -Dcom.sun.net.ssl.checkRevocation=true and -Dcom.sun.security.enableCRLDP=true . For signed JAR verification on JDK 17 and later, it provides jarsigner -verify -revcheck -strict [SIGNED_JAR] . These are alternatives, not steps that must all be applied together. The emergency alert follows Oracle’s wider patching efforts, including its September security update and August security patches . However, administrators should check this specific advisory rather than assume earlier updates cover the certificate issue. Oracle directs customers to its patch availability document for installation details and recommends moving unsupported deployments to supported releases. items.title: PwC Data Breach Claim – Everest Ransomware Group Claims to Have Stolen 590 GB of Data
items.summary: The Everest ransomware group claims to have stolen 590.69 GB of data from PwC, the global professional services firm. This alleged data theft includes human resources records, training materials, and internal documents. However, the claims are unverified, and PwC has not yet responded. The group’s listing was reported on October 22, 2026. Hackmanac’s public alert described 108,426 files allegedly taken from internal HR and learning systems. Separately, CTIWatch’s victim tracker recorded PwC appearing on Everest’s leak site that day. These reports document the claim, not independent proof of a breach. Alleged PwC Data Breach The supplied leak-site screenshot names a directory, pwc-stg.csod.com , and describes Cornerstone OnDemand platform materials, regional HR exports, e-learning courses, and integration testing documents. It lists 494 directories, alongside 1,333 original archive containers and 53 nested containers. The screenshot alone does not establish how these materials were obtained. Hackmanac reported that the alleged data spans PwC operations in Australia, China, Canada, and the UK. One HR dataset reportedly contains 213,084 records. That figure should not be read as a confirmed count of affected employees because the number of unique people remains unknown. The alert also mentions employee information, employment and training records, internal audit methods, confidential documents, and single sign-on source code and configuration files. It does not establish whether working passwords, tokens, or other usable secrets are present. PwC Data Breach Claim The screenshot threatens publication after a countdown and urges the company to make contact. A reported October 28 release deadline has not been independently confirmed. No ransom amount, initial access method, or evidence of encrypted PwC systems has been established in the reviewed material. Everest has previously used data theft claims to pressure named organizations, including its alleged McDonald’s India breach . However, its history includes both data extortion and file encryption, so this listing should not automatically be treated as proof of ransomware deployment. A separate technical analysis of Everest ransomware found no data theft function inside one examined encryptor. Researchers noted that any theft could instead occur earlier through separate tools. That finding does not explain this alleged incident. If authentic, detailed employee records could help criminals craft convincing phishing messages or impersonate staff. For now, the central questions remain data authenticity, ownership, access scope, and whether any records are current. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: Critical Cisco Expressway Vulnerability Enables Remote Code Execution Attacks
items.summary: Cisco has released security updates for a critical Cisco Expressway vulnerability that could let remote attackers run operating system commands as root. Tracked as CVE-2026-76466, the flaw carries a CVSS score of 9.8 and affects vulnerable Expressway devices configured in a cluster. Cisco published its advisory on October 21, 2026. The issue affects Cisco Expressway Core (Expressway-C) and Cisco Expressway Edge (Expressway-E). Both virtual deployments and hardware appliances are affected when running vulnerable software with clustering enabled. Successful exploitation could give attackers control over the underlying operating system. According to Cisco’s security advisory , the weakness sits in the database service and involves persistent cookies. Cisco also found that client certificates are not properly checked when clustering enables TLS Verify Mode. This means the enabled setting does not provide the expected certificate validation. An attacker who has the required cookies and network access to an affected device could connect to its database service and invoke specific remote procedure call commands. These calls could allow the attacker to run commands with root privileges , the highest level of access on the system. Cisco Expressway Vulnerability Although Cisco describes the attacker as unauthenticated, possession of the cookies remains an important requirement. The advisory does not explain how an attacker would obtain them. Readers should therefore avoid interpreting the finding as proof that an attacker can immediately compromise every reachable Expressway device. The potential impact resembles other cases covered in Cyber Security News’ reporting on critical Cisco remote code execution flaws , though the affected products and attack methods differ. Cisco lists Expressway X15.5.3 and earlier as affected, with X15.5.20 identified as the first fixed release. Customers using X14 or earlier must migrate to a fixed release. No workarounds address this vulnerability. The fix is also included in Cisco’s broader October 2026 Expressway security hardening release. That release addresses additional weaknesses discovered during an internal security review. Unlike this cluster-specific flaw, the broader hardening advisory covers affected Expressway-C and Expressway-E devices regardless of configuration. Administrators should check installed versions and cluster settings, then plan upgrades using Cisco’s compatibility guidance. Checking the version alone does not establish exposure because this particular vulnerability also requires a clustered deployment. Broader coverage is available through Cyber Security News’ Cisco security updates . Cisco credited Stefan Aleksic of Jane Street with reporting the vulnerability. At publication, its Product Security Incident Response Team said it was unaware of public announcements or malicious use. That statement does not reduce the need to patch affected clusters, given the potential for remote commands to run as root. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: Splunk Fixes 24 Security Flaws, Including Four Critical Vulnerabilities in Enterprise and SOAR
items.summary: Splunk has released security updates for 24 vulnerabilities in Splunk Enterprise and Splunk SOAR , including four critical flaws with CVSS scores from 9.3 to 9.9. Splunk published the fixes on October 21, 2026, across three advisories covering access control, input handling, exposed files, remote code execution, denial of service, and weak authorization checks. The Splunk Enterprise security hardening advisory covers four CVEs found internally. CVE-2026-76299 and CVE-2026-76302 both have a 9.9 score and involve improper access control and improper neutralization. CVE-2026-76300, scored 8.8, concerns poor control of a resource during its lifetime, while CVE-2026-76301 carries a 7.6 score for a protection failure. Splunk groups internal findings by weakness type so that each CVE may represent more than one related issue. The Splunk SOAR advisory lists eight CVEs fixed in version 8.7.0. The most serious is CVE-2026-76531, rated 9.9, which may leave files or directories open to outside parties. CVE-2026-76407 is another critical issue with a 9.3 score and involves improper access control. Other SOAR flaws include unsafe URL path checks, poor input handling, weak resource controls, and protection failures. Critical Severity : CVE Product CVSS CWE CVE-2026-76299 Splunk Enterprise 9.9 CWE-284 CVE-2026-76302 Splunk Enterprise 9.9 CWE-707 CVE-2026-76407 Splunk SOAR 9.3 CWE-284 CVE-2026-76531 Splunk SOAR 9.9 CWE-552 Splunk Fixes 24 Security Flaws A separate Splunk Enterprise advisory details 12 more flaws, led by CVE-2026-76291 and CVE-2026-76298 at 8.8. The first could let a user with scheduled-search rights bypass safeguards and run risky SPL commands. The second could allow a low-privileged user to derive the PostgreSQL sidecar superuser password and run operating system commands on search head cluster members. CVE-2026-76293 also creates a remote code execution risk. A user with the edit_manager_xml capability could run operating system commands through Splunk Web Manager XML. High Severity : CVE Product CVSS CWE CVE-2026-76291 Splunk Enterprise 8.8 CWE-284 CVE-2026-76298 Splunk Enterprise 8.8 CWE-321 CVE-2026-76300 Splunk Enterprise 8.8 CWE-664 CVE-2026-76408 Splunk SOAR 8.8 CWE-664 CVE-2026-76526 Splunk SOAR 8.8 CWE-707 CVE-2026-76530 Splunk SOAR 8.8 CWE-647 CVE-2026-76301 Splunk Enterprise 7.6 CWE-693 CVE-2026-76288 Splunk Enterprise 7.5 CWE-400 CVE-2026-76290 Splunk Enterprise 7.5 CWE-400 CVE-2026-76529 Splunk SOAR 7.5 CWE-424 CVE-2026-76293 Splunk Enterprise 7.2 CWE-94 Two unauthenticated denial-of-service bugs, CVE-2026-76288 and CVE-2026-76290, could make Splunk services stop responding through crafted web requests or repeated package downloads. The remaining issues affect REST API authorization, field extraction management, sourcetype renaming, SPL filtering, and federated search actions. Because Splunk often sits at the center of security monitoring, a compromised instance could expose logs, weaken detection, or disrupt investigations. Several flaws require an authenticated user with capabilities, but that does not make them harmless. Stolen accounts, excessive role permissions, and weak internal access rules could provide the access needed. The unauthenticated denial-of-service issues deserve attention on internet-facing systems because they can affect service without an account. Medium Severity : CVE Product CVSS CWE CVE-2026-76289 Splunk Enterprise 6.5 CWE-770 CVE-2026-76292 Enterprise and Secure Gateway 6.5 CWE-862 CVE-2026-76528 Splunk SOAR 6.2 CWE-693 CVE-2026-76527 Splunk SOAR 5.5 CWE-703 CVE-2026-76287 Splunk Enterprise 5.4 CWE-639 CVE-2026-76294 Splunk Enterprise 4.3 CWE-862 CVE-2026-76295 Enterprise and Secure Gateway 4.3 CWE-943 CVE-2026-76296 Splunk Enterprise 4.3 CWE-862 CVE-2026-76297 Splunk Enterprise 4.2 CWE-352 Organizations should review exposed interfaces and user roles while scheduling the updates. Administrators should upgrade Splunk Enterprise to 10.4.4, 10.2.8, 10.0.11, or 9.4.16 and move Splunk SOAR to 8.7.0 or later. Splunk also says CVE-2026-76292 and CVE-2026-76295 need Splunk Secure Gateway updates to 3.10.12, 3.9.26, or 3.8.73. Teams unable to patch at once can reduce exposure by turning off unused Splunk Web, Pipeline Builders, Secure Gateway, or PostgreSQL sidecar features, depending on the flaw. These steps can affect key functions, so administrators should review dependencies before making changes. Readers can also review earlier Cyber Security News coverage of multiple Splunk Enterprise vulnerabilities and Splunk SOAR security updates for wider patch history and risk context. items.title: Critical Unpatched Linux Kernel Flaws Accidentally Disclosed on Public List
items.summary: Several unpatched Linux-related security flaws were posted to public mailing lists in October, exposing technical details before fixes were ready. The reports, submitted by Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), include two critical flaws rated CVSS 9.0 that could let a remote attacker run code on systems using the Linux kernel’s KSMBD file server. Other reports describe local privilege-escalation and information-disclosure risks. The reports appeared on public lists, and Linux kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman questioned why some submissions were sent there without patches. But the reports credit Trend Micro’s AI scanner, and reporting on the disclosure points to updated kernel guidance that treats AI-found bugs as already public. ZDI had not publicly explained the routing as of October 23, 2026, so it remains unclear whether this was a simple mistake. Two Critical Flaws Affect KSMBD The most urgent reports concern KSMBD, an optional SMB file server built into the Linux kernel. It is separate from Samba, the commonly used file-sharing software. That means the reports do not automatically affect Linux systems running Samba alone. The immediate question for operators is whether KSMBD is enabled and serving files. ZDI-CAN-33774 describes a race condition in KSMBD that could lead to remote code execution. A race condition occurs when the outcome depends on the timing of tasks running at the same time. In this case, the report says that a mismatch in how the server handles queued network requests may lead to memory being read or written beyond its intended limits. ZDI rated the flaw CVSS 9.0. ZDI-CAN-33549 , also rated CVSS 9.0, affects KSMBD’s SMB Direct path. The reported cause is an integer underflow: a size value can wrap around after a subtraction, leaving the program with an incorrect length. A later memory operation may then exceed its buffer. The issue concerns SMB Direct, which uses RDMA networking, so exposure depends on the server’s configuration and use of that feature. A fix was reportedly present in a development branch intended for Linux 7.5, but that does not mean it was already available in released or distribution kernels. At the time of reporting, neither critical issue had a named fix in the mainline kernel or its integration tree, and no CVE identifier had been assigned. Kernel changes also need to reach stable and distribution releases before many users can install them. Administrators should therefore check their Linux vendor’s security notices rather than assume that a fix in a development branch has reached their systems. Four Other Reports Cover Different Components The remaining reports do not all affect the same part of Linux. ZDI-CAN-33367 involves the skb_zerocopy networking code and may allow a local user to gain higher privileges. Kernel developers had reportedly received a separate report about the same issue the previous week, with a patch expected. ZDI-CAN-34068 concerns an out-of-bounds write in the VMware graphics driver, which could also enable local privilege escalation. ZDI-CAN-34076 involves an uninitialized resource in the NVMe over Fabrics target code and may expose information. ZDI-CAN-32005 , posted a day earlier, is a stack-buffer overflow in ConnMan’s handling of search-domain TCP queries. ConnMan is a network-management service, not a Linux kernel component, so this report should not be described as a kernel flaw. items.summary_html:
Several unpatched Linux-related security flaws were posted to public mailing lists in October, exposing technical details before fixes were ready.

The reports, submitted by Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), include two critical flaws rated CVSS 9.0 that could let a remote attacker run code on systems using the Linux kernel’s KSMBD file server. Other reports describe local privilege-escalation and information-disclosure risks.

The reports appeared on public lists, and Linux kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman questioned why some submissions were sent there without patches.

But the reports credit Trend Micro’s AI scanner, and reporting on the disclosure points to updated kernel guidance that treats AI-found bugs as already public. ZDI had not publicly explained the routing as of October 23, 2026, so it remains unclear whether this was a simple mistake.

Two Critical Flaws Affect KSMBD

The most urgent reports concern KSMBD, an optional SMB file server built into the Linux kernel. It is separate from Samba, the commonly used file-sharing software. That means the reports do not automatically affect Linux systems running Samba alone. The immediate question for operators is whether KSMBD is enabled and serving files.

ZDI-CAN-33774 describes a race condition in KSMBD that could lead to remote code execution. A race condition occurs when the outcome depends on the timing of tasks running at the same time. In this case, the report says that a mismatch in how the server handles queued network requests may lead to memory being read or written beyond its intended limits. ZDI rated the flaw CVSS 9.0.

ZDI-CAN-33549, also rated CVSS 9.0, affects KSMBD’s SMB Direct path. The reported cause is an integer underflow: a size value can wrap around after a subtraction, leaving the program with an incorrect length.

A later memory operation may then exceed its buffer. The issue concerns SMB Direct, which uses RDMA networking, so exposure depends on the server’s configuration and use of that feature. A fix was reportedly present in a development branch intended for Linux 7.5, but that does not mean it was already available in released or distribution kernels.

At the time of reporting, neither critical issue had a named fix in the mainline kernel or its integration tree, and no CVE identifier had been assigned. Kernel changes also need to reach stable and distribution releases before many users can install them. Administrators should therefore check their Linux vendor’s security notices rather than assume that a fix in a development branch has reached their systems.

Four Other Reports Cover Different Components

The remaining reports do not all affect the same part of Linux. ZDI-CAN-33367 involves the skb_zerocopy networking code and may allow a local user to gain higher privileges. Kernel developers had reportedly received a separate report about the same issue the previous week, with a patch expected. ZDI-CAN-34068 concerns an out-of-bounds write in the VMware graphics driver, which could also enable local privilege escalation.

ZDI-CAN-34076 involves an uninitialized resource in the NVMe over Fabrics target code and may expose information. ZDI-CAN-32005, posted a day earlier, is a stack-buffer overflow in ConnMan’s handling of search-domain TCP queries. ConnMan is a network-management service, not a Linux kernel component, so this report should not be described as a kernel flaw.

Start by checking whether KSMBD is active and whether the system needs it. If it is not required, disabling it reduces exposure to the two remote-code-execution reports.

If it is needed, keep file-sharing services away from untrusted networks, review share access, and monitor the Linux distribution’s security updates for fixes. These steps reduce risk but do not replace installing a vendor-approved patch once it becomes available.

The reports also show why public disclosure before a fix can create pressure for maintainers and system operators. Public details can help defenders understand what to check, but they can also give attackers useful information before updates reach users. For context on earlier KSMBD risks, see Cyber Security News’ coverage of a Linux KSMBD remote-code-execution flaw and its report on an AI-assisted discovery in the Linux SMB server.

For ongoing protection, administrators should follow their distribution’s advisories and apply fixes as soon as they are released.

items.title: 1Password recognized in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Privileged Access Management
items.summary: 1Password Privileged Access was named an Honorable Mention in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Privileged Access Management. 1Password Privileged Access eliminates standing access for human and non-human identities across cloud and hybrid environments, databases, and Kubernetes. It provides just-in-time, just-enough privileges created at request time, scoped to the task, and automatically deprovisioned when the work is done. This secures production infrastructure and sensitive data for every identity and resource. We feel this honorable mention in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Privileged Access Management reflects the recognition that privilege should be created for the task at hand and removed when the work is done. Why standing access persists Standing access emerges as a byproduct of daily operations. What begins as a quick fix to remediate a bug or launch an AI agent often leaves a long tail of access risk and manual cleanup. Today, every engineer, service account, and AI agent in your environment carries more access than needed, and each permission is an opportunity attackers can exploit. Consider a team that brings on a contractor for a three-month project and grants access across its cloud environment, K8s cluster, and database. When the engagement ends, the access remains because removing it requires checking several systems and confirming nothing else depends on the account. Permissions granted for legitimate work outlive the work that justified them. Across the infrastructure, an organization may manage an AWS role, a K8s RBAC binding, and a database account through separate tools with no shared policy layer. Each new system adds another inventory to maintain. When the project ends, the contractor leaves, or a workload changes, teams must manually track and trigger cleanup, which quickly outpaces what they can secure or manage. In AI-agent workflows, standing access is harder to identify and contain. Many organizations still manage agent access through IAM solutions designed for human employees and static identities. But agents can use API keys, service accounts, and backend integrations and may move between different access paths within the same workflow. When an agent inherits a person’s or workload’s permissions, it becomes harder to see what is acting, what authority it has, and when that authority should end. In a June 2026 1Password survey of IT and security professionals on how organizations adopt and govern AI for their most technical workers, 40% of developers reported granting AI agents persistent access to systems or credentials that were not revoked when a task was completed. Among developers who use AI agents, 33% reported their organization had experienced a security incident or breach from overprivileged non-human identities. Security teams need to answer four questions for every human, workload, service account, or AI agent: Which identity, agent, or workload requested access? Which production resource, system, or customer data could it reach? Which role, policy, approval, or business justification granted that access? What happened during the access window, when did it expire, and can the team prove that it was revoked? Until access is governed with a clear attribution chain showing which identity received access, why it was granted, and when it was revoked, standing permissions leave a larger attack surface and exposure risk when an identity or workload is compromised. From standing access to runtime privilege The four questions above help teams transition from granting access to governing it. Privileged Access addresses them by mapping existing permissions, evaluating each request in context, creating only the access required for the task, and recording what happened afterward. It begins by mapping identities and permissions across cloud and hybrid environments, Kubernetes, and databases. This helps security teams identify dormant accounts and permissions that are broader than required. When access is requested, Dynamic Guardrails run contextual approval workflows to evaluate the request and determine whether and under what conditions to grant access. The policy considers who or what is requesting access, what it needs, the environment and resource involved, and the risk of the requested action. Lower-risk requests can be approved automatically. Higher-risk requests can be routed to a human reviewer. When access is approved, Just-in-Time Access creates the required permission in the target system’s existing policy layer. That might be an AWS IAM role, a Kubernetes permission, or a scoped database account. Privileged Access automatically deprovisions those permissions at the end of the approved access window. Developers can request access from Slack, Teams, the CLI , Backstage, and supported MCP workflows. The system automatically logs requests, approvals, granted resources, access events, and revocations. Where session activity is supported, security teams can also review what happened, when it happened, who approved the access, and which policy authorized it. Why AI agents need behavioral control Just-In-Time Access addresses excessive or persistent authority and limits what an agent can access and how long that access remains available. Nondeterministic agents also need contextual controls to ensure they act within the scope of the task that created the access. Without time-bound, scoped permissions, an agent asked to investigate a production error may start by reading logs or inspecting a service configuration outside the original request. If that action falls within the permissions attached to its role, a conventional permission check treats it as authorized. AI Agent Control in Privileged Access gives each agent a distinct identity and a role scoped to its task. The system provisions permissions when the task begins and removes them when the task is complete. With Intent-Based Access Control, currently in beta, Privileged Access compares an agent’s declared intent with the actions it takes in real time. If the agent deviates from that intent, access can be restricted or revoked before the action executes, subject to the capabilities of the supported integration. An adaptive model for privileged access In our view, the recognition in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Privileged Access Management comes as security and infrastructure teams are asked to adapt least-privilege controls to cloud infrastructure, machine workloads, and AI agents. As the parameters defining identity shift, privileged access can no longer depend on permanent roles and manual access reviews. To keep human and non-human identities working efficiently without expanding risk, organizations need task-specific, time-bound access and controls that consider their behavior. 1Password Privileged Access helps organizations move toward that model and gives teams a way to secure cloud environments by keeping access scoped to the task at hand and removing it when the work is done.
